THE DAUGHTER-IN-LAW. When I lived in my father's dwelling Good macaroni was my food. Now I am married there's no telling If macaroni's bad or good. When in my mother's house I tarried On finest paste I need to dine. I scarcely Imow since I am married Whether the paste he coarse or fine. And while the mistress and her daughter The macaroni all devour, The son's poor wife, with pail and water, Stays in the corner pots to scour. And while the daughter and her mother May drink good wine and have their Ling, The eon's poor wife can drink no other Than water from the nearest spring. And while the mistress and her daughter May go to balls, and dance, and play, The son's poor wife must have it taught her To rock the babe the livelong day. '6—ltalian Folk Songs in Gentleman's Magazine. Tarittito.

We show little judgment by exhibiting our annoyance in 4far looks, and less by bursting into a passion about them. Noble are they who are not too lazy to work, or too proud is be poor; who only eat what they earn and wear what they pay for. It is impossible to make people nnderstand their ignorance for it requires knowledge to perceive it; and, therefore, he that can perceive it, hath it not. The law of harvest is to reap more than you sow. Sow 1 an act, and you reap a habit and you reap a character; sow a character, and you reap a destiny. Have the courage to face a difficulty, even though it should trick you harder than bargained for. Difficulties, like thieves, often disappear at a glance. Never hold any one by the button, or the hand, in order to be heard Out; for if people are unwilling to hear you, you had better hold your tongue than them. Daniel O'Connell, the Irish orator, was applied to by a friend for his autograph, to which he replied :—" Sir, I never send autographs.—Yours, Daniel O'Connell." What we call health in the body is a very fair analogical interpretation of what we call religion. Religion is to the llonl what the organs of a man are to the body.—Beecher. He has just started another, and named it "Kind Words," 'because, he says, "kind words can never die." A MIGHTY hirrw.—Some time since a woman delivered a lecture in Lancashire, against Christianity, in which she declared that the Gospel narrative of the life of Christ is a myth or fable. One of the mill-bands who listened to her obtained leave to ask a question. "The question," said he, I want to ask the lady is this :—Thirty years ago I was s curse to this town, and everybody shrank from me who had any respect for himself. I often tried to do better, but toed not succeed. The teetotalers got hold of me, but I *broke the pledge so often that they said it was no use try- ing me any longer; then the police got hold of me, and I was taken before the magistratee' and they tried; and next I was sent to prison, and the wardens tried what they could do, and though they all tried, I was nothing better but rather worse. Now, you say that Christ is a myth. But when I tried, and the teetotalers, the police, the magistrates and the wardens of the prisons, all tried in vain, then Christ -took hold of me, touched my heart, and made me a new clan. And now lam a member of the church, a class- -leader, a superintendent of the Sunday-school; and I ask, if Christ is a myth, how comes it to pass that that myth is stronger than all the others pat together ?" The lady was -silent. The geologist. if he be fairly in earnest, is far too tired after his day's work to trouble himself about the aristo- oratic air of his quarters, and, besides, generally manages 40 put his outer man into so uncleanly a condition that a Wand hotel would have some scruple in taking him in. rrofeseor Sedgwick, after a bard morning's work, betook daimaelf to a village inn for a lunch of bread and cheese. When he asked what he had to pay, he was told fonrpence. Ile could aot avoid remarking on the smallness of the charge. " Ah, air," said the landlady, "I should ask eight- pence from anyone else, but I only asked fourpence from you, for I see that you have known better days."—A well. known geologist, long secretary to the Geological Society, was once taken up while at his vocation, and dragged off to the Bristol Asylum for an escaped lunatic. On another oc- casion, tired, and with his pockets fall of the day's trea- .-siures, he mounted a stage-coach, and fell fast asleep. Waking at his journey's end, be was horrified to find his .Ipockets as empty as when beset out. An old woman who sat beside him, feeling the pockets f all of stones, took him tot a madman, who had loaded himself more effectually to eosin drowning, so she slyly picked out the fossils, one by one from the drowsy philosopher, and tossed them on the soadside. David Price, a man of meek and kindly spirit, had long suffered from the patter-clatter, never-ending scolding tongue of his worser half. One day a herb doctor greeted David at his work with a "Well, Master David, and how

be you ? " "Oh! I be very well, thanks to ye; bat my -wife not so very nicely." "Indeed!" said the gatherer of simples, with a quick ear for an ailment; "what may be -tile matter wi' she, Master David? " "Well." said David, sin his usual dry and quiet way, "she hey a bad breaking vat about her month every now and then, that troubles her -and me varry sore, I 'sure ye, Master Doctor." "Well." said the latter, "I could make a grand care of her, I'll war- rant. I hey a salve 'at I makes fra the juice of the juniper tree, and by boiling up a vast o' different kinds o' things, 'at quite cure that in no time!" "Deed," said David, le an' what might your charge be, now, for a box of that 'int- ellect. 'at would quite cure her?" "Oh!" said the her- Isalist, looking anxiously up in David's face, " only a matter 'of a shilling." "Well, that's dirt cheap," said David; "If iota cures her, I'll give you eighteenpence, there now." With this offer, the doctor set off home to prepare his nos- Arum, and straightway hied the very next day to David's **souse, box in hand. There he found Mrs. Price, and went -ISt once to business. "Well, Mrs. Price, your master tells Ade you hey betimes a bad breaking out about the month, and I've brought a box of fine 'intment 'at will quite cure We!" With this announcement, Mrs. Price, firing up—at race seeing her husband's jest—raised the brush with -which she was sweeping the floor, and pummelled the doctor to her heart's content, even following to boat him A field from her house, he screaming out all the while, 4. Oh I Missus Price, be you gone mad!" From that day, Sbowever, Mrs. Price has been wholly cured of her scolding habits. David has only to look up In her face and say, -Nru get a box of that 'intment," and there's an end of the 'Clatter. David honourably paid the doctor his is. 6d. to auks him forget his pummelling. _ question of housing the poor in New York has been treated with so much energy in recent years that the example 4igivec on the other side of the Atlantic might be studied with advantage by those who are interested in the problem ct home. An excellent opportunity is afforded at the 'Health Exhibition for this purpose. Notice was not re- -actived in snfficient time to secure a general representation .of American sanitary work, nevertheless the editor of the American Scsnitary Engineer collected, in answer to a sable =telegram received four days before sailing, plans from the 'Kew York Board of Health and other sources, which he has -exhibited at his own expense. By this energetic act of ipatriotism we have now official documents and plans illus- =trating what has been done in New York. There the diffi- culties were even greater than those that beset us in Loc- ation. What is known as the city lots are covered with the poorest tenements. The lots are situated back to back, with streets 60 feet wide. Each lot has 25 feet of frontage, and runs back a distance of 100 feet. It was customary to =build over 90 feet, so that the back yard was only 10 feet wide. When we consider that the houses are five storeys

lhigh, with four tenements on each floor, it is easy to imagine the unwholesomeness of these huge dwellings thus rowded together. Interested persons succeeded, however, is impeding legislation on this subject till the year 1879, -when the opposition was broken down. The Sanitary Engi- steer had offered a prize for the best plan which, while -.securing light and air, would pay for investment on the 4Lenal city lot. The exhibition of more than 200 plans ex- +sited exceptional Interest: committees were formed, and. in response to the efforts of devoted citizens' an Act was restricting the building to 65 percent. of the lot, so that the -tack yards now measure 35 feet. The following year the Attune committee obtained the enactment of another law, by which all plumbers had to be registered, and were not allowed to execute any work that was not approved by the Board of licalth. The text of these laws and drawings, illustrating their practical application, are now to be seen at the Health _Exhibition, and should be examined by medical officers and -sanitary legislators. It will be found that the regulation, affecting plumbing are much in advance of anything we "have in England. For instance, the through ventilation of soil-pipes is compulsory, and New York plumbers who have !ailed to carry out these principles have been arrested and fined as mnoh as £so.—Laneef. Ds. Baules. Bt. Matter, in Zeitschrift dos Fereines Deutsche? In-I gorieure, is thoroughly examined as to his investigations on the absorption of gases by steel. The results arrived at may be thus summarised :—The gas liberated from steel in the liquid state before solidification is chiefly carbonic oxide. The rising of steel, and consequently the formation of blow-holes, is attributed to hydrogen and nitrogen, and to a small extent to carbonic oxide. A CONGEALED EARTHQUAILIL—I have already, in pre- vious notes, referred to the activity of the Japanese in the study of earthquake phenomena. In a recent number of the Transactions of the Seismological Society of Japan is a contribution by Mr. Gergene, entitled " A Note on a Con- gealed Earthquake," from which it appears that an iron casting with open surface was just solidifying when. an earthquake occurred; the metal was rippled by the agita- tion and solidified while in this condition, leaving the ripple marks as a record of the event. —Gentleman's Maga:mtg. The dialectal uses of the word "allow" are varied and carious. Sir W. H. Cope notices that in Hampshire it is used in the sense of consider, think, suppose, as of distance, "I allow it to be so far." Mr. C. G. Atkins, in the Nation, mentions a peculiar use of the same word in some parts tof Ohio, notably in Hardin County, where he spent a few weeks in 1862. It was almost universally used instead of intend—thne, "I allow to go home to-morrow." A little girl watching her brother dawdling over some work in the garden, warned him of paternal intentions in these words: "Pap 'lows to whip ye if ye don't pitch in." If the little girl had lived in Maine she would perhaps have expressed herself thus "Father is goin' to give you a good liekin' if ye don't work smart." The word smart would be reserved by the Hardin County people for the combination of " right smart," and one might hear a farmer boast of rais- ing "right smart of oats." Amongst the wonders of the age is M. Chevrenl. The veteran, who is now in his 99th year, is spoken of as having been the success at the recent meetiog of the French National Society of Agriculture. The occasion was the annual distribution of prizes, and M. Chevreul delivered "an eloquent and impassioned" address in praise of science which, "equally avoiding pessimism and optimism, pursues truth alone." M. Chevreul reviewed recent discoveries, dwelling specially on those of Pasteur and M. Joseph Boussingault, the latter of whom has lately produced a re- markable analytical report on wines. Amidst repeated ap- plause, M. Chevrerd brought his discourse to a close by expressing apprehension that if he continued longer his hearers would consider that he was nearer to the period of extreme youth than the end of his century. It is not long since M. Chevreul complained that his memory was failing because he could not remember the exact name of a student who made an experiment before him about three-quarters of a century ago. INTERESTING Discovertv.—The Rev. C. W. Markham, of Saxby Rectory, Barton-on-Eltimber, writes as follows :—I beg to send you a brief description of a singular and inter- esting discovery in this neighbourhood. Some brickyard labourers, in excavating clay on some level land in the Valley of the Ancholme, near Brigg, in Lincolnshire, have ' recently discovered, about seven feet below the surface, a very ancient wooden way. It consists of massive beams of oak laid traversly, and fastened into the soil below—which is the glacial drift—by oak pins. This structure, which it Is thought extends nearly a mile across the valley (which in bygone ages was no doubt generally covered with water from the Humber), is thought by some archteologists to be a relic of the Neolithic man. Its age must be enormous— almost beyond calculation—as on the top of the wooden way is about Oft. of solid clay, and above the clay about lft. of peat; and this peat was there in the time of the Romans as the Roman roads in the neighbourhood are laid upon it. This most interesting discovery can now be seen, but it is to be covered up shortly, unless some steps should be taken by any learned society to preserve it. It is, I believe, on land belonging to the Earl of Yarborough.

DR. SCHLIEMANN'S DISCOVERY AT TIRYNS. Fresh facts have come to light concerning Dr. Schlie- mann's extraordinary discovery of a vast prehistoric palace or castle at Tiryns, in the Peloponnese. From further ex- cavations this remarkable building appears even older than was thought at first. Its oldest portions are now assigned to the thirteenth, perhaps even the fourteenth century be- fore our era, whilst the partly rebuilt portion is attributed to the eighth or seventh century B.C. In this way it would be of even higher antiquity than the heroic graves of tilycens. The vestige of a terrible fire by which the palace at Tiryns was destroyed are yet visible everywhere. At the door and window openings the atone has been burnt into a chalk-like, the clay into a brick-like, mass. Otherwise the ruins are in a good condition. The places of the columns are still discernible by slight circular elevations of the floor where the bases of 27 columns, formed of hard limestone, have been found; also a most ancient Doric capital. Near the gate the Cyclopean circumvallation still overtops the castle, and there, in the narrowness of the gloomy gate- way, the masies of stone, heaped up on all sides, are doubly impressive to the eye. At this place the onlooker gets a truly overpowering sensation of the whole prehistoric settle- ment. A feeling is created that we are here onthe threshold of an architectural development which forces a transition to the Lion Gate of Mycense, so that the latter archaic work, though it gives rise to such wonderment, already appears to be something more recent and more refined. Near the threshold of each room, the bases of two columns, as well as the faucet-holes of the folding doors, are still to be ob- served. In a large ante-room there is a square structure, to which steps lead up from the door. Dr. Schliemanu holds it to be an altar of the house-protecting chief deity (Zeus Herkeios), in accordance with the custom mentioned in Homer. A great many rooms, divided by intervening walls, evidently formed at first a single hall—a throne- room, as the phrase would be now. In the centre of this splendid room there is a large circular cut in the floor, with four bases of columns set in a square, probably a seat for a king, or a receptacle of house-gods. Under the western wing of the hall there is a bathroom, proved to be such by a large atone slab at the bottom, and by a still well-pre- served waste-pipe. Whatever remnants there are of wall paintings are very fresh in colour, of strikingly bright and gay tints. The colours need are black, red, blue, yellow, and white. One of the wall paintings repre- sents a bull in full career. On its back a small nude male figure is to be seen, agitating itself in curious fashion as if engaged in some acrobatic performance. The proportions of the bull are faultlessly rendered, the details given with naturalistic fidelity; the movement of the human figure is most exaggerated, almost as if it were on the wing. The back-ground is dark red; the bull yellow; the human figure white. Seeing how exceedingly rare any mural paintings of Greece are, these archaic pictures are of incalculable value. A mass of pottery and terra-cotta figures, many of them of extraordinary freshness, have been discovered as well ss some slabs of alabaster with relief sculptures—sparse remnants of a once splendid inner de- coration of the rooms. Many knives of obsidian and rudely formed hammers of diorite and speckled marble have been found; little metal—no iron, but a great deal of lead. Charred grains after a close investigation by Professor , Wittmack, have been recognised as the remnants of grapes. ,1 At the foot of the rock on which the castle stands Dr. Schliemann has discovered Cyclopean house walls. Here there must once have been the dwelling-places of a rival population, seeking shelter under the castle like a herd near the herdsman. Besides these pre-historic dis- coveries, Dr. Schliemann found the ruins of a Christian church from Byzantine times—probably from the sixth century. In Greek antiquity the men of Tirvas were noted, curi- ously enough, not only for their bravery, but also for their Bacchic habits, and, last but not least, for their drollery, their waggishness, their uncontrollable propensity, towards hoaxing practices and laughter. The Tirynthians once con- sulted the Oracle at Delphi in order to get rid of their bent towards side-splitting jokes. The performance of a sacrifice having been imposed upon them by the Oracle for the object in question, a little boy unfortunately straddled across the procession, when his infantine remarks forthwith led to a repetition of the inveterate laughing habit on that sacred occasion. The sacrifice thus came to nought, and the Tirynthians continued laughing until their town was de- stroyed by their rivals, the Argive& This destruction was wrought soon after the Persian invasion, daring which the Tirynthians had bravely taken part in the battle of Plataiai, whilst Argos had held aloof In treacherous neutrality. Their name was therefore engraved among those of the other cities that had fought there on the bronze column with the golden tripod stand which the Spartans dedicated as the tithe of the booty to She Pythian Apollo at Delphi. That column, it may be noted in passing, is at present preserved at Constantinople. Tiryns, like Mycenss Midea, and some other towns of Argolis, was originally of "barbarian," foreign, Lydo-Phrygian, that is Thracian (hence, according to one view, Eastern Teutonic) foundation. The rivalry and hostility between Tiryns and Greek Argos may thus explain itself all the better, though in course of time the Tirynthians became fully Hellenised in language and feeling, it really looks as if a still latent sentiment of hostility had finally led, on the part of the Argivee, to the annihilation of that once dangerous Thracian stronghold. What a vista this opens into grey antiquity! And what a background do we thus get for Dr. Schliemann's wonderful discovery

At the assizes in Carrickfergus in 1821, a prisoner was indicted for stealing a quantity of liaen in the town of Belfast. There was no direct evidence as to his stealing it himself, but many of the police proved that they found the linen concealed in his house. He, however, declared he was utterly unconscious of Its being there, and protested his innocence in the most solemn manner, asserting at the same time that his character before this accusation had been un- impeachable. Tuesday, Earl of Winchelsea. Earl Harrowby. Duke of Wellington. Wednes- day, Earl Dudley, Marquis of iLondonderry. Earl of Had- dington. Thursday, Viscount Falmouth, Earl of Camar. von. Friday, Lord Wynford, Earl of Eldon, Lord Lynd- hurst, Lord Tenterden, Archbishop of Canterbury, Duke of Gloucester, and the Earl of Harewood. The main argument of the Opposition was that the ten- dency of the Ministerial plan was to concentrate the power of the State in the Commons, to elect the latter into a chamber of delegates, and thus to pave the way for the destruc- tion not only of the Peers but the Monarchy. The arguments against the bill, says a shrewd observer, sought to establish the following conclusions :—" That though the grand virtue of the British Constitution is its representative character, yet neither King nor Lords can exist unless they control the Commons; that though the wishes of the people ought al- ways to be attended to, yet neither petitions nor votes can be received in proof of what they want; that when the people ask earnestly they are not to be heard, because that shows excitement; that when they do not ask earnestly they are not to be heard because that shows re-action, and that whether they are excited or not the only way to satisfy them is to give them little or nothing." The intel- ligence that the Bill had been thrown out of the House of Lords produced an extraordinary sensation throughout the country.• A series of great demonstrations followed. The members who had supported the Bill met at the Thatched House; the common Council of the city of London assem- bled; the conduct of the Ministers was approved by a meet- ing of merchants and bankers at the Mansion House, and the King was petitioned to continue his Ministers and have recourse to a new creation of Peers in number sufficient to carry the bill. On October 9th Lord Ebrington moved in the House of Commons a resolution declaratory of un- abated confidence in the Ministers, and this was passed by a majority of 131. On the 20th of October Parliament was prorogued to the 22nd of November, and meanwhile ad- dresses and petitions poured in upon the King from all ranks and conditions of his people. The Lord Mayor and Corpora- tion of the City of London went up to St. James's with an address to the Throne in favour of the bill, accompanied, it was supposed, by sixty thousand persons. The grandest movement, however, appeared at Birminga ham, when the Political Union, consisting of 150,000 per- sons, assembled—a sublime spectacle of power and peace. That historical gathering was presided over by Thomas Attwood, Elea, who delivered a most powerful address, in which he said :—" When the Union was first formed they were told by his friends that they would have no power— that the Oligarchy were too strong for them, and that all their efforts would be in vain. Bat when he had been informed that the Union would not be able to control the Oligarchy he had said, We will get two millions of strings, and we will place each string in the hands of a strong and brave man, and we will twist those strings into a thousand large ropes, and we will twist those ropes into one immense cable, and by means of that cable we will put a hook in the nose of Leviathan and guide and govern him at our pleasure.' Now,' continued Mr. Attwood, "have we not put a hook in the nose of Leviathan and have we not twisted the strings, and the ropes, and the cable well—have we not thwarted that atrocious influence behind the throne which Lord Chatham said was stronger than the Throne itself.' He would explain that atrocious influence of the oligarchy which had governed the King, the Lords, and the People. He did not say it was the House of Lords—that hon- ourable and illustrious House, composed of an aristocracy associated with so many great and glorious recollections— hmademsecbersretlyof and dat f rraiugdhutlenhtolnyouursaubrlpeedHthouesep, powers d but it was a junta of 150 individuals, some of whom owwtheroathe King, Lords, and Commons, and had, in fact, governed everything in England with a despotic sway. These were the " oligarchs " whose dominion was now com- ing to an end. In accomplishing this great end no violence was required, for by obeying the law they became powerful to control the law. They had united two millions of men peaceably and legally in one grand and determined associa- tion to recover the liberty,the happiness, and the prosperity of the country, and he should like to know what power there was in England that could resist a force like this. In con- clusion he asked all to take off their hats and to cry with one voice, God bless the King. In an instant every head was uncovered, and at one moment a hundred thousand voices answered to the exhortation, "God bless the Bing." The continuance of Earl Grey in race had a powerful effect in preserving the peace of the country, his lordship having pledged himself to carry a Reform Bill if he re- mained in office. The King, too, declared that he had the highest confidence in the Ministry, and that every means in his power should be used to secure the success of a measure so essential to the interest, happiness, and welfare of his people. Parliament re-assembled on the 6th of and the King urged a speedy settlement of a Reform ques- tion so necessary to the security of the State and the con- tentment of the nation. To accomplish this a new bill must be introduced, and this was accordingly done by Lord Russell in a few days afterwards, but with some material improvements. Again was the bill subjected to a fiery ordeal, but its second reading was carried by two to one, and the House adjourned to the 17th of July, 1832. The bill was now pushed in committee, and again vigorously assailed, Lord Russell moved the third reading. Warm debates en- sued, Mr. S. Percival, in his harangue, telling the House that he was sent in God's name to warn them of impending destruction. Two days afterwards the House divided, when the decision was—For the third reading, 355; against, 239; majority, 116.
