ANCIENT FITED AT FARNWORTII. A feud arose in the reign of Philip and Mary, sometime before 1555, betwixt certain parties in the neighbourhood of Farnworth, near Prescot, in this county, which termi- nated in a lawsuit in the Duchy Court, in which the plain- tiff, John Lister, laid a charge of assault against Henry Henryson. The "Calendar to Pleadings" of the 4th and sth Elizabeth contains a record of the transaction, which is curious enough for extract as a local Note. The documentr preserved in the Public Record Office are described as' In- terrogatories and Depositions on a Charge of Assault by the Defendant (Henry Henryson) upon the Plaintiff (John Lister)." The Interrogatories are "solely administered to the Plaintiff, John Lister," whose dispositions state in sub- stance as follows:

John Lister deposeth "that he was at Farnworth. and that there was a Court of the Fee of Wydnes holden there; that John Layton took the presentment of the Jury for certain Surrenders and other things then presented, and divers of the Tenants complained for the stopping of their , Ways; that a Jury of the Homage of the said Lordship, empannelled and sworn, were afterwards, together with Bryan Travers, on the North side of Farneworthe Church, and communed together; and that the said Bryan Travers informed the Deponent that they had so communed concern- ing a Surrender to pass between Ralph Thomasson, Clerk, and Richard Thomasson, for a Tenement which the said Ralph did surrender to the use of Gilbert Gerrard before . . .

that' time; that the Defendant, Henry Henryson, was one of the said Jury; that Deponent was, after Mass, going to Kewrdley Chapel, when the said Henry Henryson assaulted hire, and that Deponent thereupon struck him again; that thereupon the said Bryan Travers caused a Jury to inquire of the assault, who found and presented that the said De- ponent had struck the said Henry Henryson ; and for the Deponent saith that many of the Jury were akin to the said Henry Henryson ; that after the finding of the Jury the said Bryan Travers willed Deponent to put in Sureties for the Peace; which he did, and the said Bryan Travers would have bound Defendant to a Fee Court, which Deponent re- fused, as against the custom of the Lordship of Wydnes, but offered himself, with Sureties, to be bound to the Hal- mote; that the said Bryan Travers thereupon awarded Pro- cess against the Deponent to the Bailiff of Wydnes, to bring him to Halton Castle, there to remainuntil the pleasure of Sir John Savage Knight, Steward of the Lordship, should be known; and that Deponent put in sureties to answer within the Lordship, but that he made no Rescue nor escape from the Bailiff otherwise than he lawfully might do. Further that the Servants of the said Sir John Savage, namely, George Vernon and others, did afterwards lie in wait for Defendant in a Shepecole, and took him, as he was going to Farneworth Church to teach his Scholars, and assaulted him, and by violence brought him to Halton Castle, where he remained Prisoner nine days, and was then delivered out of the Castle by virtue of the King's and Queen's Majesty's Writ of Corpus cum cousa, directed to the Constable of Halton, from the King's and Queen's Majesty's Exchequer at Chester, and that after Deponent was so delivered Out of the said Castle, the Right Honourable the Earl of Derby sent for Deponent, and commanded him to come and speak with hita, and Deponent went over the Water [river Mersey] to the said Foul, being in Lancashire. And the said Deponent further deposes, that the Lordship of Wydnes was parcel of the Duchy of Lancaster, and that Henry Duke of Lancaster gave the said Lordship to the Tenants there, as parcel of his Castle and Manor of Halton; and that he supposed the said Sir John Savage was Steward there; that the Steward for the time being had empannelled Juries at the Halmote in Wydnes, for the inquiry of offences there, and such as were found offenders were fined in the Court there for their said offences; and that he never knew but that such offenders within the said Lordship were put to a fine by the direction of the Court, and nowhere else, saving that the Deponent was taken and punished in the Castle of Halton. Also, that if any Man was convicted for Debt, detinue, or the like, tke party convicted was to pay the said Debt, or else to remain with the Bailiff till the Debt was paid, or else to be brought to the said Castle of Halton, at the Bailiff's election, and there to remain till the Debt was satisfied; and that if any person was taken by a Caplas to answer to an action In the Court of Wydnes, or else in the Halmote Court there, and the person so attached, Jtc., could not or would not put in pledges or sureties, that then it was at the election of the Bailiff there to keep such person so attached to answer for the same, or else to bring him unto the said Castle of Halton, being the place accus- tomed for such persons to be imprisoned. And lastly, he deposeth, that when certain persons inhabiting within the said Lordship of Wydnes had acted against the Steward there, he had sent for them over the Water into Cheshire, and then committed them to prison in the said Castle of Halton; and that, for any offence committed against the Order of the Court of Wydnes, he knew of no person that had been punished but only by Fine in the Court there.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. REFORM DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. GREAT MEETING ON THE COMMON.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES. REFORM DEMONSTRATION AT RUNCORN. GREAT MEETING ON THE COMMON.

An open air demonstration in favour of the Franchise Bill was held at Runcorn, on Saturday afternoon. When it became imminent that the House of Lords would throw out the Bill for the Extension of the Suffrage, introduced by Mr. Gladstone, a working-man who occupies a position of influence amongst his fellows, mooted the desirability of the unenfranchised in Runcorn giving the denial to the state- ment se often iterated by Conservative politicians, that those who were now outside the pale of fall citizenship had very little desire for the measure. He suggested a proces- sion and an open air meeting as the most effective kind of demonstration. His proposal was received with favour; and a committee of working-men was formed and set to work, in conjunction with the Liberal Committee, who consented to lend their aid by obtaining speakers. All the arrangements requisite for a successful gathering were made, and nothing further than a fine day was to be desired. To add interest to the procession several bands had volunteered their ser- vices, and about half-past two they paraded the streets of the town. Mill Brow Wesleyan brass band started from the school, and proceeded along Halton-road, and then returned to Devonshire-square, through the streets adjoining St. John's Presbyterian Chapel. Camden Wesleyan band visited Duke's Field; Weston band entered the town by Greenway- road, and the Frodeham fife band arrived by train at three o'clock. Shortly after three o'clock Devonshire-square was crowded with a large assemblage of people, and then the I march to the Common commenced. Borne aloft in various parts of the procession were boards bearing the phrases " The franchise for the people," "Taxation without repre- sentation is unjust," "The people's rights," drc. It was com- puted that there were about 1,200 people in the procession,l which reached the rendezvous by way of Greenway-road and Moughland'e-lane, hundreds of spectators lining the way. IA spot near the reservoir of the Mersey Brine and Salt COM- pany had been chosen for the place of meeting, and here a - large concourse of people, standing on their own common land, and covered by the blue vault 1 of heaven, surrounded the platform—a couple of lorries provided with forms. One Liberal computed the number present at 4,000, but it may be stated I with confidence that upwards of 2,000 took part in the de- monstration and they exhibited much enthusiasm. The ac- commodation provided for the press proved of too insecure a character to stand the pressure of the crowd upon it, and 1 the table collapsed with a crash in the midst of the proceed- I ings, note taking being a matter of consider- able difficulty throughout. During the afternoon a donkey in the neighbourhood several times gave forth a discordant bray, and there were immedi- ately cries of " Salisbury " from members of the audience, followed by loud laughter, whilst several speakers made the animal the medium of good points against the House of Lords. Mr R Shaw, of the Highlands, who we may observe entertained the speakers to luncheon, presided over the as- sembly, and he was supported on the platform by Mr I 3 Leadam (Liberal candidate for Mid-Cheshire), the Revs Geo Hack, J D Thomas, F Carter, tir Vause, J Pickwell ; Messrs T Snaps, If S Hall, JP. Jas Handley, J P, G Rooke, JP, Wm Long. JP. A E Paterson, A Fletcher, T Handley, W Handley, T Norman, H Hurst, 33 Dixon, J Cross, .13 Yapp, .1 Edwards, A Nicholson, W Armstrong, Jepson, F .7 Norman, G Arrowemith, J Curzon. and 0 Leak (secretary to Runcorn Liberal Association). The Crummier, who was cordially greeted, said they had met that day on very important business. (Hear, bear.) There were a number of persons in the town of Runcorn and that division of the county who were not at the present time permitted to vote ire the election of a Parliamentary representative. The Liberal party had been endeavouring te carry a very moderate bill to remedy this anomaly. They had succeeded in passing the Franchise Bill in the House of Commons by a large majority, which would enable a large number of those present who had sufficient intelligence and, who had to bear their fair share in the taxation of the coun- try, to have a voice in choosing their representative in the people's house, but this measure, which would have simply done justice to these who are at present debarred from their just constitutional rights, had been ignominiously thrown out by the upper house. They were met to protest against this action of the upper chamber of the Legislature, and he was pleased to see that they had mustered in such large numbers. (Loud cheers). Mr. JEPSON moved the following resolution :—" That in view of the full and exhaustive discussion which the Franchise Bill received, the overwhelming majority by which it main features were affirmed, and the practical unanimity with which it passed the House of Commons, this meeting has to express its disappointmeat and indigna- tion that the majority of the House of Lords have refused this measure of electoral justice and reform, for the factions and inconsequent reason that it was unaccompanied by a redistribution arrangement; and this meeting also emphati. cally approves of the decision of the Government to hold an autumn session, thus showing their determination to give early effect to the repeatedly declared will of the people on the question. That copies of the foregoing reso- lution be sent to the Prime Minister, Earl Granville, and such members of Parliament as may be selected." (Cheers.) Mr. Jepson said that the great audience which be bad the honour of addressing must, he supposed, be taken to repre- sent "the great unwashed"—(laughter)—" the swinish mul- titude "—(laughter)—those who had been lately spoken of as men without intelligence. (Renewed laughter and ap- plause.) But there was not a man amongst them but could tell when he was hungry. (Much laughter.) There was not a man amongst them but could tell when his rights were I trampled upon, or who did not want and claim the fran- I chise. (Hear, hear.) They were willing to uphold the arms of the grand old man. (Three cheers for Mr. Glad- stone.) Their purpose that day was to let Lord Salisbury know that they wanted the franchise, and intended to have it. (Cheers.) He expected the bill would be passed through with a sweep in the autumn session, and he was glad to think that before long two millions of people will be put on a par with the three millions that now exercised the

right of voting for a member of Parliament. Taxation with- electors of Runcorn. He (the speaker) should never forget out representation was tyranny, and so long as they paid the kindness and consideration which they had shown him their just share towards the govenment of the country they self, the leniency they had shown to all his faults, and the demanded that they should have a voice in chosing the men manner in which they had exaggerated those few merita who should represent them in Parliament. (Cheers.) which he possessed. (Cheers.) He asked then as the best Mr. W. Anion/ONG was proud to second the resolution, thing they could do for him to transfer that confidence with and as a working-man to have the opportunity of protesting which they treated him to his Wend Mr. Leadam, who be against the thousands of his class having their constitu- believed represented the highest class of Liberalism far tional rights withheld from them any longer. (Hear, better than he could ever do, and be sure that in him Mid- hear.) He characterised the Reform Bill of 1867 Cheshire would have a representative of whom the con- as a grand piece of class legislation, and said stitnents might be proud. (Cheers.) Lord Beaconsfeld's idea was to keep the cootie! Mr. William Milne, Mr. Killick (who observed that the ties in such a condition that they would continue to be present electorate of Mid-Cheshire was 10,000, but if the bill Tory strongholds. He, on behalf of the working-men of had passed it would have been increased to 23,000), Mr. J. T. this county, stood up there to vindicate their right to be , Brunner.and Mr. W. Long also spoke in favour of the resolti- admitted to citizenship. (Cheers.). The Monarchy was , tion. At this point the Chairman read the following tale- limited, the House of Commons Was limited. The result ; gram from Mr. Thomas Rigby, the second Liberal candidate of this was that the members of Parliament had to appeal to , for the division:—" Sorry I cannot attend meeting this alter" the people for power, but there were only half the people noon. lam suddenly prevented. Kindly apologise for me." who could vote—there was only a very limited number of Three cheers were then given for Mr. Rigby. electors. But the rights of the constitution, the rights of The CHAIRMAN then put the resolution to the meeting, the nation were established in the House of Commons, and it was carried unanimously with loud cheers. which had at its head one of the finest and noblest statesmen On the proposition of Mr. T. Norman', seconded by Ur. that had ever adorned humanity—(cheers)—and he hoped T. HANDLInr, a vote of thanks was accorded to the bands for they would leave the business in the hands of Her Majesty's their presence and aid; and on the proposition of Mr. Roosts, Government, which had carried it on so honourably up to seconded by Mr. NICHOLSON, a vote of thanks was passel to the present time. (Cheers.) the Chairman by acclamation. Mr. I'. SHAM who was received with loud cheers, said Mr. Slim suitably replied, and the proceedings con- they were commencing that day one of the gravest, but he eluded. was glad to think, one of the last of the many struggles for liberty in which their forefathers had in centuries past been engaged. They were about to crown the edifice and to con- summate the liberties of the people by doing something more than pass the Franchise Bill, viz., by the sweeping away of the hereditary House of Lords. (Cheers.) He referred to the speciousness, the insincerity, the hollownese of the pretexts the Lords had advanced for throwing out the bill, and the people felt that there was nothing they had done and nothing they had said which deserved consideration at their (the people's) hands. If their lordships had the con- fidence in the people which they professed to have, they could not have too many of the enfranchised to express an opinion upon what a redistribution bill should be. (Cheers.) If the Franchise Bill had been passed they had reason to suppose that the great bulk of the 2,000,000 additional voters would have been drawn from the counties, except in towns like Runcorn, and would have been followers of the Lords. They would have been drawn from the agricultural districts, from the classes that had been supposed to be con- tinually receiving benefits at the hands of the aristocracy, and if anybody ought to have had confidence in these two millions surely it ought to be the House of Lords. (Cheers.) But he fancied there were spectral memories of ill deeds done in the past to these classes which haunted their lordships—(hear, hear, and laughter)—and be thought it was because they were afraid to appeal even to their own near friends and dependants that they had rejected the Bill. The House of Lords had taken the first step towards politi- cal suicide. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) The princes of the royal blood never ventured to take part in a political debate, or to give a vote on a question affecting the liberties of the people, but what the princes and the Queen herself would not have ventured to do, these men in all the arrogance of their position, because they were the sons of their fathers and gradfathers who were perhaps by no means respectable in their origin and in their character—(hear, hear,)—they had ventured to put down the people's rights. (Cheers.) What did the Lords want to impress upon them that the people were in earnest in this matter? Did they want them is do as they did in 1831, and storm Ansley House, or as in 1867, and pull down Hyde Park railings? (Cheers.) But the people knew better to-day. They had something stronger than pikes and bayonets, and guns and stones—there was the force of public opinion—(hear, hear,)—which even these Lords dare not defy, and which they could never resist. But that anachronism, the House of Lords, must be put out of the way. It seas out of all reason in a land of liberty, and in days of progress like these' that an irresponsible body could obstruct legislation and hinder progress. (Cheers.) They knew the lines— Hereditary bondsmen! know ye not Who would be free themselves must strike the blow /. (Hear, hear.) That blow they struck that day, and they would strike it home. (Rear, hear.) The speaker referred to many beneficial measures Of progress and reform that the House of Lords had opposed, and he added that the country wanted to know why a house like this should be allowed to stand in the people's way, and why they should Mt in their gilded cage like a squirrel in his revolv- ing barrel thinking that whilst they were tuning round they were serving some good and toilful purpose. 1 hese foolish creatures like that very squirrel thinks he climbs on higher and higher, turning wood and wire, and he never gets five inches higher. (Laughter.) He rather thought that it was very much the same with refer- ence to any attempts at legislation that the House of Lords might put in force. This baneful incubus must be put out of the people's way. Before the autumn the House of Lords —even Lord Salisbury—would wish to heaven that they had never thrown out the Franchise Bill and provoked agitation, for so sure as the House of Lords had had all those privi- leges for no many years, so sure bad the day come when these privileges must be brought to an end. The Reform Bill would pass, and the House of Lords must be set in order. Its power of veto must be taken away; Some representative basis must in future be its foundation, or else it must be banished to the limbo, where lay all dead and useless things. With all reverence he used the words of Holy Writ in reference to this crisis, and he said to them, his countrymen, that "Now is the ac- cepted time," and now was the day of their political salva- tion. (Loud cheers.) Mr. I. S. LBADAM, who was received with loud cheering on rising to speak, said he must congratulate them upon the imposing assembly which the enthusiasm of the working men of Runcorn had brought together, and went on to ob- serve that there was a difference between the old and the new Toryism. The new Toryism, of which he believed Mr. John Brookes professed to be a representative, was not, in all particulars, like the old. When the people under the old Toryism demanded entrance into the constitution that Tory- ism had the pluck to put up its back and refuse the de- mand; but the new Toryism, to clear the doer of the house, put the key in its pocket, slunk round by the back way, and expressed wonder as to what on earth the obstruction was all about. (Laughter and cheers.) When in 1866, the Liberal Government brought in a Reform Bill, dissevered from redistribution, at which the gravest dissatisfaction was expressed because of the separation, it was agreed to bring in another measure in which the extension of the franchise and redistribution were coupled. As soon as the Tories had the two bills together they tore them into shreds, and the collapse of the Government followed the fate of the bills. He believed that the Government had adopted the present course as to the Franchise Bill because they desire to do more adequate justice to the intelligent masses of the North ot England than had hitherto been done. The Gov- ernment had offered to meet the Lords half way. They offered to summon Parliament in November to discuss the question of redistribution, but the Lords refused to accept this proposal. Why, the Liberals went in for redistribution long before the Tories woke-up to the fact that there was any necessity for redistribution at all. (Cheers.) He should like to know what a Liberal Government had to ob- tain by ill-faith with the constituencies in this matter. (Hear, hear.) Why they should deprive the intelligent masses of the North of the power which their intelligence entitled them to? The speaker referred to the unconstitu- tional means which Lord Salisbury had adopted for forcing a dissolution, and added that the aristocracy had too much power in this country. They were not only represented in the House of Lords, but they flooded the House of Com- mons. The members of Mid-Cheshire at this moment were the nominees of an aristocrat, and one of them was a mem- ber ot the aristocracy. He trusted that neutral politicians in the conflict which was arising would stand by the Corn- MODS—that they would send the members for Mid-Cheshire back to the aristocracy to which they belonged by birth, and that they would choose in their places men who were Com- moners, and Commoners only. (Hear, hear.) For genera- tions past the people of England had stood by their repro- ' mutative& The representatives for Mid-Cheshire were now betraying the interests of those who elected them and he trusted that electors at the general election which would shortly be at hand would vinoicate now as they had vindi- 'cited in the past the traditional independence of the Com- mons of England. (Cheers.) Mr. G. W. LATHAM was greeted with enthusiastic cheers, He remarked that Lord Salisbury with considerable sarcasm had said that the Liberal party were perfectly welcome to walk up and down the streets until the next meeting of Par- liament. Well, they from Runcorn had got as far as Run- corn Common, but he trusted that if they did not get what they wanted they would be prepared to go a step further and go to London and ask for it at the hands of their representatives. (Hear, hear, and cheers.) They would not get what they wanted by stopping at Runcorn and shouting. They must take some active measures to show that they were in earnest. Lord Salisbury had himself said that except there was a violent agitation he should not be convinced that the people were in earnest. (" There will be one," and cheers.) He did not counsel any active measures of that sort. He simply said they must show they were in earnest, me reminded them that in modern days the walls of a beleaguered city did not fall merely because a trumpet was sounded, lie allowed that at the present moment the House of Lords was obstructing their liberties; it was pre- venting the free progress of Liberal opinion; but they must , not be angry with the House of Lords for that. An engineer when he was making a railway did not get angry because there was a big rock in his way. He simply regarded it as an obstacle he had to conquer somewhow. If they watched a railway in a mountainous country they would see how cleverly the engineer could manage. He went now and then with a gentle curve round the obstruction. If it was very much in his way he blew it up, but he never blew up more than he was obliged to do, and he left a certain part of the obstruction to look picturesque for future ages. (Laughter.) Well, he counselled them to do this—not to do any more destruction than they needed. Simply to be firm and deter- mined that the course of Liberal progress should not be obstructed for a moment. They would have the franchise let what obstacle came in their way, and it would only be by the undue obstinacy of those who were in power if they were not able to get past all obstructions with very little difficulty and blowing up at all. (Hear, and laughter.) The measure passed in the House of Commons was of the mildest and most Conservative description, and if it were rejected the next that was passed would ha of a much more drastic character. He for one, as a Liberal amongst Liberals, as a Radical amongst Radicals, should not be sorry to see the bill obstructed a second time, so that they might have a more perfect one hereafter—that they might see the equality vote throughout the country ; and a more perfect represen- tation of the people. (Cheers.) He was glad that his friend Mr. Leadam had made his first- speech before the

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting was held on Tuesday under the presidency of the Rev. Canon Barclay. Present: Revs. .1. W. N. Tanner, J. Lockwood; Messrs. J. Ashton, T. Norman, E. A. Wallington, R. Ashton, Derbyshire, Knowles, Warbur- . ton, Mclntyre, W. Handley, J. Hightield, H.Linaker (desk), and W. EL Lin tker (deputy clerk.)—The Finance Com- mittee recommended the payment of accounts amounting to £252 Os 10d.—The Rev. J. Lockwood moved the adoption of the recommendation, and it was carried.—The Master re- ported that there were 157 inmates in the house against 177 corresponding week last year. There were four vagrants relieved during the week. There were 16 imbeciles in the house. Twenty boys and 23 girls were in attendance at school, stud six boys and 14 girls were receiving an indus- trial training. The Visiting Committee reported that they had inspected the Workhouse and found everything in a clean and satisfactory condition. They recommended the erection of a shed with galvanised iron roof for the protee- Hon of coke, and also a shed building in men's yard for joiners and other industrial work.—Mr. Handly moved tbe adoption of the report, and observed that he thought the in- mates would be happier if they had more industrial work.— The report was adopted unanimously.

TWO CHILDREN MIIIIDERED.—A cabinetmaker named Edwards and his wife are in custody at Plymouth charged with murdering their two children, aged one eight years and the other ten months. The wife's story seemed to show that the husband had cut the children's throats, and the coroner's jury has returned a verdict of " Wilful murder" against _him alone.

THE SHOE MAHER AND THE AUCTIONEER. A RUNCORN DISPUTE. Before Captain C. W. Ilazlehuret and Mr. J. Brundrit, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Samuel Yarwood, auc- tioneer and cab proprietor, was summoned to answer a charge of using obscene and defamatory language towards Thomas Cooke, shoemaker, calculated to provoke a breach of the peace. Mr. Hitchen defended.—The complainant said he lived in Church-street, next door to the defendant. Between eleven end twelve o'clock on the 14th July be locked all the doors and went upstairs to bed. His wife was downstairs puttine things by. His daughter called out to him, "Father, there's someone in the entry," and he went downstairs and found Mr. Yarwood ond his wife in the entry. Mr. Yarwood was using very abusive language to- wards the complainant's wife and threatened to "knock her -- face off." Mrs. Rutter then came across, and the de fondant said "That -- has been painting my property, but I will make the -- bastard sit up yet." He was re• ferring to him (witness). The defendant added that he had got £5OO and he would spend the whole of it in law. Wit- ness replied that perhaps he would have his belly full of law. Defendant said he would remain in the entry until the lights went out. He would annoy witness as long as be could and have a band of musk there rather than be done by him. The defendant swore he would not have the entry' 1 door locked, and he cut the cord to which weights for the purpose of making the door s sing to.—ln reply to Mr Hitcben, witness said there had been no dispute about the right to the entry, and nothing was said about Mr. Yarwood not coming that day. He never said "Sam, if tha doesn't go out of the entry I'll knock thee out of it." Mr. Yarwood bade his wife bring him a cigar in a commanding sort of way, and said he should smoke it in the entry to show his rights.—Mrs. Cooke said she heard someone " pretending " to unlock the door, and heard Mr. Yarwood sly he would knock the door down. She opened the door and told him that it would look better if he would stop in his own yard. whereupon he used language not fit to be mentioned.—By Mr. Hitchen: There was a pigeon cote overhanging the door inside the entry. She knew defendant had a right of road through the entry, and he had a key for the door.—Mr. Hitchen: Was anything said about Halton Club P—l said I had not been to Halton Club —What did you mean by that ? That I was at home.—What had that got to do with it I,—l says "If you have got anything to say come at a proper time and not at this hour of the night; and come sober." In answer to farther questions witness said her husband never spoke to Mr. Yarwood. There bad been some dispute about a wardrobe which overhanged Mr. Yar- wosd's yard. She knew it.was a grievance to Mr. Yarwood and that he wanted it to be removed. She never called Mr. Yarwood a dirty scamp.—Mr. Hitchen here took a technical objection which was overruled by the Bench, and Mire Fanny Cooke, daughter to the plaintiff was called, and cor- roborated the previous evidence—Mr. Hitchen then ad- dressed the magistrates for the defence. The defendant was sworn and said he was sorry to say be had property next door to the plaintiff. On the night in question be came home from business about eleven o'clock and his wife said "Oh Sam I have found the key belonging to the entry door." This key had been lost for a length of time, and they had not been able to use the entry. His wife handed him the key. Ha said be was certain that could not be the key as it would have been rusty. They decided to go and try the key and see whether it was the right one. He found that the door had been fastened with cords and pulleys, and as these interfered with his right of way and had certainly no right there, he cut the cords. The key proved to be the ' right one. Immediately he had opened the door Mrs. Cooke came out and said "You old scamp" what are you do- ing there. You have been to Halton Club and you have come here to kick up your rows." He replied that she would excuse him if he said that he bad not been to Halton club, and that he had not come there to kick up any row. He said he should, however, maintain his right to the entry, whereupon Mrs. Cooke said he must go the other way. He then told his wife to fetch him a cigar, which lie smoked in the entry to show that he bad a right there. He inquired where Mr. Cooke was. and Mtn. Cooke replied, "He is in bed where you ought to be, you old scamp." He told her she must understand he was not a scamp, nor would he hear such language from her. if. then intimated that he should have the door knocked down as it was overhanging his premises, and they had taken no heed of his notice to remove it. At this point Mr. Cooke same upon the scene and said he would knock witness oat of the entry if he did not go, and he replied that he did not think a "blooming bastard" could at all events knock him out. Mr. Cooke then said In should make him pay for it. He alleged that Mrs. Cooke used very abusive language to him, and added that he had lived next door to Mr. Garnett, ' the last occupant of Cooke's house, for seventeen years, and ' a wrong word had never passed between them. Beyond the expression he had stated, he had used no defamatory language, and the charge of threatening Mrs. Cooke was ' concocted.—By the complainant: He had been subjected to every annoyance possible about the entry —On leaving the box, defendant said "A more proficient blackguard I have never seen for years than Tom Cooke's wife."—Captain ' Haelehurst said the Bench could not help but feel satisfied ' that the case was proved. If these people had done any- thing against him personally he had the option of taking out a cross-summons—Defendant: I have been negligent in that part.—Captain Hazlehurst : We have nothing to do with that. We have simply to deal with the case as we have it before us. You must be bound over in your own reeog- nizancee of £lO to keep the peace for six months, and pay the costs.

OLD "KING Coat."—Theophratus, a Greek writer who flourished in the fourth century before the Christian era, in a work entitled "Book on Stones," describes an earthly substance which would kindle and barn, and which was used by smiths. There can be no doubt that he refers to coal, and that this is the earliest passage in which that substance is expressed or mentioned. IRELAND —Mr. Edward Richards, a landlord of county Wexford, who was one of the foremost in resistance to the Land League in bygone days, publicly complains in a latter to the Daily Express that the League is not dead, for that two of his most friendly tenants, his nearest neighbours, have declined through fear to hire him a horse to finish some mowing.—Last week, Mr. H. M. Philips, on his return home from business connected with Mr. B. St. Joule's property at Meenacluddy, county Donegal, of which he is the agent, found that some miscreants, taking advantage of his absence, had mutilated a fine calf immediatelr below the bough of one of its hind legs, leaving the limb dangling by one inch of the skim—A man named Peter Breen, bog- ranger on the estate of Archdeacon Bland, in county Kerry, has been seriously wounded, but not shod dead as at first re- ported. ROYAL AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY: PROPOSRD TRAVELLING DAIRY.—In connection with the dairy proceedings it may be mentioned that the subject of the establishment of a per manent dairy conference was discussed in Shrewsbury last week, a committee of the dairy conference held at Glouces- ter a few weeks ago having met under the presidency of Col. Kiegscote, M.P., at which after due discussion it was re- solved to form an association under the title of the "Dairy Conference Association," to hold a conference in various parts of the country, to promote the establishment of dairy schools and other educational purposes, and generally W spread information on all matters connected with dairy in- dustry. Dr. Bond, of Gloucester, was appointed secretary 'pro tem., and it is proposed to establish, as soon as practic- able, a travelling educational dairy, similar to that which. in the hands of Canon Bagot, has done such good work in Ireland. It is proposed to hold the first meeting, which will be held in London, simultaneously with the show of the Dairy Farmers' Association. The daily attendances,although not coming up to last yea's successful meeting at York, have materially exceeded those at Beading in 1882.
IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.

_ HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair shortly before 4-0. CHOLERA PRECAVTIONS.—A further question was pat as to the cargo of rags from Marseilles which had arrived at Hull. Dr. CamEnon wished to know if the rags had ac- tually been landed nar Hull. Sir Citentas DIME replied that the Local Government Board had telegraphed that morning to ask what had been done with the cargo, and the reply was that the rags had been transhipped into lighters *a the Humber, and were now awaiting the decision of the consignee whether he would send them back or not. If he declined to send them back they would be destroyed. It was added that the rags were now tailors' cuttings, and that they were all on board the steamer before the outbreak of cholera at Marseilles. In reply to a question whether an order would be issued against the importation of rags from France, Sir C. DILIII said he could not issue such an order, but one had been issued prohibiting importation from Tou- lon or Marseilles. Rags had conveyed smallpox and wool sorters' disease, but the most careful inquiry had failed to elicit the fact that cholera had been so conveyed. Tau DEFENCE or Elam, &c.---Phe Marquis of Han- TINGITCYN informed Sir F. Milner that some increase of ex- pease would be caused by British troops being stationed at Amman, but he was not able at present to say what it would be. The noble marquis told Lord E. Cecil that he was still in communication with the Chancellor of the Ex- chequer on the propriety of introducing during the present session a supplementary estimate for the cost of the relief of General Gordon and the defence of Egypt.—Lord E. FITZ. MAURICE stated that £3OO had been granted for distribution by the Mansion House Committee amongst the families of such of the crew of the Nisero as were in need of as- sistance. Tan Fitencuisa Dratonsraerion.—Mr. CHAPLIN corn-1 plained that in consequence of the Hyde Park demonstra- tion he bad been compelled to reach his place in the House , by an underground passage.—The SPEAIIER expressed his regret that in exceptional circumstances the hon. member had been put to inconvenience, and the HOME SECRETARY bore testimony to the extraordinary good sense and good humour of the crowds of people. As to the approaches to the House. he did not think there was anything to complain of, and he thought the police had suc- ceeded admirably in their duty.—Mr. J. LOWTHER com- plained that he had been stopped in his carriage, and was , told by Sir W. Harcourt that he would not have been I stoppel unless his progress wag considered to be inconsistent with public order.—Mr. CHAPLIN gave notice that "in con- sequence of the gross neglect øf the Home Secretary" he should put a farther question on the subject, and if the an- swer was not satisfactory he should take an early oppor- tunity of calling attention to the matter, but the SPEAXER declined to let the question appear on the paper in those terms. SUPPLY.—The House again went into Committee of Sup- ply on the Civil Service Estimates. On the vote of £30154 for the office of Chief Secretary to the Lord Lieutenant, Mr. O'Brainx moved to omit the salary of the Chief Secretary. and complained at lengjp of the cruel wrong done to himself by the prosecution of Ottited Ireload for its charges against Mr. French Various other topics were raised in connection with the vote, conversation upon I it being carried on by Irish members until 20 minutes past two, when the vote was at last agreed to.—Progress was then reported, and the House resumed. HOUSE OF LORDS—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. ANOTHER BILL RENIECTED.—Two divisions were taken on the Sheriff's Court House (Scotland) Amendment Bill, the second reading of which was moved by Lord Dalhousie. Lord Abinger moved its rejection, and on a division the second reading was refused by 26 votes against 24. Lord Granville, Lord Kimberley, and the Doke of Argyll pro- tested against the practice of moving the rejection of a Bill on the second reading without notice, more especially as in the present case the measure in question was a money Bill. The Lord Chanceller put Lord Abinger's motion that the Bill be read a second time that day six months. The House again dividing. Lord Abinger was now defeated by a major- ity of three, 29 voting with him, 32 against. Lord Dalhousie gave notice that he will put the Bill down for second reading ea Thursday. Lord Abinger intimated that he will again move its rejection. Tau FRANCHISE BILL, &c.—The Hours of Polling Bill was read a third time, as were several other measures.— Lord REDESDALE, reverting to the position e the Franchise Bill, explained for the information of the processionists of the previous day that "the House had not in any way re- fused the franchise to those to whom it was proposed to ex- tend it." They had only practically thrown the Franchise Bill out on the second reading. He now proposed that the Bill should be brought up again at the autumn session in two parts—one dealing with redistribution. The Franchise Bill might then be dealt with, and the redistribution scheme adjourned till after Christmas.—Earl GRANVILLE expressed hi disappointment with this speech. He had hoped the noble earl was going to say something: new. For himself, he had nothing to add to his former speeches.—After some remarks from the Duke of ARGYLL the subject dropped, and their lordships adjourned at five minutes to seven. HOUSE OF CONIMONS.—TUESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at a few minutes to four. THE REFORM DEMONSTRATION —There were a series of questions with respect to the popular demonstration of Mon- day. Mr. DAWNY attired by whose orders the iron hurdles, posts, and seats in Hyde Park had been removed, and by whom the expense was paid. Mr. LEFEVRE, amid inter- ruptions from Mr. Warton, explained that the posts were removed by his order, with the object of avoiding injury and damage to the public. The work was done by the or- dinary labourers of the park, and there would be no extra expense. Mr. Tatton Egerton, who had a seties of questions on the same subject, drew from Mr. Shaw Lefevre the an- nouncement, loudly cheered, that there had been no damage done to the park. Mr. Lowther persisting in knowing whether the men employed in removing the hurdles were public servants, Mr. BROADHURST, amid prolonged cheers from the Liberal side, asked whether the men employed in removing the hurdles for public convenience are the same 1 men who are employed continually in keeping as a special' tract a large portion of the 'Ark for the use of a select class of horse riders. Sir Wm. HARCOTJRT, IO Whom further ques- tions on the matter were addressed, sugz,ested that as Mr. Lowther had given notice of his intention to raise the mat- ter by moving the reduction of the vote for the metropoli- tan police, it would he more convenient to reserve questions till then. "Of course," he added, "a motion of that kind, coming from the front Conservative bench, is a very serious matter." Mr. LowrnEn endeavoured to explain that he only took that course because he could not get at the Home Secretary himself. MISCELLANEOUS.—Mr. CAMPBELL•BANNERMAN said the information which had reached the Admiralty with respect to the collision of the ironclads did not go further than the statement already made in the newspapers The ships would proceed to Plymouth, where a cot rt,aa lola would be held.—Lord EDMOND FITZMAURICE read an additional telegram describing General Gordon as being in a dominant position at Khartoum. Major Chermside telegraphed that the Arabs were much afraid of Gordon, who had defeated four of their tribes between Berber and Khartoum.—The House then went into Committee of Supply, resuming con- sideration of the Civil Service Estimates.—The Irish votes being again taken very little progress was made, though the committee sat till a late hour. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNISDAT. The Speaker took the chair at half-past twelve. CIVIL SERVICE ESTIMATES.--The Hone, Which rose on Tuesday morning at a quarter to three, met again at noon and resumed consideration of the Civil Service Estimates, which occupied it throughout the sitting. The chair was taken by Sir Lyon Playfair. A long discuss'on took place on the vote for the salaries and expenses in connection with the General Valuation and Boundary Survey of Ireland. Mr. SEXTON moved to reduce the vote by the sum of £4OO, the salary of Mr. George Bolton. The hon. memoer made a detailed attack upon Mr. Bolton, who it was mentioned in the course of the conversation is at the present time a party to an untried action at law in which the defendant is Mr. O'Brien.—Mr. HARRINGTON repeated and enforced the allegations against Mr. Bolton.—Mr. COURTNEY re- minded Irish members that this gentleman's salary as Crown Solicitor for Tipperary would come under considera- tion next week. and appealed to them to defer controversy till then. He pretested against members using the privileges of the House to prejudge a case now awaiting trial. Mr. Arnold supported the motion on the ground that Mr. Bolton had presented a petition in bankruptcy. Mr. Courtney greatly aggravated members below the gangway on the Ministerial side by undertaking to prevent such " another flood of easy declamation." He subsequently apologised for this language, but its effect was seen in the division. For some time discussion of the vote was averted by pro- tests against the language of Mr. Courtney and his manner of conducting business. Matters looking serious, Mr. Glad- ' stone interposed and supported the vote on the grounds alleged by Mr Courtney in his first speech.—On a division the vote was confirmed by 116 against 55. Amongst those who , voted in the minority were Mr Labouchere, Mr Rylands, Mr Collings, Mr H Fowler, Mr Caine, Mr S Buxton, Mr Villiers Stuart, Mr O'Connor Power, Sir W Lawson, Mr Storey, Mr Arnold, Mr Richard, Mr Anderson, Mr Craig, Bit George Campbell, Mr S Smith, Mr Roberts, Mr Grey, Sir George Balfour, Professor Bryce, and Mr Williamson. Several Conservatives also voted for the reduction of the vote, among them being Mr Ritchie, Captain Aylmer, Mr Puleeton, and Baron de Worms. About half-a-dozen votes were agreed to before, at a quarter to six, progress was re- ported. The House resumed, and the Superannuation Bill was read a second time. The Ulster Canal and Tyrone Navigation Bill was read a secoud time. The HOUSE adjourned at five minutes to six. HOUSE OF LORDS.—THDRSDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter-past four o'clock. MISCELLANEOUS.—Lord Salisbury's proposed amendment of a standing order so as to provide tbat la the constructioni Of any railway through the Metropolis or elsewhere there should be compensation given to the poor and working classes who are evicted from their houses, and that the amount of the accommodation available should not be diminished by works of that kind, was ordered by the House of Lords to be printed and taken into consideration on Tues- day.—Lord CARLINGFORD moved the second reading of a bill which had come up from the Commons to establish voting by ballot at elections of Poor-law Guardians in Ire- land, and to make other changes.—fhe rejection of the bill was moved by the Earl of Lonoronn, and upon a division the motion for the rejection was carried by 110 to 41.—Lord Btuaiwnt brought in a bill for the codification of the law of arbitration, and it was read a first time.

I Their Lordships adjourned at a quarter after six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.•—•THORSDLY. The Speaker took the chair shortly before four o'clock. MISCELLANBOUS.—The Marquis of Hartington expressed a fear that a supplementary estimate would be required in connection with the defence of Egypt.—Mr. Dixon-Hartland returned to the subject of the police arrangements for the recent Hyde Park demonstration, for the purpose of com- plaining that be had been stopped on attempting to cross a street at Waterloo Bridge.—The Home Secretary pointed out that a certain amount of inconvenience was inevitable on such an occasion, and the general opinion was that the Ipolice did their duty admirably.—Mr. E. Ashley announced that the Colonial Office had received a telegram from the Governor at the Cape announcing that a resolution had been carried in both Houses of the Legislature affirming the expediency of opening communications with a view to submit a measure for the annexation of Becbuinaland, which would include Stellaland and Goschen.—The Mar- quis of Hartington informed Mr. S. Leighton that the ap- proximate loss of life in Egypt since the occupation was 20,000.—The Prime Minister, who was questioned respect- ing the Conference, stated that the negotiations had not ar- rived at such a point as to enable him to make a statement. Ha hoped after another meeting of the Conference on Mon- day to be able to give some definite information.--Mr. Trevel- Tan announced that the Irish Local Government Board bad determined to dismiss Mr. Elliott from his post as collector for the Blackrock Poor Law Commissioners, who had fallen into arrears and was unable at present to pay up the amount. —The House again went into Committee of Supply, Sir L. Playfair in the chair, and several votes having been agreed to, progress was reported at five minutes tit twelve o'clock. MUNICIPAL ELECTIONS (CORRUPT PRACTICES) BILL.—On the consideration of the Municipal Elections (Corrupt Practices) Bill, Mr. WHITLEY and Mr. S. &diva complained that the maximum scale of expenditure provided in the fifth clause was inadequate.—Mr. NORTHCOTE proposed to amend the clause by increasing the maximum scale of expenditure from £2O to £2s.—The Committee divided—For the amend- ment, 42; against, 95; majority against, 53.—Mr. WARTON proposed several verbal amendments, all of which were nega- tived, and the Bill was read a third time. The House continued sitting until a late hour.

div.head: COTTAGE GARDENING
div.p: COTTAGE GARDENING

CHOPPING BETWEEN POTATOES —Where the most is made of the ground the above arrangement is usually taken advantage of. It answers beat in the case of early and second early crops as they are ready to clear away before the intermediate crop is too far advanced to be interfered with. When the tops of the potatoes grow so as to meet in the rows (which late crops are sure to do), we lay them down in the same direction as the row, so as to admit light and air to the other crop. We are also inclined to think that the potatoe crop is also improved by the operation. When the crop is taken up the tops should be removed either by pulling or cutting them at the surface of the soil. If this is not attended to the operator will discover himself in a fix as he proceeds, and in the end he will see that he has "given himself an extra amount of labour, and has probably destroyed most of the plants forming his inter- mediate crop. AU weeds should be cleared as the potatoes are dug, and the ground left with an even surface. Most planta of the cabbage tribe are all the better for the ground being made firm round their stems, especially the broccoli. It is, therefore, an, excellent plan to tread the soil round them. A few days afterwards the hoe may be ran amongst them just to break the surface. All the crops will be bene- fited by the use of the hoe, as the heavy showers that have descended have a tendency to solidify the surface of the soil. Vegetable marrows, as they come in flower, should have some fresh litter spread on the surface of the soil under them, as it will enable them to set their fruit much better than when they are in contact with the naked earth. I Especially will this be the ease in cold showery weather. The litter on the surface serves another purpose; in dry weather it prevents evaporation, and thus saves a consider- able amount of watering. STRAWBERRY Rurnwsne.—Every effort should be made to layer these, so that the plants may be sufficiently strong to produce fruit next year. The runners that shoot out round the outskirts of the beds are by far the strongest and the most accessible. If, therefore, some rich loose soil is laid three or four inches thick on the ground surface, and the layers placed on, with stones to keep them in their place till rooted, it will be an advantage. Pegs will answer the same purpose as the stones. The layer' will root in about three weeks, when they may be cat off and planted in rows or beds. If the first method is adopted, sufficient should be layered to put three plants where one is usually put. By this means a crop may be expected next year equal to any produced by a two year old plant. Strawberries planted in the ordinary way would yield scarcely anything the first year.

Tag Faoyr Greanxti.—Malching—which signifies the introduction of some additional matter to the surface of the soil, either for the purpose of preventing water escaping from it by evaporation, or with the view of increasing its fertility. If the latter should be desired, the mulching, or top dressing, should contain fertilising ingredients, which may be washed down within reach of the roots. If we applied guano or Clay's fertiliser to the surface of the soil, we would cover it over with an inch or two of soil or some light manure. That may not have much virtue in it, and when any farther applications are needed it may be re- moved and replaced again. It is evident that on a dry, sunny day, after the manure has been previously dissolved by rains or waterings, its strength will be diminished, and the liquid which holds it in solution, before it can be ab- sorbed by the roots, will have escaped in the air. Fresh horse manure, such that has' not undergone fermentation, has proved an excellent material for mulching, inasmuch as it is a certain source of fertility and intercepts evaporation. Roses and Dahlias are benefited by its use, and its efficacy has been perceptible on most herbaoeous plants in the open ground, which form a number of strong roots. We would therefore advise the cottager to avail himself of its assist- ance, for after it has laid on the surface and all the goodness washed out it will still be of service to dig into the soil at the right time. THE WiNnow.—We find some of the Geraniums in the boxes have grown so high that it is unsafe to allow them to remain any longer without support. For neatness no- thing can excel wire, of the desired strength, and painted a pale green. This should be inserted in the soil at the back of the plant, or the side nearest the window, and to these all shoots requiring it should be secured. Geraniums in boxes should not have their tops pinched out at any period of their growth, for that would tend to retard their flower. ing until fresh shoots formed. They usually get bushy enough without having recourse to stopping. This class of plants, which are grown inside the window, should not be allowed to expand any trusses till about three weeks before they are required to be at their best. If they have been placed outside tarn the most defective part of the plant towards the sun and keep it well supplied with weak stimu- lants.

I wonder if I've lost that comb. I wouldn't part with it for a good deal." Replied the youngster: "Why, mamma, what good would a comb be to you if you couldn't 'part' with it ?"—Americanyarer. ,

div.head: FOREIGN NEWS.
div.p: FOREIGN NEWS.

EGYPT AND THE SOUDAN. NEWS OF GENERAL GORDON. Cara% StrstaKw•—•The Maclir of Dongola telegraphs that he has received a despatch from General Gordon, dated June 22nd, stating that Khartoum and Senaar were safe. Gen. I Gordon, who had 8,000 men at Khartoum. asked for rein- forcements. A telegram was received here from Assouan I stating that Colonel Taylor hae made a recognaisance as far as Kourkour, 50 miles distant, but had found no trace of the enemy. Konoszo, SIIIMAY.— General Grenfell and staff arrived here yesterday on a tour of inspection. Native traders are still passing to and from Dongola and Wadi Haifa. They report all quiet and the road safe. Several emissaries of the hiandi have arrived at a village in the neighbourhood of Korosko, and have been dealt with by the police. CAIRO, MONDAY —Lia official telegram from Aesouan says that a merchant has arrived there who reports having left Kordofan two months ago, and Dengola 17 days ago. While in Kordofan he was a good deal with the Mandi, and he ul- timately escaped with Bedawi Khalefa, who was one of Hicks Pasha's lieutenants. The latter, however, only accompanied him as far as Dongola, where he preferred remaining. No objection, the merchant says, was made to his leaving Don- gola, the Madir and inhabitants of which are, according to his report, loyal to the Egyptian Government and hostile to the Mandi. The merchant further states that many of the men of Hicks Pasha's army are now in the hills, aril that the Roman Catholics in the Mandi's power are safe. The artist who accompanied Hicks Pasha's army is also safe. With regard to General Gorden, the merchant states that Khartoum had been surrounded by followers of the Mandi, but that Gordon had defeated them and compelled them to retreat, their leader having been killed. The Mandi's in. Iluence is declared to be declining. The merchant also alleges that letters pass almost daily between General Gordon and the Mabdi. CAIRO, TUBSDAY.—A. company of the 46th Regiment will shortly proceed to Assioat from Kench. It is expected that Major Kitchener will shortly proceed to DOngola. A99017AN, TIIESDAY.—Tbree war steamers, under the com- mand of Captain Boardman, are now being fitted out here for patrolling the Nile. REPORTED 'VICTORY AT DEBBAB. . .

PORTIMOUTH, WIIDNESDA.Y.—The transport Hartkow left here shortly after noon, having on board the 27th Hamp- shire Regiment for Malta, where it will take the place of the Yorkshire Regiment, which is under orders for service in Egypt. Cam, WEDNISDAY.—.4 telegram has been received here from the Mudir of Dongola, in which he states that he has gained a victory over 5,000 followers of the Mandi close to Debbah. A large number ef the rebels were killed, and 300 Remington rifles were captured by the Egyptian trooops. This report is received with some reserve here. The trial by court-martial of the first of the mutineers of of the Turkish battalion was concluded to-day. Judge- ment has not yet been pronounced. SIIMEIM WEDNESDAY.—A Gella spy captured at Saakim was hanged this morning. He admitted that he was justly condemned. Reports are generally current that General Gor- don keeps the rebels between Khartoum and Berber in con- stant terror with his war steamers. Osmal Digna's people do all in their power to counteract this feeling in the district. THE CHOLERA. SPREADING.

PARIS, SATURDAY.—Four deaths from cholera have oc- curred at Arles, in the department of the Bounties du Rhone, two at Sisteron (Basses Alpee), and one at Nimes (Gard.) There have also been three cases of cholera nostrae in Paris, two of which ended fatally. TOULON, SATURDAY.—The Due de Chatres has arrived here from Marseillies, and in the course of the day he visited the St. Mandrier, Bon Rencontre, and Civil Hospitals. In passing through the wards he addressed a few words of encouragement and sympathy to many of the sufferers. lie left with the Mayor 4,000 f, 2,000 f. with the Maritime Pre- fect, 4,000 f. with the principal Catholic clerymen, 500 f. with the Societe des Savateurs. and 200 f. with the Protes- tant clergymen for the relief of the sick and indigena. Twenty-one deaths from cholera have occarred since ten this morning. One of the victims was a Sister of Mercy.—Sun- day, 10 a.m.: There were 31 deaths from cholera here last night, five of which occurred in the Bon Renzontre Hospital, seven in the suburbs, and 19 in the town. The mistral is blowing violently, 6 p.m.: Since eleven o'clock this morn- ing fifteen deaths from cholera have occurred ,here. Eigh- teen more persons have been admitted to the hospitals, where there are 171 cases under treatment. Seven patients have been discharged completely cured. There have been three deaths from cholera at Bignoles.—Monday There were 28 deaths from cholera here last night in the city and suburbs. The mistral has now ceased blowing, and is suc- ceeded by an east wind. 6 p.m.: Twelve deaths from cholera have been registered since ten o'clock to-day. Three cases haveappeared at the village of Vidauban. The record of St. Mauaier Hospital to-day is—Admission 14, con- valescents, 11, deaths two, under treatment 122. The mistral is again blowing. MARSEILLES, SATURDA.Y.—The official bulletin issued this evening gives the number of deaths during the last twenty- four hours as 119, of which 65 were from cholera.—Sunday: The Chamber of Commerce has voted 10,00 francs in aid of the sufferers from the epidemic. The official bulletin issued this evening gives the number of deaths during the last 24 hours as 118, of which 61 were from cholera. Wasatworrole, SUNDAY.—The Cabinet has decided to take prompt and vigorous measures against the cholera. The State and Treasury Departments will act in concert in en- forcing the regulations. The importation of rags from in- fected countries will be prohibited for 90 days or longer. MARSEILLES, TUESDAY, 6-35 P.M.—Since 11 O'clock this morning 11 additional deaths from cholera have been regis- tered here, making a total of 49 since eight o'clock yester- day evening. Toe position shows a slight improvement. TOULON, TUESDAY.—There were 28 deaths from cholera in the city and suburbs last night.--6.30 P.m.—Fourteen deaths from cholera have occurred to-day in the city and suburbs. Thirty•eight cases are under treatment in the Bon Rencontre, and 128 in the St. Mandried Hospital. A Local Government Board order is gaaetted prohibiting the import of rags exported from Marseilles and Toulon. PARIS, TUESDAY.—The Director of Public Aid formally announced yesterday that no Asiatic or sporadic cholera had been reported in the hospitals. There has been no case ot cholera here since yesterday. One case is reported from Lyons. ROME, TUESDAY.—The Italian Government has resolved to maintain the quarantine on the Swiss frontier. MARSEILLES, WEDNESDAY, 940 a.m.—Tvrenty-one deaths from cholera were registered here last night. MARSEILLES, WEDNESDAY, 11-20 A 1.1. Nine deaths from cholera have been registered here since nine o'clock this morning. TOULON, WEDNESDAY, 10-15 AM.—There were 15 deaths from cholera here last night, of which eight occurred in the city. Several chemists and druggists threaten to close their shops in consequence of the gratuitous distribution of medi- cines by the Municipality. FRANCE AND MADAGASCAR. - - -

Pints, MONDAY.—A long discussion took place in the Chamber of Deputies to-day upon the credits asked for by the Government on account of the Madagascar expedition. M. Perin criticised the report of the committee, m hich he thought had a warlike tone. Mgr. Treppel, Bishop of An- glers, approved the policy of the Government with regard to Madagascar, and declared that a protectorate over the whole island ought to be proclaimed, and a grand blow struck. Admiral Peyron, Minister of Marine aud Colonies, stated that, in addition to Tarnatave and Majanga, Admiral Miot would occupy such points as be might deem necessary. M. Jules Ferry reminded the Chamber of its vote of March 27th with reference to Madagascar, and felt sure that the House would not wish to change its policy or show any signs of hesitation. With a credit of five millions of francs there could be no question of carrying out a more extended programme, which, moreover, the Government had not at the present moment any reason to take into consideration.— The credit of five million francs was then adopted by 372 votes to 93.

div.head: FRANCE AND CHINA.
div.p: FRANCE AND CHINA.

- SHANGHAI, MONDAY,--A respite of five days has been granted, pending ndgotiations between the Viceroy at Nan- kin and M. Patendtre, at Shanghai.—Tidies. PARIS, SATURDAY.-At a Cabinet Council held this morn- ing, M. Ferry explained the state of the negotiations with China. It appears certain that China will shortly give satisfaction to France in regard to the indemnity demanded by the latter Power. 'The Tempt of this evening says it
t.oPt 111 E EXA

has reason to believe that the reply of the Chinese Govern- ment to the French ultimatuJa will be laid before the Cham- bers next week. PARIS, TURSDAT.—At the Cabinet Council to-day, M Ferry announced that negociations with China were pro- gressing favourably, and a prompt solution was expected. THE PORTE AND THE POSTAL SYSTENI. CONSTANTINOPLB, SUNDAY.—The Porte has sent a cir- cular-note to the six great Powers to the effect that, all the necessary measures having been taken for the regular convey- ance of the mail-bags between Constantinople and Varna, the Porte intends to do away with the foreign post offices in Turkey, which up to the present have been tolerated, but not authorised, by the Imperial Government. Turkey has never failed to protest against the existing state of things, which is an infringement oi the sovereign rights of the Sultan. CONSPIRACY AT WARSAW.—ARREST OF 100 PERSONS. BRRLIN, SATURDAY.—A private telegram from Warsaw reports that the discovery of the plot against the life of the Czar has led to the arrest of upwards of a hundred persons, including Russians, Servians and Bulgarians. VIENNA, MONDAY.—lntelligence received from Warsaw states that the large Schostenski gunpowder mill in the Czeringov district has been blown up by Nihilists and en- tirely destroyed. SOUTH AFRICA. DURBAN. MONDAY.—The present condition of the Znln Reserve is described as being deplorable. About 1,000 rebels have collected there, centred in Inkankhla. under Dabala- manzi. These roam about as they please. simply evading the troops when in movement against them by passing round them. It is confidentally believed that the Usutus will fall out with the Boers when the latter assume the occupancy of their farms in Central Zululand. FRIGHTFUL RAILWAY ACCIDENT IN THE UNITED STATES. Nsw YORE. SUNDAY:A fearful railway accident, resul- ting in great loss of life, occurred late on Saturday night, near Canton, Ohio. A train was returning by the Canton Valley line from Ctiyahoma Falls with a party of two thou• sand persons. who had been pic-nicking at the Falls. The holiday-makers were chiefly men employed at Aultman's Agriculture Works, Canton, with their wives and families, and they had been out for their annual pleasure excursion. As the train, heavily laden with its freight of human beings, approached Canton, the second section left the rails and top- pled over the embankment, into a pond below. Many were crushed to death, while others were drowned. A telegram received here states that two hundred persons have been killed and injured, but the proportion of loss of life does not appear to be yet ascertained.

THE SUEZ CANAL. PARIS, TITIISDAY.—M. de Lesseps has Informed the French Academy of Science that the International Technical Com- mission has pronounced in favour of widening the Suez Canal and against the construction of a new one. THE CAPTIVE CREW. AMSTERDAM, TUBSDAY.—Despatches are published to-day concerning the Nisero affair. In the last despatch, the Dutch Minister advocates the closing of some of the ports near Tenour, in order to induce the natives to co-operate in the Anglo-Dutch Ultimatum. THE PANAMA CANAL SCHEME. Pants, WEDNESDAY.—A general meeting of shareholders of the Panama Canal Company was held to-day. The re- port of the directors and their proposals were adopted unanimously, M. Dingier, Director of Works, affirmed that the Canal was making excellent progress, and would be ready for opening in 1888. Holders of 100,000 shares attended the meeting. WRECKS OF STEAMERS.—REPORTED LOSS OF 90

LIVES MADRID, WEDNESDAY—NO further particulars have been received concerning the collision between the Spanish steamer Gijon and the English steamer Laxharn, near Cor- onas. It is stated that of the 56 persons picked up by the Spanish steamer Santo Domingo, 11 are English. Accord- ing to intelligence from Comma, dated Monday evening, the English steamer Huelva has been wrecked off Calmar. boss. The crew were saved. An official despatch states that before the steamers Lax- ham and Gijon foundered they launched their boats, in which 160 persons, passengers and seamen embarked. Of these 56 were picked dp by the steamer Santo Domingo, but nothing has vet been heard of the two boats, containing up- wards of 90 people. Several boats have been sent out in search of them. MADRID. WEDNRSDAY.—Among the persons saved from the steamer Laxham and landed at Corunna were two ladies. Up to the present no news has heel received of the fate of the remaining passengers and crew of the steamers Gijon and Durham. It is estimated that there must have been some 200 personiNon board the Gijon. The mails were lost. The number of persons on board the Laxham is un- known. CONFERENCE OF INDEPENDENT REPUBLICANS. NEW YORK, TUESDAY EVENING.—The Conference of In- dependent Republicans met here to-day. Resolutions were adopted deprecating the organisation of anew party, favour- ing an appeal for honest government, and endorsing tke can- didature of Governor Cleveland for the Presidency.
BELGIUM AND TEIE VATICAN.- BRUSSELS, THURSDAY AFTHRHOON.—In the Chamber to-day, the Government introduced a bill providing for the resumption of diplomatic relations with the Holy Sea.
THE MANCHESTER_ SHIP _CANAL.

---- -- On Monday the Manchester Ship Canal Committee en- tered upon the third week of the inquiry and proceeded to hear further evidence in support of the petition presented against the scheme by the Mersey Dock and Harbour Board. Mr. Sclater•Booth was in the chain—Captain Graham Hills, marine surveyor to the Mersey Dock and liarb mr Board, who was under examination the greater part of Friday, in continuation of his evidence entered into details of the works on the river Seine, and said that in consequence of the construction of the training walls, there bad not only been enormous accretions behind the training walls, higher than the walls themselves, but also accretions in the river below the training walls, and a silting up of the entrance to the harbour of Havre. . .

On Tuesday Mr. Pember resumed his cross-examination of Captain Graham Hills, R.N.—Mr. George F. Lyster, engineer to the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board, stated that there were fifty-ene docks at Liverpool. The acreage of the Birkenhead system of docks was 506 acres, and the combined area of the two dock estates on both sides of the river was about 1,584 acres. Witness said his objection to the canal was that it would interfere with the upper reaches of the Mersey, and if that plan was carried out, it would ultimately destroy the efficiency of the dock estate and the approaches to the river. On Wednesday the committee heard farther evidence in opposition to the bill. Sir W. Thompson, F.R.S., was ex- amined with the view of showing that the proposed estuary works would be exceedingly injurious to the bar and to the port of Liverpool.—Mr. R. Manning, chief engineer to the Board of Public Works in Ireland, said he had carefully ex- amined the estuary of the Mersey. The proposed works would cause silting up and reduce the effect of the scour. The present channel was a wandering one, and in its action had a beneficial effect. The works would, no doubt, be in- jurious to the bar. He thought there would be great diffi- culty in completing the undertaking.—Mr. Vernon Harcourt, CE., London, agreed with the previous witness that the re- sult of placing training walls in the estuary of the Mersey would he to cause accretion behind the walls, and owing to the reduction of the tidal capacity, the channels beyond Liverpool would be injured. It would lead to a reduction in the depth over the bar.

div.head: PENISTONE RAILWAY ACCIDENT.
div.p: THE PENISTONE RAILWAY ACCIDENT.

At Penistone, on Saturday, the inquest on the bodies of the persons killed in the recent disaster was resumed. Mr. Charles Sacre, chiet engineer of the company, in his evi- dence, said no examination by the engineman or other per- son could have revealed the flaw in the crank axle before the engine started. He believed it was a growing fracture. The inquest was again adjourned. Major Marindin, the Board of Trade Inspector, visited the scene of the accident on Saturday. The work of clearing the wreckage from the embankment and highway at the scene of the railway accident has been completed. The injured persons under treatment at Manchester Royal Infirmary were reported on Monday to be on the whole in rather an improved condition. The interment of the re- mains of Mrs. Rawlings, one of the victims of the Penistone disaster, took place at the Willow Grove Cemetery, Red- dish, on Monday afternoon, in the presence of several thou- sand spectators.

On Wednesday, at the half-yearly meeting of the Man- chester, Sheffield, and Lincolnshire Railway Company, re- ference was made by the Chairman (Sir E. W. Watkin), to the recent accident on the Company's line at Penistone. To everybody concerned that accident had, he said, given the deepest pain and sorrow. On the mere pecuniary question —which, after all, paled into insignificance in the presence of the suffering that had occurred—they were advised that the accident was one which could not have been foreseen or provided against, and that, therefore, there was no pecuniary liability; but he had instructed the secretary, for himself and not for the shareholders, to oiler relief in different direc- tions in urgent and sad cases of poverty and difficulty. It would be satisfactory to the shareholders to know that so far as the inquiry, which had been searching, had gone, no blame was attributed to the company. The Chairman made some noteworthy observations on the question as to whether the speed of trains might not be reduced with ad- vantage.

Klux', By LICRITNISG..—. Nottingham was on Thursday visited by a severe thunderstorm. James Harris, a milk- man, was selling milk to some men, when he was struck by lightning, which set fire to his hair and passed down the left side of his body, causing instant death. THIIRIMB ATTEMPTED DOUBLE MIIRDEII.—At the Thames Police Court, London, on Thursday, Thomas Sullivan, labourer, of Blackwell, was charged with attempting to mur- der his two children on Wednesday, by cutting open their heads with a chopper. The children are in a dangerous condition. The prisoner, who had been drinking, was remanded. TIM CROWN PRINCE AND PRINCESR OE GERMANY.— The Crown Prince and Princess ot Germany, with their three youngest daughters. arrived at Sheerness on Thursday morning fron Flushing in the Royal yacht Osborne. A large naval and military staff were present to receive their Im- perial Highnesses, but as they were travelling incognita no formalities were observed. The Crown Prince and Princess proceeded to London.
