(Cheers.) MR. CHAMBERLAIN AT Tan DEVONSHIRE CLUB. Mr. Chamberlain, M.P., was present on Wednesday night at a house dinner of the Devonshire Club, and made an interes- ting speech on public topics. The right hon. gentleman chiefly dealt with the rejection of the Franchise Bill by the House of Lords. After a powerful and telling criticism of Lord Salisbury's speech at Sheffield, the President of the Boyd of Trade proceeded to sum up the advantages that would accrue to the Liberal party from the present agita- tion. They should educate the new voters before they were called upon to exercise their political rights to distinguish' their friends from their foes, and they would not be slew to see the difference between Tory professions and Liberal performances. Another result would be that Lord Salisbury would not be able success- fully to assert his claim to dissolve the House of Commons whenever it was not servile enough to agree with the House of Lords. He could not, however, escape the challenge he had thrown down, and in the course of the next autumn on every platform, in every household, there would be a discussion as to the past history and the future prospects of the House of Lords. In any case the course of the Liberal party was clear. They had in all the calmness of conscious strength, and in the assurance of cer- tain victory, to pursue the constitutional issues wh:ch Lord Salisbury had raised, and to sweep away the obstacles which now cut off a vast multitude of unenfranchised men from the political rights to which by universal consent they were entitled. They had also to assert the supremacy of popular rights and representative institutions over personal authority and hereditary privilege. MR HERBERT GLADSTONE, M.P., AT LEEDS.—E. demons- tration, convened by the Leeds Liberal Association and at- tended by about 15,000 or 20,000 people, was held on Sat- urday, in Victoria-square, Leeds to protest against the action of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franchise Bill. Mr. Kitson, the chairman of the association, presided.—A resolution pledging the meeting to support the Government was supported by Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., who warned his hearers that they must not confuse the issues which were before them. Mr. Goscben bad said that there were two questions—one of the Reform Bill and the other of the opposition of the House of Lords. That was true.l But they must not join those two questions together. Let 1 them deal with one and finish it before they come to the I other. The House of Lords had been guilty of incredible' and astonishing stupidity, and if he mistook not, before that venerable House was much more venerable it would have re- pented of its mistake in dust and ashes. There one object of the present time should be the passage of the Reform Bill. To divert the attention of the party from that one all-impor- tant point must essentially weaken their position. For the present at any rate their one motto should be "Victory for reform." (Cheers.)—The resolution was carried amid great cheering.

LETTERS FROM TORY LElDERS.—Letters have been re- ceived by Mr. E. Waddington from the Marquis of Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote in answer to the resolutions which were passed at an open-air meeting at Barrow :—Lord Salisbury says: The working-men fully undqrstand that the House of Lords is not opposing in any sense the exten- sion of the franchise, but that they are contending that the representation which that enlargement of the franchise pro- duces shall be equitable and genuine. I concur with you in earnestly hoping that the House of Lords will not yield.— Sir Stafford Nortlacote writes: "I am confident that if the working-men of this country are independent enough to ex- ercise their own judgment at the present crisis they will see that the real contest lies not (as is foolishly said) between the Peers and the people, but between the country and the Caucus. There is no difference of opinion as to the pro- priety of extending the Franchise; the question is whether the Reform measures are to be manipulated as to suit the purposes of the wirepullers, and to cover the faults of the Ministry."

A stormy meeting was held on Monday night in Darling- ton Town Hall, convened by the Conservative party, and addressee in support of the action of the House of Lords were delivered amid considerable interruption and increasing excitement. Upon a resolution being submitted, a working man offered an amendment, but he was hustled off the plat- form.

1 Mr. Gladstone's " Midlothian campaign" is, as at present I arranged, to consist of two speeches, both to be delivered in the city of Edinburgh, one on Saturday the 30th August,„. and the other on Monday the Ist September. 1 Mr. R.. Leaks, M.P. was the principal speaker at two de- monstrations held on Thursday evening in support of the , Franchise Bill, and in condemnation of the conduct of the House of Lords, at Wardle, near Rochdale, and at Heywood. 1 Resolutions were passed urging the Government not to dis- solve until " the Peers have yielded to the just demands of the people," and expreasing the opinion that the unchecked powerof impeding and obstructing the popular will at present exercised by the House of Lords is not conducive either to the welfare of the people or the peace and prosperity of the country. The General Committee of the Widnes Liberal A9SOCiII. tien, at their meeting on Thursday, resolved as follows : " That an open-air public meeting be bald to protest against the acticn of the House of Lords in rejecting the Franchise Bill, and to support the Gevernment in their intention of holding an autumn session to reintroduce the measure, and that Saturday, the 2nd of August, be the date fixed." A franchise agitation demonstration, attended by many thousands of persons, was held on Thursday night in the Market Place, Leicester, in support of the Franchise Bill. Processions, headed by bands and carrying banners, , marched from the seven wards of the borough to the place of meeting, where two platforms had been erected. The Earl of Sandwich presided on Thursday at a meet- ing of the Huntingdon and Godmanchester Conservative Association, and explained that be voted against the Fran- chise Bill only because it was incomplete without redistri- bution. He thought the recent demonstration in London would have no effect at all upon the House of Lords. The Marske and Saltburn Conservative Associaticn have resolved that the House of Lords has acted in the true in- terests of the country, and has earned the gratitude of the people. At a meeting of Liberals, held on Thursday night at Ex- eter, a resolution of confidenee in the Government and cen- suring the action of the Lords, was carried by a large majority. Disorderly proceedings took place on Thursday evening at Bournemouth, at a meeting convened to protest against the rejection of the bill. On the doors of the Town Hall being opened, there was a rush for the platform. Fighting ensued, and the disturbance lasted without intermission for an hour and a half, chairs and tables being smashed, and several gentlemen being, roughly handled. Eventually, some hun- dreds of Liberals proceeded to the pier, where speeches were delivered by Mr. H. Davey and Mr. Bryce.
HINTON.

.SIIDDEN DEATH.,--AS Isabella Hewitson, 47 years of age, wife of a gardener named Henry Hewitson, was going about her work on Thursday morning week, she complained to her daughter of feeling unwell, and immediately fell down; medical assistance was obtained, but she died that afternoon about four o'clock, without having recovered consciousness. Her death was certified as caused by paralysis. The remains were interred in Huvton cemetery on Monday afternoon by the Rev. Canon Pen*rhyn. A preliminary service at her late residence was performed by Mr. Varley, Wesleyan Min- ister. A large circle of sympathising friends were in atten- dance.

SEIPWRICCE AND Loss OF NINE Livits —A Wick tele— grain reports that the ship Vicksburg, of Leith, has gone. ashore on Pentland Skerries, and to,come a total wreck. N in, of the crew were lost. The captain and elevsn men were saved.

On Thursday at the County Magistrates' Court, Liver- pool, Mary Ellen Pennington, a cook in service at Waterloo, was committed for trial at the assizes, charged with the wilful murder of her infant child, on the night of the 20th May last. BROILERS IMPRISONHD.—David APGregor and Alexander James Pringle, wool brokers in Leith, were indicted in thn High Court of Justiciary in Edinburgh, on Monday, for fraudulent trading. They pleaded guilty to some ot the accusations, but attributed their default to the desire to prevent a stoppage of their business. The Lord Justice Clerk passed sentence of twelve months' imprisonment upon , each.
DEATH OF AN OLD FaXEMASON.—PhiIip Chethare, the

_ oldest Freemason in England, and it is supposed, in the world, has just died at Southport. He was in his 97th year, and was initiated a Freemason in 1811. He had been past master of Lodge 322 since 1811, and was secretary for over 50 years. In 1802 be volunteered on board his Majesty's guardship Phoebe, and was at Trafalgar, though not in action.
WINDFALL TO A BANK Poi:alma —Letters nf administra-

ton have been granted to the heir-at-law of the late Mr. F. J. Sumner, mill proprietor, Glossop, who died intestate,. suddenly, in London, a few weeks ago. The personal estate is sworn under £570,000, and will he divisable among the first cousins, of whom five or six are known to be alive, and one of them is William Sumner, porter for many years at the National Provincial Bank, Newcastle, an elderly man with a, family.

Tiles SENDERLAND MURDER. —A. young man named - James Soulsby was sentenced to death at Durham on Satur- day for the murder of T. Ledwick, at Sunderland. The, prisoner killed the man by striking him on the head with a. hammer. The jury recommended him to mercy, but Mr. Justice Manisty characterised the murder as cruel, cold— blooded, and cowardly, and warned the prisoner not to hold out the slightest hope on the recommendation given by the- jury.

EXTRAORDINARY ACCIDENT TO A YOUNG WaxAsr.—On- Wednesday night, in Caleder Works, Dundee, Agnes Call, a young woman, was combing her hair and was throwing it back over her bean, when the tresses, which were un— usually long, were caught by a revolving belt and the poor girl was caught up and thrown several times round tbie shaft before tbe machinery could be stopped. She was. nearly scalped, and lies in the Infirmary in a precarious/ state. A ROMANTIC ELOPEMENT.—A young gentleman, the Mb Of wealthy parents, residing near Northop, Flint. who has just seen his 17th birthday, fell in love with a charming young lady of Mold, three years his senior, and, as the con— templated union was not likely to receive the paternal bene— diction, the interesting couple eloped to Liverpool. The parents, however, got scent of their whereabouts, hurriedly- followed them, and succeeded in inducing them to returta home. The young wanderers still swear unalterable fealty and love.

PRESENTATION TO GENERAL GRAIIAM.-011 Saturday Jarrow was filled to overflowing by people of all sorts and. sonditions met to witness the presentation of a sword of honour to Lieut.-General Sir Gerald Graham, in recognition of his distinguished services to the country. The gift was subscribed for by the officers and men of the Newcastle Engineer Volunteers, of which corps Lie.t.-Colonel C. M. Palmer, M.P., is the commandant. Colonel C. M. Palmer, M.P., in making the presentation, referred to the former con— nection of General Graham with the volunteer movement is the North of England, and to his brilliant achievements is the Soudan.

ACCODCHEMENT OF THE DUCHESS OF ALBLEY.—The. Court Circular, dated "Claremont, Sunday," says :—" The. Queen, attended by the Hon. Horatio Stopford, arrived at Claremont yesterday evening at twenty minutes before nine. The Dutims of Albany was safely delivered of a prince at twenty-five minutes past eleven. her Majesty was wit!) Her Royal Highness the whole time. Both the Duchess and infant prince are going on as well as possible. The Right. Hon. Sir W. V. Harcourt. Secretary of State, certified the prince's birth. This event bas caused the Queen the most lively satisfaction, and is a cause of deep thankfulnes to Her Majesty."

CONSEREATIER CONFERENCE. A Conference of the National Union of Conservative Associations was held on- Wednesday at Sheffield, under the presidency of Lord Ran- dolph Churchill, M.P. The proceedings were private, but reports have nevertheless been published. A resolution was- adopted on the motion of Mr. A. B. Forwood, of Liverpool. expressing a wish to see the National Union more truly re- presentative, and remitting to the Council the task of pre- paring a scheme of reform. Out of the 36 members elected.- for the new Council it is understood that fully two-thirds.- are prepared to support the member for Woodstock when her shall be proposed as chairman, in opposition either to Earl Percy, M.P., or any other gentlemen. The Duke of Nor- folk was elected President of the Union in succession to the Earl of Dartmouth. FLOODING OF A FLINTSHIEH COLLIERY.—Mostyn Colliery, lying between Rhyl and Chester, was suddenly flooded on Tuesday night. Fortunately 11000 of the miners were at work at the time, but all the animals kept underground were drowned. Powerful pumps were set to work, and late the same night two men went down in the cage to see whether they were having any effect in reducing the depth of water. Before they had descended far, however, a tremendous ex plosion of displaced gas took place, and the cage with the. two men in it was blown high into the air. One of the men fell back into the shaft, and his body has not since keen recovered. The other is shockingly burnt about the face. On Wednesday night the water was gaining, ard the- [colliery is now closed. Nearly 400 workpeople are thrown- out of employment by the occurrence. MILL FIRE AT WIGAN: £20,000 DAY AGES. What is known as Old Mill, forming part of the Sovereign Spring , I Mills, Wigan, the property of the execmo-s of the late Mr. Thomas Knowles, M.P., was destroyed by fire on Thursday morning. The mill, which was a handsome structure, has been almost refilled with new machinery on being purchasert by Mr. Knowles. and in it employment was found for some. - 250 hands. Flames broke out at half past eleven in the- mule room on the third storey, and although the mill is only a few hundred yards from the fire station, the whole room was one mass of flames before the engines reached the- spot. Efforts had to be directed to saving the surroanding buildings, and these were successful. By one o'clock little remained of the burning mill except two ends, the side walls falling on the burning debris. The property is insure& The damage is roughly estimated at £20,000. The operatives managed to make their escape from the mill in safety. Pannwm. DINNER To Witsros.—On Monday night a dinner on diet reform principles was given to E. P. The 3rd Lanark won the Belgian Challenge Cup, and the 2nd Midlothian the. Battalion Sweepstakes. For the Vizianagram Challenges Cup the Commons were victorious, beating the Lords' team by 63 points, and with a total of 450 points out of a possible • 500. On Monday the most interesting competition was that for the Mal lens Prizes. Twenty-nine teams, representing various Volunteer battalions, took part in the contest. They advanced at the word of command over unknown distances, firing from three points of their advance, first in any posi- tion, next kneeling, then standing at movable targets repre- senting Men. The let Berks, who won last year, again gained the first prize of £lOO with 38 hits. the 50 Lance.- natreheLdibalriisnoi-.1.17r shire taking the second prize of £6O with 37 hits. On Toes- P. In the competition for the United Service Cup. the Volunteers were successful, and in that for the Chan- cellor's Challenge Plate the Cambridge University team beat the Oxford team. The Elcho Challenge Shield was shot for at Wimbledon on Thursday. Again it goes to Ireland. The snores were :—lreland 1,583; Scotland, 1,476; alad. England, 1,414.

ODDFELLOWS' ANNITESSIOZY AT ROBY —On Monday, Club day at Roby was disappointing in regard to the weather, which materially interfered with the annual display; but in spite of the rain about forty members marched in procession, headed by the Huyton Volunteers k2nd Engineer) Band, through Roby and Huy. ton, calling at the vicarages, and eventually reach- ing the Stanley Arms Rotel, where an excellent dinner awaited them. The chair was taken by Mr. H. Makin, treasurer of the Prescot district, vice-chairman P.P.G.M. Brennand. The usual loyal toasts were duly honoured. That of the bishop and clergy was replied to by the Rev. G. .1. Banner, and the Rev. Canon Penrhyn also briefly spoke. This was followed by "The Manchester Unity," and "Board of Directors," coupled with the name of Mr. J. Mater, who suitably responded. The " Prescot District and Officers " was responded to by P.P.G.M. Makin. Lie said the position of the district was very good. Their nett gain in funds for the past year amounted to £471, making their cash and pro- perty value now £10,410; average worth per member in the district £8 7s 6d, their members numbering 1,243. The "Loyal Lord Stanley Lodge" was well received, and the secretary, Mr. Henry Mame, gave a summary of the ac- counts. The proceedings were enlivened with songs and music, and afterwards a dance was kept up till the early hours, to the strains of Pinnington and Atherton's String Band.

CLAIM FOE Pnitscrrat the St. Helens before Mr. T. P. E. Thornp- County Court, on Wednesday, son, judge, a tub dealer named Patrick Murphy, residing IR Waterloo-street, sought to recover £7 from George Barker, a labouring man'residing in the same neighbourhood, for per- sonal injuries sustained through the action of the defendant. —The plaintiff was represented by Mr. Swift and Mr. Riley appeared for the defendant —lt was stated that some time ago the plaintiff was taking care at some pigeons at the public-house of Thomas Mills, Bridge-street, and the defen- dant entered with a pigeon in his hand, stating that it was one of Mr. Mills's. The plaintiff and defendant accordingly went into the back yard, and the former mounted a ladder to look . into the pigeon cote. It was alleged that whilst he was on the ladder the defendant for a bit of *devilment," as it was termed. pulled the ladder away, and the plaintiff fell. Ile alighted with his face on some bricks, and sustained such injuries as necessitated medical attendance for three or four weeks.— The defence was the occurrence happened accidentally. It was stated that a man was " swilling " the yard with water, and the defendant, in order to escape the water, jumped on the ladder, which fell over.—After hearing the evidence, His Honour took the defendant's view of the case, and gave a decisien accordingly.

div.head: EXAMINER.
div.p: THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JULY 26, 1884.

THE Reform Agitation is all that it should be ; it is far-reaching, resolute and strong, and is being conducted with the moderation and good temper of men who are confident of victory. The demonstration in London on Konday was unprecedented in many ways; it was unprecedented in the vast numbers who took part in it, reaching into hundreds of thousands; in the orderly character of the processions and meetings; in the " wit and wisdom" of the mottoes on the banners; and in the self-sacrifice of thousands of agricul- tural and other labourerewho denied them- selves so much in order to swell the ranks of

the reformers and give the lie to those who have again and again asserted that they were indifferent to the Franchise Bill. There is the same feeling all over the country; great meetings have been held and others are about to be held. Warrington showed itself in earnest last week, though it has yet another word to speak on the subject; the working- men of Runcorn gathered together in their thousands in the open air on Saturday; the men of Widnes meet on Saturnav next; and St. Helens, which has had one large meeting in support of the Government, is about to have another. Birmingham and Bristol have spoken with no uncertain sound; Man- chester is to make its voice heard to-day. with JOHN BRIGHT, the tribune of the people, in the front, as of old; and, as Lord WEMYSS admitted would be the case if the Lords refused to surrender, Reform is in the air from John O'Groats to Land's End. The Conservatives, on the other hand, are dis- couraged and dismayed. The bulk of them are wiser than their leader; they hesitate to follow Lord SALISBURY in his mad career; they are more in touch with their countrymen, and hence the ludicrous response to the " order " for "indignation meetings," which has been issued from the "Conservative Central Office at Westminster." It is true there have been a few meetings at which vague resolutions of protest against the con- duct of the Government have been carried, but these have been passed for the most part within the entrenchments of political clubs. Toryism does not want to fight in the open; it is not prepared just at present to take the field. But Lord SALISBURY is militant; he has crossed the river and burnt his boats, and we do not doubt that he is ready to sac- rifice both himself and his party rather than yield. We give him credit for knowing what he is struggling for; he wants to be Prime Minister of England, and he believes he will have a good chance of attaining the object of his ambition, if he can force a dissolu- tion upon the present register. It is nothing to him that his course is unconstitutional; for the new-fangled Tory is undeniably a Revolu. tionist. Conservatives in the House of Com- mons have violated the Constitution, and still violate it,by preventing a duly-elected member taking his seat; and why should the House of Lords not have a turn? There are some Conservative supporters of Lord SALISBURY —real Conservatives—who do no see at pre- sent all that is involved in the issue; but they will open their eyes by-and-by; and then, we fear, his lordship will be left in the lurch as he has been before. We say we fear this will be the result, and be use the word advisedly, for if Lord S A LISBURY'S followers refuse to follow when the Franchise Bill is re-presented to the Upper House in the autumn session, this, as any rate,.vvill follow —that the Bill will become law, and there may in consequence be an, end fora time of the agitation against the House of Lords The best thing that could happen for the Liberal party, and therefore for the country, is that the Peers should continue antagonistic to the People sufficiently long to put the agitation against them on such a basis that Mr. GLADSTONE would be returned to power pledged to the Reform of the House of Lords. It is a work that must be done soon or later, and better soon than later. Indeed, as matters now stand, it is made evident whilst we are at the beginning of the conflict that the nation will not be at rest until such a change has taken place that it will be no longer posssble for an irresponsible body of men to mar and mutilate, "without either rhyme or reason," the , work of the responsible representatives of the people. Lord SALISBURY'S reference to the House of Lords as the fly-wheel of the mac- hine of State is far-fetched and prepos• terous ; for whoever heard of a fly-wheel that was allowed to bring a machine to a stand just at the busiest time and when most work was required of it? A fly-wheel in any of our Lancashire mills or workshops with such pro- pensities would quickly be relegated to the room for old lumber, which is perhaps the best thing that could be done with the House of Lords Lord SALISBURY, in his speech at Sheffield, on Tuesday, further said that "the other House was interfering with its own con- stitution," and "encroaching on the powers and rights of the people who sent them to it." And whose constitution should it inter- fere with, if not its own ? And how does his lordship make if out that it is constitutional for the Upper House to interfere with this so-called interference? It will be soon enough for the Peers to cry out when their "own constitution" is being revised, and we I trust they will have occasion ere long. Can it be that they perceive the shadow of coming events, and think it as well to cry out before they are hurt? But what an abuse of terms to speak of an extension of the fran- chise as an encroachment on the powers of the people! As well tell hungry men when they are being fed that the means taken to supply them with food is a trespass upon their rights. Lord SALISBURY may, as Lord BEACONSFIELD said of him, be a master of flouts and jibes and jeers, but he is not a sound reasoner, and he is often so utterly in- sincere that there is no wonder the astute Jew, with such men in his eye, should at one time have described the Conservative party as an organised hypocrisy. It will be a sorry day for England if ever Lord SALISBURY is appointed Prime Minister, and, believing this, it is the duty of all men who wish well to their country to labour hard and long at the present juncture to prevent such a calamity.

The Miners of St. Helens are on strike not only against the propos ,c 1 reduction of wages, I but against the decision of their representa- tives assembled in Conference at Wigan last week. The men met on Saturday and were practically unanimous in protesting against the decision of the Conference that work should be resumed at the ten per cent reduc- tion except at four firms in the Wigan district. The plan of the delegates would seem to be to fight the battle in detail, having little or no hope of winning if the strike at the pre- sent juncture is to be on an extensive scale. The Conference met again on Tuesday, and after what is described as "a long and dis- orderly debate," it was resolved by gz votes to 70 to adhere to the policy of bringing out the men at four large firms which were named. On Tuesday forenoon there was a mass meet- ing of colliers at Parr, and another in the afternoon at St. Helens, at both of which the advice of the delegates was rejected. It may be said that the representatives themselves were not united, and that the majority by which the decision to resume work in certain districts was carried was not a lame one. Still there was a majority in its favour, and it may fairly be put to the miners of St. Helen whether the minority or the majority should rule. No doubt they feel it will be a great hardship to submit even for a time to a ten per cent. reduction, but better that, with a chance of winning in the end, than, through ill. organis ed resistnce, find themselves

beaten in a short time all along the line. Our sympathies are certainly with the men in the struggle for maintaining the old rate of wages. The collier's life is a hard one; he wastes, as SHELLEY has it, "a sunless life in the unwholesome mine," and certainly deserves all he gets. But if they would succeed, .the miners must be united. "A house divided against itself cannot stand ;" and we can see no hope of success if the decisions of a representative body are to be set aside by district meetings. If it be true that less than one fourth of the colliers of St. Helens are members of the union, how can they hope to achieve a victory, after cutting themselves off, as they will have done, from the miners of other parts of the country? 'United, they may stand; divided, they will certainly fall.

The Manchester Ship Canal scheme is un- doubtedly a heavy undertaking, but it would seem after all to have a light side ;• it is a grave subject, and vet it is not without its comic aspects. This at any rate would ap- pear to be the opinion of the people of War- rington, for they devoted Wednesday evening last to two farces with the Ship Canal as the basis of them. No. r, which was the longer and the more entertaining, was that in which Mr. WILLIAM DIG GLE appeared as author and leading actor, at the Co-operative Hall. There was a tolerably large audience who had paid for admission—all of course "for the fun of the thing," and they had plenty for their money. Nobody takes Mr. DIGGLE seriously, although he has terrible things to say about the Canal. The audience chaffed, and DIGGLs chaffed, and there was chaff all round. The piece ran, as Lord SALISBURY would say, "charmingly ;" or, as the " professionals" would say, it went "immense," considering that it was unrehearsed and a "first night." Farce No. 2 was " produced" at the Town Hall, and was played by Councillors and Aldermen, who had met to contribute, if need be, £5OO towards the Ship Canal Scheme in the shape of " ane penny in the pound on the rateable value of the borough." This piece had been particu- larly well advertised, for had not our "neutral " contemporary turned resurrec- tionist for the occasion, disinterring cer- tain skeleton speeches by way of " beat- ing the big drum ?" But the fun of it all was that "it did not come off' according to the announcement. "The LORD CHAMBERLAIN," or somebody, nr something, had interposed, and given notice of prohibition. The Esoo could not be given in this way, and there was nobody in the humour just then to steal a march on his fellows by giving it in any other. Some of our "most potent, grave, and reverend , seigniors " saw where the laugh came in, but there were some who couldn't, mistaking the farce evidently for a tragedy It was patent to all, however, that they had nothing to do. and they did it. They were in the pickle that one of the heroes of "The Ingoldsby Legends" found himself, and acted accord- ingly—
Thcre was naught to be done, There was naught to be said, So rey Lori Tornnoddy went bonne to bed:

FAMILY DESERTION AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Ses- sions, on Wednesday, before Messrs. H. S. Hall, F. H. (Jos- Sage, and John Brock, a labourer named John Towkov Pleaded guilty to deserting his wife and family.—Mr. John Scannell, the relieving officer, said the prisoner deserted his Wife and three children in December last, and they became chargeable to the Prescot Union. Two of the children were removed from the house in the course of a couple of weeks, bat Mn. Towkey was maintained out of the rates for three months. Pierpolnt Tms ROBBERY OF IRON BY BOYS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Edward Shields, 13 years of age, was charged with stealing from the Widnes Marsh a quantity of old iron, the property of the trustees of the late Mr. John Hutchinson.—lnspector Wood remarked that two other boys who were concerned in this robbery were flogged I on Wednesday last.—Thomas Dennett, foreman platelayer for the trustees, said he resided at Hale Bank. At seven o'clock on the 10th instant he saw a number of railway chairs lying Oa the Marsh. On the following morning be missed them, and from ihformation received he proceeded to a closet in Pear-street and found the stolen property there —Sergeant Clarkson deposed that he watched the place and saw the prisoner and two others come away with bags con- taining the iron. The prisoner escaped.—The Bench ordered the boy to receive nine strokes with the birch-rod. FATAL FALL OF A CHILD AT RUNCORN —Mr. T. J Ridgway, the Coroner for the honour and fee of Halton, held an inquiry at the London and North-Western Hotel on I Tuesday, into the CRU9O of death of Hannah Davies, two ee. years and nine months old, the daughter of Samuel Davies, blacksmith, 23, Lowland-road. About the Bth of June at seven o'clock in the evening the deceased was playing with her brother in the kitchen when she fell against the door With her forehead. The blow made her very sick, and Dr. McDougall was called in and pronounced the girl's brain to be injured. She remained very unwell until Sunday even- ing, when she died. The doctor gave a certificate stating that the primary e -fume of death was concussion of the brain, but under these circumstances Mr. Coleburn, the registrar, refused to register the thath until the coroner had been communicated with. The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the child died from injuries received to the brain accidentally. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD : PROPOSED HOSPITAL. —On Tuesday afternoon a special meeting of this Board was held in the Board offices, Alforde Chambers. There were present Messrs Gossage (chairman), Dr O'Keefe, E Carey, H indley, Wright, Midwood, Dutton. Houghton, Martley, Johnson; Allen (clerk), Coops (medical officer), Higginson (surveyor), and Dickson (nuisance inspector). The seal of the Board was affixed to the General Dietrict Rate, on the motion of Mr Handley, seconded by Mr Wright. --Tt was agreed to sc- cept.the tender of Messrs Ashmore and White, of £250, for the supply of patent screens te be used at the gm works in place of scrubbing boards.—The chief busineve of the meet- ing was, however, the selection of a site for the proposed in- fectious diseases hospital, but on this subject coming up for consideration the reporters were requested te retire. We un- derstand, however, that after a somewhat prolonged discus- sion the meeting adjourned without anything further having been done in regard to this matter. A PILFERING, LODGER AT Win/ans.—Patrick Hogan, a labourer, was brought up at Widnes Police Court, on Mon- day, to answer a charge of stealing 78 6d, the money of Jas. 11Iauley.—The prosecutor said he lived in Wellington-street, and the prisoner lived with him. On Saturday night they Went to bed about the same time as each other. Witness awoke at day-break on Sunday morning, and saw prisoner in his bedroom with his (witness's) trousers in his hands. On seeing that he was noticed, prisoner said "Hew are you Letting on ?" and witness said "Oh, all right." Before going to bed he counted his money, and he had 7a 6d in silver and Al 10d in copper. He then put it in his trouser's Pocket. On getting up he found the silver was gone, but the coppers were left. He gave information to the police. After dinner on Sunday he saw the prisoner, who asked him if he had lost any money. Witness replied that he had, lied held his own opinions as to who had taken it. The prisoner then struck him.—Sergeant Clarkson proved apprehending the prisoner, who said, in answer to the usual charge, "I am quite innocent."—William Holbrook, also a lodger with Mawley, said that on Saturday night the prosecutor came into the house "blind drunk," and showing him (witness) 5d in copper said This is all I have left."—The prisoner was fined 21s. or 14 days in default. Viounres IN A. Reetoteset SLree—On Saturday, at the Runcorn Police Court, before Captain Haelehurst and Mr. G. L. Davies, a powerfully built fellow named Thomas Sharkey was brought up under warrant charged with un- lawfully assaulting Petrick Coffee. The prisoner pleaded not guilty.—Coffee said he lived in Back Mersey-strest, next door but one to the prisoner. On Saturday night, the lth inst., he was coming down the street, when the Prisoner's wife commenced to beat him about the head. She then fetched her son to fight him. The prisoner then came al), saying he was ready to "do " for him, and followed him Into the houee, where he got him down and kicked hint aavagely about the body. He did all he could to "finish him," and since then he had not been able to go to his work. --The prisoner questioned complainatit as to whether on the Previous Thursday night he did not come to his house with a Poker and threaten to murder them ell. Coffee said the allegation was untrue —The complainant's wife gave con- firmatory evidence. She said that when Sharkey came into the holm he picked up the poker with which he struck her husband, slitting his ear. When her husband WAS on the floor Sharkey kicked him several times about the lower part of the body.—P.S. Whalley said on the night of the assault he saw the complainant. About the thighs and abdomen he was bruised in a shocking mermen—The Chairman said the prisoner had undoubtedly been guilty of a disgraceful assault, and he would be sent to gaol for one month. Ammeum ROBBERY OF ROPE AT WIDNES.—On Wednes- day, at Widnes Petty Sessions, James Grey and John Taylor were charged with having on or about the 11th in- stant stoles 120 yards of rope, value 20s, from the flat William, the property of Messrs Paris and Co., of Liver. Pool.—From a statement by Inspector Wood, it appeared that the flat William was at present lying in the St. Helens canal at Widnes. On Saturday Grey sold the rope to a marine store dealer named Frederick Bibby, and received Os from Charles Atherton a boy in Bibby's employ. The fol- lowing day he was taken into custody, and on Monday Tay- ler was also apprehended. Taylor, who is brother to the captain of the "William," and mate on board that craft, stated "All I can say about it is I went home on Friday, and I told Jem here to keep his eye on the ropes. When I came back on Monday morning the ropes were gone from the main hatches. I went to Frederick Bibby's shop and taw the ropes there.—Charles Atherton said he had given sed to James Grey for the rope.—Grey stated John Tay- lor asked me to take the rope, and I got fis for it, and I cave ,Taylor the meney. He gave me 2s out of it. The captain of the "John" was present when he gave me the rope.— Inspector Wood informed the Bench that the captains of the Rats John and Nelson had promised to attend at court at 11 O'clock that morning to prove that Taylor was in Widnes on Saturday when the rope was stolen, but they had not done so. He should therefore produce sufficient evidence for a remand.—Thomas Taylor and P.C. Thompson were called, and the Bench remanded the prisoners for a week.—ln the meantime the captains will be summoned as witnesses. TIIII ATTEMPTED SUICIDE OP A SAILOR AT RIINOORN.— At the Runcorn Police Court, on Saturday, before Captain Hazleharst and Mr. G. L. Davies, Arend Smit, a tall, good- looking seaman, 24 years of age, was charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide by cutting his throat on Sunday the 13th instant.—P.C. Morris said that at twenty minutes past five on Sunday morning he found the prisoner lying in Hol- loway-road. Thinking he was asleep be tried to wake him. Re got the prisoner upon his feet twice, and be fell down again. He then noticed that in his throat there was a great gash. He took the prisoner to the police station where be told him that he had cut his throat, and lithe knife with Which he bad done it had been sharper he would have killed himself. He further said that be bad thrown the knife away, and on going back to the Holkway-road he found the knife produced not far from the place where he had found fruit lying. After the man had been seen by a doctor he was taken to a house in Bridgewater-street, where he had been since.—The prisoner,who was not able to speak ,itglish, had the statement of the constable interpreted to nirn by the captain of the vessel Tasmania, upon which he Se-id it was all true.—William Schwth, master of the Tas- Mania, said the prisoner, who was one of his crew, had been strange in his manner far the last day or two that he was on board the vessel.—Dr. McDougall said ha was called to see the prisoner. MS manner seemed to be peculiar. Be ex- aminsd him and found a gash in his throat cutting through Portion of the windpipe. From what he saw he believed that the prisoner had been suffering from the effect of sun- stroke, and being excited through not being able to get some money owing to him he had been led to commit the rash act. In reply to Mr. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, Dr. McDougall said he believed if the magistrates s tav fit to discharge the prisoner be would be perfectly competent to look after himself.—The Bench discharged the prisoner, and %eked the superintendent of police to exercise some care over him while he remain,d in Runcorn.—The prisoner thanked the Bench for his discharge, and through the cap- of the vessel said he should nut make another attempt 11Po0 his life.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 26 1881.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 26 1881.

• C.R.T.S., WIDNES.—The weekly meeting was held at • the National Schools on Thursday evening, the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, presiding. The chairman and Mr. J. Foley, the lay reader, delivered addresses, and an enter- tainment of songs and recitations was taken part in by Messrs. G. Hesketh, G. Thomas, and the two speakers. FRAUDULENT REMOVAL ON GOODS AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, Michael Kilroy was summoned to answer a charge of fraudulently removing his goods in order to avoid a (distraint ter rent.—Patrick Quinn said he was agent for Taylor's mortgages, and prior to the I.Bth June the defendant occupied a house belonging to the mortgagees at 3s I per week. On that day he owed £1 34 ed for rent, and without giving notice he removed the whole of his furniture without giving up the key.—The Bench made an order upon the defendant to pay the sum owing at the rate of 5s Per week. AN AMBULANCE 7031 RUNCORN UNION.—The Guardians of the Runcorn Union have recently obtained at the moderate cost of £45, an ambulance for the conveyance of p qeons suffering from infectious diseases to the Workhouse Hospital at Button. It is in every way adapted for the pur- pose intended, and will prove to be of great service. The patient can be removed from bed into the vehicle with the minimum of risk and inconvenience, and the journey to the Workhouse accomplished without atigue, as the motion of the ambulance can scarcely be felt, and there is accommo- dation for attend rnts. lalszliontsr FREI CHURCH, RUNCCRI.—The anniversary of the establishment of the Sunday School in connection with this church was celebrated on Sunday, when the Rev J • Billington, of Birkenhead (formerly of Runcorn), preached two seimons to crowded congregations. At the evening ser- vice the choir rendered, under the conductorship of Mr John Holford, and aided by an excellent string band, ch ruses ' from Mendellsohn's "st. Paul" and Beethoven's "Mount 1 of Olives." In the afterieson a service et song, entitled " The Giver and his Gifts," was rendered by the scholars. ' The collection in aid of the school funds amounted to over

£2O. " PROFESSOR " FLETCHER ON HIS DEFENCE AT RUN- CORN." Professor " Fletcher, the herbalist, on Wednesday evening delivered a lecture on the tnarket ground, with re- ference to the woman named Baker who died from erysipe- lee last week under circumstances published in the Exam- iner. The professer narrated numerous instances of the wonderful cures he had effected in cases that had keen con- sidered hopeless by the faculty, and delivered a lengthy eulogy upon his medicines. He alleged that the woman Baker, when he paid his last visit to her, was in a favour- able condition, and contended that if she had been left under his care, she would have now been alive. MILL &tow WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL, RUNCORN.— The scholars attending this school had their annual treat on Wednesday, when they were conveyed in a covered boat to Keckwick, where they matched in processional order, ac- companied by a brass band, to a field kindly lent by Mr Bennett. Games of all descriptions were indulged in, and the teachers and officials distribuzed prizes for racing, leap- ing, &e. During the afternoon tea was provided. Before departing for borne in the evening a cordial vote of thanks was accorded to Mr and Mrs Bennett for entertaining the scholars. Messrs J R Frith, S Pope, and T Cayg,ill, super- intendents of the school, accompanied the children. THE SALVATION ARMY AT RuNconN.—The members of this army held a festival on Sunday and Monday last. when 111ajor Taylor paid a visit to the town to perform the C'rerueny of presenting colon, s. On the former day four meetings were held, and on Monday morning a holiness meeting took place in the Public Hall. In the evening a procession took place, the principal officers, attired in scarlet suits riding in front, whilst the inferior officers wore the usual red jersey, walked is the usual fashion, to the beat- ing of tambourines. A meeting in the Public Hall fol- lowed, when Major Taylor presented flags to the Captain and Lieutenant in command of the Runcorn corps. At 11 o'clock an all night prayer meeting was commenced, and passed off successfully. FARNWORTH C.E.T.S.—In connection with this society, a ; lecture was delivered in Bold schoolroom on Thursday even- , ing by Mr John Abbey, of Oxford, on the use of beer in the ; bay and harvest field. The Rev. G. Bond, M.A., presided, ; and there was a good attendance. The lecturer urged that - the practice of giving beer to men in the harvest field had ; been one great national school in which the rural popula- tion bad been taught habits of intemperance, and said that ; when total abstinence had been pot to a trial on the hay ; and harvest holds, it had proved satisfactory to both masters' ; and men. On the proposition of Mr. J. W. Davies the fol- lowing resolution was unanimously carried : "That in the ; opinion of this meeting it is desirable in the interests of , both niastere and men to diecontinue the giving of beer in , hay and harvest work, and to give an equivalent in money, and some non-intoxicatieg drink instead. DAMAGING PROPERTY AT RUNCORN. On Monday, at 4 Runcorn Petty Sessions, John Williams, Timperley, Alfred ; Steinway, William Leeson, and John 'Wigan were sum- , moned on a charge of having on the 7th July wilfully dam- aged, to the extent of fld each, the property of, the Mersey , ;Salt and Brine Co, Limited, by trespassing upon the em- bankment of the reservoir on Runcorn common. The de- fendants pleaded guilty—Mr W Ii Lineker appeared to pro- secute, and observed that the company wished to put a stop to persons trespassing upon the banks of the reservoir, but as this was the first case, they were willing with the permis- sion of their worships, to withdraw the summonses on the defendants apologising and paying costs.— The defendants left the court with Mr Lineker to arrange matters ; and later in the proceedings the latter said Timperley, Stanway, , and Leeson had acted as desired, but Radigan said he would "go to the pumps" before he would pay the costs. He was, therefore, told to stay in court, but he bad ; decamped, and Mr Linaker, therefore, applied for a war- I rant —A warrant WAS granted ANOTHER BATHING FATALITY AT WIDNES. Whilst bathing in the Mersey near the Accident Hospital, Widnes, , on Tuesday evening, Thomas bole, 12 years of age, son of , Samuel Heole, of 25, Irwell-atreet, wee drowned. Hook, 1 It appears, was in the water with several companions, but 4 got out of his depth. A youth named Edward Jones, who lives in Beamont-street, saw the boy's predicament and went to his aid, bat was unable to bring him to the shore until he ; was in a very exhausted condition. He was at once con- veyed to his home and Mr Richards, assistant to Dr McDon- ; nel, sent for, but when that gentleman arrived all human ; efforts were without avail. This is the second bathing fa- ; tality that has occurred at Widnes within a few weeks.— i Yesterday morning Mr S Brighouse, the county coroner, held an inquest on the body of the deceased at the Britannia ; Inn. The evidence showed that Hook and his companions were bathing in what is known as a sand hole in the river. ; Hoole, saving he could swim, dived into the water, but he I did not rise to the surface again. A young man named , Littler then dived after him, and found him with his bead ; sunk in the quick sand. He was brought on shore, but the , efforts made to resuscitate him were of no avail. The jury , returned a verdict of "Accidental death." WARRINGTON LIBERAL ASSOCIATION.--Lad evening there ; Was a largely attended meeting 01 the Executive of this 1 Association, Mr. C. Broadbent; J.P.. occupying the chair. The first business transacted was the appointment of a depu- tation of five to the National Liberal Conference to be held in London on Wednesday next, the gentlemen finally nomi- nated to represent the party in Warrington being Messrs. McMinnies (M.P.). C. Broadbent, W. Pierpoint, F. Roberts, and H. Roberts. Afterwards the meeting proceeded to consi- der the desirability of having demonstration to support the Government in the present crisis, and more particularly to give expression to the feeling of the working-class on the conduct of the Hones of Lords. The matter was freely discussed, the general opinion being that it was advisable to have an out-door de- monstration some Saturday afternoon before long, and it was ultimately resolved to leave the arrangements in the hands of a Sub-Committee. Mr. William Crosfield, the Liberal candidate for the borough at the next election, was I present, and briefly addressed the meeting on the policy to , be pursued in conducting the election campaign. The pro- ; needing., which were distinguished by heartineaa and 1 unanimity, closed with the usual votes of thanks. EXTRAORDINARY ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Petty Sessions on Monday, Robert Moores, a powerful-look- ; ing young fellow, was summoned to answer a charge of as- saulting John Dimelow, an elderly man. The complainant stated that on the sth July, about a quarter past eleven, he. I was going over the "cemetery fields" on his way home, when he heard a woman shouting as if in distress. He went to her assistance and be found two men were illusing her. ; He asked them what they were doing, when they turned noon him, and the woman ran away. The men then "leathered" him by striking and kicking him, and so on, 1 but at length he got away and ran down the field. The de- , fendant was one of the men.—The Defendant informed the ; Bench that he left Wilson's Hotel about ten minutes to eleven, and walked over Doctor's Bridge and over the fields. ' He heard a bother himself. When he got to Poole Bridge he saw the complainant standing there. The complainant said "I think you are one who has been hitting me." De- fendant said he did not know anything about it, whereupon the complainant said "Well I wish you would fetch my basket and cap. There has been some fellows laying on me." Defendant fetched these things, and then they walked away together. Defendant added that he did not hit the com- plainant 'if he were never to go away alive."—Both com- plainant and defendant wished to call witnesses who were not present, and the Bench therefore adjourned the case for a week. SAVAGE ASSAULT ON A RUNCORN SRRGRANT.— Yester- day at Runcorn Police Court, before Mr J Brunirit and Captain C W Hazlehurst, Thomas Hole and John Mackey, seamen, were brought up in custody charged with being drunk and disorderly. Hole was also charged with assaulting PS Whalley whilst in the execution of his duty.—? Whalley stated that about 11-20 on the previous night he was on duty at Waterloo Bridge, when he saw a crowd of about 40 sailors. In the centre were the prisoners, who were stripped. and fighting. He arrested Mackey, and gave him in charge of PC Breeze. He then seized Hole, but the atter resisted him violently, throwing himself on the ground Hole struggled with great determination, and kicked him (witness) on the legs several times causing abrasions of the skin. The prisoner also attempted to incite the crowd to attack the police. Both the prisoners were drunk, and the greatest difficulty was experienc,a in bringing them to the police station.—Constables Sullivan and Breeze corrobora- ted. Hole, who pleaded not guilty, stated that there was a row amongst the sailors, and one of them drew a knife to stab him, when he was pulled away by his friends. His coat was pulled off in the row. The next thing he found was someone seizing his throat, and he began to kick. He did not know it was a police officer he had kicked. He cal- led three witnesses in his behalf. Mackey was fined lOs and costs 5s 44 for b4ng drunk and disorderly. Hole for being drunk and disorderly was fined 19e and costs 8e 4d • and for the assault upon the sergeant he was fined 40s and costs Bs.

TER HALTON PARISH CHURCH CHOIR had their annual excursion to Llandudno, on Monday, the vicar and church- wardens aecompanying them. A pleasant day was spent. WIDNES AND THE STRIKE OF COLLIERS,—The strike of Lancashire colliers has proved so far bat a slight hindrance to the trade of Widnes, and the colliers having resolved to resume work, all danger of a stoppage of the chemical man- factories is at an end. MILTON CONGREGATIONAL CHAPEL, WIDNES.—We under- stand that the Rev. It. G. Hughes has been appointed to the pastorate of the above chapel, and will commence his duties tremorrow (Sunday). He has frequently preached before the followers of Wycliffe at Widnes. AN OPEIN-Alle PRHONSTRATION Will be held on the ground near the Market Hall, Widnes, next Saturday, to protest against the action of the House of Lords in re- jecting the Franchise Bill. The chair will be taken at four o'clock by Mr. E. K. Mnspratt, J.P. SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN IEACHEW—MiSS Agnes Edith Howard, a pupil teacher in Runcorn National Girls' School, has this week received a prize from the Diocesan Board of Education in recagnition of her having obtained a first class in all subjects at the examination in religious subjects, held oa the Sib December, 1883 A SUCCESSFUL WIDNES STUDENT.—We are glad to learn that Mr. William Sadler, son of Me Thomas Sadler, builder and contractor, Widnes-toad, has succeded in winning at the National Art Competition, South Kensington, two bronze medals for a study of drapery on figure, and the other for the study of an anatomical figure. IP MYSTERIOUS DROWNING CASE AT WESTON.—AI Weston on Thurslay morning, James Mather, 12 years of age, was drowned in the Old Basin under circumstances which are at tee present surrounded in mystery. Mather, who was employed on the steam tug Regulator, was seen on hoard that vessel about eleven o'clock. After the lapse of a few minutes he was mused, and his cap was seen floating on the water. Naturally it Was suspected that he had fallen into the basin, end grappling irons having been brought into use, toe dead body of the boy was brought to the surface in h if an hour.—At the Weaver Hotel, Weston Point, last evening, Mr T J Ridgway, the coroner, held an inquest touching thc death of the boy ; but no fresh light was thrown upon the case, and the jury returned a verdict of " Fund drowned " A SAILOR DROWNED AT RUNCORN.—About half-past eleven on Wednesday night, Henry Fife, a seaman on board the schooner James, at present lying in Runcorn Docks, WES on his way from the town to the vessel when he fell into the water and was drowned. It seems that Fife and two other seamen named Angus McClenuan and Andrew McKoy went to Runcorn Post °nice about eight o'clock, and then stayed drinking at a public-house nntil nearly closing time, when they started for the decks. When approaching the slope at Parr's Lock,Fife ran away from his companions,who shortly afterwards heard a splash. One of them remarked that "Harry was in the water," and they hastened to the spot, but according to their statement the deceased was "smothered ' at once. Information of the occurrence Was conveyed to the 'James," and Was. Ross launched a boat, and the body was recovered in about half an hour.—Mr T J Ridgway, coroner, keld an inquest on the body at the Police Court, yesterday afternoon, and the jury after hear- ing the evidence returned a verdict of " Accidentally drowned."

IHE FATAL ASSAULT AT RUNCORN. INQUEST AND VERDICT. Yesterday, Mr. T. J. Ridgway, coroner for the honor and fee of Halton, held an inquest at Runcorn Police Court upon the body of William Stringer, an elderly man, who died on Tuesday night from injuries received on the afternoon of the 17th May, through being thrown over the head of Michael Murphy, captain of the schooner Eclipse, of Fleet- wood. Mr. W. Handley was feremen of the jury. Mr. W. H. Linaker watched the proceedings on bekatf of Murphy, and Mr. Superintendent Leali was present to represent the police.—Joseph Stringer, 30, Portland-street, Duke's Field, dock labourer. said the body the jury had seen was that of his father. He was 58 years of age, and followed the occu- pation of a dock labourer. He remembered ble father going to his work on Saturday morning, the 17th May, and on the afternoon of the same day he was sent for to the Darwell Vaults. He went there, and found his father in the lobby in a kneeling position, and he, with the aid of Thomas Howard, placed his father in a barrow, and wheeled bias home. 29, Portland-street. He did not think the " old man" was so bad, and he did not go for a doctor until mid- night. Ha went for Dr. Robinson, but that gentleman re- fused to have anything to do with the case as it was likely to reselt in a l+w suit. On Sunday morning Dr. Bagnall was called in, and he had attended Stringer up to the time of his death at half an hour after midnight on Tuesday,— By the foreman: His father bad enjoyed very good health, and he was certainly in good health on the morning of the ' day lie was hurt. He was perfectly eober when he (witness) took him home from the Vaults.—Nl.r. F. Johnson, deputy magistrates' clerk, produced the depositions of the deceased, which were taken before Mr. W. Henke!, J.P., in the pre- sence of the man Murphy, his sister, and Mr. Robert Edmondson, solicitor.—The deposition, which has previa ugly been published in extenso in The Examiner, is to the effect that on the afternoon of the 17th May he went into Dar. well's Vaults, where Murphy and several other persons were. , During the time he was there he had a pint of beer, and be bad had no liquor previously. He had no conversation whatever with Murphy ; but when be was about to leave the house Murphy seized hold of him, and placing his foot in his stomach threw him over his head. He did not know that Murphy had any ill-feeling towards bins. He had not given Murphy any provocation. Wm. Hardley, shipwright, of 4, Bentinckt-street. Runcorn, said he went into Darwell's Vaults on Saturday afternoon, the 17th May, about 20 minutes or a quarter to four o'clock. When he had been in the tap-room auout ten minutes, the deceased, who was quite sober, got up to go out. The de- ceased went to the fireplace and lighted his pipe, and was going out of the house when Murphy suddenly caught hold of him with both hands either by the breast of his coat or by his arms, placed his bead in his breast, still re- taining his hold of him. Murphy then slipped down on his back purposely, and placing his feet on the belly of the de- ceased, threw him over his head. The deceased' fell on his head and shoulders on the flags in the passage, his legs and feet striking against the wall. The deceased was thrown through the doorway and across the passage. Murphy got up and sat down in the tap-room, but Stringer lay groaning in the passage until Mrs. Bradburn went to him. She said "Ott, Captain, whatever is to do; who has done this ?" Stringer was then placed ins chair by Mrs. Bradburn and Murphy. Stringer seemed quite conscious and he said "I am badly hurt," Slid asked them to send for his son to help him home. He did not seem to be able to move. His son came, and witness arcl James Howard carried the deceased out of the house and placed him on a barrow, in which he was wheeled home. When Murphy got hold of deceased be did not speak, nor did deceased speak to Murphy. Neither Murphy nor Stringer spoke to each other while he (witness)' was in the house, except it was in general conversation. So far as be could judge, Murphy was quite sober.—By Mr. Hankinson: He never heard anything said about feats of ' strength or. wrestling. Joseph Bradbury, landlord of the Harwell Vaults, Ben- tinckt-street, gave corroborative evidence.—ln answer to the Foreman, he said Murphy had several glames of beer. It seemed to witness as though Murphy had been drinking the day before, and was taking liquor then to sober him. He was quite steady when he left the house. By Superintendent Lash: The deceased had no chance of resisting Murphy, as the whole affair only took about two minute& Jane Bradburn, wife of -last witness, said she asked Murphy what be had done it for, and he replied that be didn't know. Murphy said hot ale would do Stringer good, and in about a quarter of an hour afterwards she asked him to send for some brandy for the injured man. Ile refused, saying Stringer wae only foxing. She told him he had given Stringer his death blow, and that if anything hap- pened to the man he would be brought into trouble. Murphy replied that if anything happened they would have a spree. She had asked Murphy to help her with Stringer, bet he refused —By the Foreman : Murphy was quite sober. He bad been to the house before, and had always conducted himself right before. Dr. Bagnall deposed that when he saw the 'deceased en the 18th May he formed the opinion that he was suffering from concussion of the spine. The deceased was paralysed in his legs and arms. On the previous day (24th instant) he had made a post-mortem examination of the body. Ex- ternally there were no marks of violenee to be noticed, the bruise which he had seen before having disappeared. The body was much emaciated. In the chest there was not much to notice, except that the heart was flabby, and there was some adhesion to the right lung, but nothing of any importance. The witness then described the other portions of the body, and stated that the brain was fairly heathy. He examined the upper parrot the spinal cord, and found an Injured portion in the neck. He took out the injured por- tion and found that the external membrane was thickened, and inflammation had extended inwards tawards the cord itself. His opinion was that the injured portion of the cord was the seat of the injury, having first caused paralysis, then resulting in other disorders and death: Tbe fall he had heard the deceased had was quite sufficient to account for the injury to the spinal column. P.S. Whalley proved apprehending Murphy on a charge of doing grievous bodily harm. Murphy said " I didn't think of hurting him. I don't know what made me do it." The Coroner said it was now for the jury to say bow the deceased met with his death. They would have to consider in arriving at a verdict the most serious point which a jury could consider, whether or not the man Murphy was guilty of murder or manslaughter. The question of pure accident was beyond consideration. The Coroner described , bow Murphy threw the deceased, and pointed out that the Medical evidence conclusively showed that the deceased met his death through the act that took place in this beer- house. He thought they must find that what Murphy did was an unlawful act. There was no consent or approval given by the deceased, and even if the act could be termed a trick, could it be held to be a lawful trick. It was not like where two parties Were agreed to enter into a wrestling match, which was a trial of skill, and which had been decided often enough to be a lawful game in England. He thought the jury must affirm that this was an unlawful act on the part of Murphy. Then the question for them to decide was whether Murphy was guilty of the murder of the deceased. He read to the jury one or two definitions of the word murder, amongst them being the following : " The malice necessary to conetitute the crime of murder is not confined to an Mention to take .way the life of the deceased, but includes aid intent to do any unlawful act which may prubably end in depriving the party of life." " If a man kills another without any or considerable provocation the law implies malice."

1 I "If an action unlawful in itself be done deliberately and - with intention of mischief, or great bodily harm to particu- lars, or of mischief indiscriminately, fall where it may, and l death ensue, the original intention of the party, it will be ! murder."—Murphy, continued the Coroner, was much sur- prised at the serious assault he had committed when arrested by the police, but to him (Mr Ridgway) Murphy's conduct after he had done the act seemed most callous. He seemed to have had no feeling at all for the deceased, and simply I to have thought that the deceased was shamming. Murphy committed the act in such a place, that if he had taken the trouble to think of what the result would be, he must have known that something serious would ensue. He was, how- ever, utterly reckless as to the result, and it was for the jury to say what their verdict should be. The jury then retired into the magistrates retiring-room, and after an absence of five minutes returned into court— The Foreman said the verdict cf the jury was that the man Stringer met his death as a result of the fall received in Darwell's Vaults at the hands of Michael Murphy. The Coroner: Then do you say that that was intention- ally caused or not.—The Foreman: We don't say it was in- tentionally caused, but it was the result of the act of Michael Murphy. We say tnat Michael Murphy caused his death by throwing him over his head, and that he is responsible fir his death—The Coroner: Then do you consider it has been wilfully done.-- The foreman said the jury were not agreed to bring in a verdict in the bare naked words wilful murder, because they did not think there was any malice : ! aforethought. They were all of the strong opinion that Michael Murphy was in such a state himself that be could ' have prevented himself from giving this man a throw and ' oaght not to have done such an act.—The Coroner: In that eise I think yourverdict icons of wilful murder.—The foie- 1 man said the words he had used were those in which the jury preferred to give their verdict. He (the coroner) could ' enter it as he thought fit.—The Coroner said he was bound I to ask whether they found Murphy guilty of murder or man- slaughter.—The jury then retired again, and remained absent I for about a quarter of au hour. The foreman raid: We lied ' that the deceased came by his death in the manner described 1 in the evidence, but without any premeditated malice on 1 Murphy's part.—The Coroner : Then you say that Murphy is guilty of the manslaughter of the decaasett—The Fore- i man : We do.—The verdict was then formally recorded, the I inquiry having occupied five hours.

HEALTH OF WARRINGTON.
Dr Gornall, medical officer of health, supplies us with the following details as to the health of Warrington during

the quarter ending June 28th, 1884 : During the second quarter of 1884 471 births were regis- tered in the borough ot Warrington, equal to an annual rate of 423 per 1 000 of the estimated population, which is now about 44,500. Warrington still cmitinues to hold a pre- eminent position in respect to its high birth rate, for whilst the London birth rate in the some period was only 33.8, the 28 larger towns averaged 35, and the 27 provincial towns The birth rate in these towns ranged from 28.0 and 290 in Brighton and Huddersfield to 406 in Cardid, 41 in No - tingham, and 453 in Sunderland. The deaths for the quarter were 178, equal to a death rate , of 159 per 1.000, against 268 and 233 in the correspond- ing quarters of 1882 and 183. In London this death rate WAS equal to 199 per 1,000, whilst in the provincial towns it averaged 21•6. The ether low death rates in the same quarter were—Brighton 16-1, Derby 168, Bristol 17 2, and Leicesttr 17.7. whilst the rates ranged upwards to 248 in Liverpool, 24.9 in Wolverhampton, 25.5 in Manchester, and 25 6 in Oldham. In Warrington to the principal zymotic diseases 19 deaths were referred. or 108 per cent. of the total deaths, equal to an annual rate of 1 7 per 1,000. The corresponding rates in Vie 28 large towns from zeinotic diseases were 15.1 per cent. and 313 per 1000. The lowest zymotic death rates last quarter were 082 in Brighton, 092 in Derby, and 12 in Hull ; the hie eA were 381 in Leeds, 416 in Oldham, 422 I in Portsmouth, Sod 4.64 in Liverpool. The 19 deaths from zymotic diseases in Warrington in- cluded 1 from enteric fevert 11 from measles, 2 from whoop. tom cough, and 5 from diarrhosa. Under oar Notification Act the following Cases of infec- tious disease were reported :—Small-pox 2, scarlet fever 3, enteric fever 5. Of these, the eases of smallpox and scar- let fever and one case of enteric fever were removed to the Hospital. The weather during the quarter has been remarkably fin 9 and warm. The mean temperature of the air in the quar- ter was 46 6, against 47.3 and 47-1 in the corresponding quarters of 1882 and 1853. Rein fell on 14 days in April, 11 in May, and 4 in June; in all 29 days of the 91 days of the quarter. The rainfall wets equal to 3.99 inches, against 104 and 492 in the corres- ponding quarters of 1882 aud 1883.

div.head: DRUIDS' ANNIVERSARY AT HILL CLIFFE.
div.p: DRUIDS' ANNIVERSARY AT HILL CLIFFE.

More good stories are told about Whistler than any pro- minent man in London society. Oscar Wilde, who at one time shared with him this attention, has now dropped into the difficulty of the married state, and the good things that were either said by him or attributed to him have ceased to circulate. But Whistler still keeps the ball rolling. The latest good thing is his reply to one of the numerous syco- phants who worship at his shrine. "There are, Mr Whistler," said his admirer, "only two painters in the world, yourself and Velasquez." "Why drag in Velaaquez ?" said Whistler with exquisite humour, probably lost upon his worshipper. A story of a similar kind bracketed him with another artist even of higher standing than the great Span- ish painter. I was sailing down the river the other day from Westminster to Chelsea," said a lady. "I saw Whistler everywhere, Whistler in the clouds, Whistler in the dim outlines of the houses, Vs, histler in the haze that lloatedson the water. Whistler, Whistler all along the banks." TEE LATE LIBERAL Murrittos.—The following commu- nications have been received from Mr. Gladstone and Lord Granville in acknowledgment of copies of the resolutions which were passed at the Liberal meetings held in Warring- ton on Wednesday week:- 10. Downing-street, Whitehall. 24th July. 1884. Eiir,—Mr. Gladstone has had the honour to receive the elm- munication which you have been good enough to forward to him. on the subject of the rejection of the Franchise Bill by the House of Lords. lam directed to express his thanks through you for the marks of approval and support afforded by this communi- cation.
I am, Sir, your obedient servant, E. W. HAMILTON.

Henry Roberts, Esq., Secretory of the Warrington Liberal Association. Foreign Office, July 22nd. 18ftt. Sir,—l am desired by Lord Granville to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of yesterday, incMsing the copy of a reso- lution passed by large Liberal meetings held at Warrington on the 16th inst. Lord Granville has received with much gratification the cordial expression of confidence in Her Majesty's Government, and assurances of support conveyed in the resolution which you have been so good as to communicate to him, and for which he desires me t.) return his best thanks. I am, 81r, your obedient servant. MIRY MERVEY. Henry Roberts, Esq..'
Warrington.

WAWEINGTON CONSERVATIVE CLUE BUILDINGS CO., LIMITED.—An annual- ordinary meeting of the shareholders ef this company was held in the Conservative Club, Academy-street, on Monday evening. The business of the meeting was the election of directors and auditors and the transaction of ordinary business. The balance sheet and accounts were submitted to the meeting, explained by the auditor and Messrs. Francemb and Sutton (directors), and unanimously adopted by the shareholders. In accordance with the articles of the association of the com- pany, the following directors retired from office, viz., Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., Messrs. W. Atherton, James Smeth- urst, William Dickens, and J. A. Simpson, and the following gentlemen, two of whom had just retired, were elected to the directorate, viz. : Sir Gil- ' bert Greenall, Bart., Messrs. William Dickens, John White, Robert Isherwood, and J. E. Wright. A Pre- liminary Committee for making arrangements for the framing of rules, enrolment of members, opening and management of the new club were elected, and it is expected that the new club will be opened by some of tiae,leading members of the Conservative party in September or October next. About 600 working-men and tradesmen of the town have taken up nearly 3,000 shares in the Club Company, and the direc- tors hope to receive applications from about 200 more working-men.
