div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY._
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY._

The fornightly meeting was held at the Dutton Work- house on Tuesday, Mr J Ashton presiding. There were present the Revs J Lockwood, J W N Tanner, Messrs R Ashton, Knowles, Warburton, Weir, Derbyshire, Mclntyre, Adams (medical officer), H Linaker (clerk), W Ii Linaker I (deputy clerk), and Farrington (nuisance inspector). Tan CUOLBRA OUTBREAL—A letter was read from the Local Government Board respecting the precautions to be adopted with regard to the cholera outbreak on the con- tinent, to prevent infection in the Anthoritv'e district —Tee Clerk said he had got information from the Bridgewater Navigation Company that they had given instructions to their servants at Liverpool not to permit any vessels to pro- ceed to Runcorn sinless they had a clesn bill of health,—A committee was appointed to take all necessary action, and it was understood that bills containing instructions how to pre- vent infection would be distributed. THF 6Taerrrox Nuisawca.—The committee appointed to meet and report on the cendition of the cattle drinking ittml belonging to the Lower Hall in the township of Stretton belonging to and complained of by the owner, Mr James Maroon, J.P., as being highly polluted, examined the pond, and, ascertaining the different sources of pollution, they were of opinion that Mr Ramon was quite justified in making the complaint, yet failed to see that the chief cause of pollution arose from the liquid which flowed into it from Stratton Hall, as it received ttie whole of the sewage, &c from Lower Stratton, including that from the Lower Hall. The pond was without doubt greatly polluted, and must be highly dangerous to cattle drinking therefrom, and the only remedy the committee could suggest to improve it was to extend the existing sewer to a distance of about 300 yards, the connection to be made with the present sewer in land belonging to Mrs Poole at a point where it discharged at present. The line of the extension would be through a plot of land helonging to the Vicar of Stretton, and across two plots owned by Mr Meson, and it would discharge into an open ditch, which would receive and sontain the :solid matter, and could be cleansed occasionally. In the opinion of the committee no nuisance would arise therefrom.—lt was decided that this scheme shmild be carried out if Mr Marson had no objections to raise. Tstn FEYEEL PLAGUIC.—The Medical Officer of Health re- ported that Mark Rawlinson, aged ID years, son of Mr. Samuel Rawlinson, had been attacked by typhoid fever at a house situated on Preston Brook Canal Tunnel. The pa- tient was properly. isolated, and the usual precautionary measures adopted. The disease had been imported from Hartford where the patient had worked. Ile had therefore notified the outbreak to the medical dicer of health for that district in order that he might investigate the canes of the outbreak. He was glad to be able to state that no in- formation of any extension of the outbreak at Sutton had reached him since the last meeting. Tun AUTITOIIITY AND THY CANAL BOATS ACT.—Mr. Far- rington asked to be permitted to make a few observations with respect to a statement made before a Select Committee of the House of Commonsabout the Canal Boats Bill. It was stated by an individual who is part promoter of the bill that no canal boat inspection took place between Middle- wich and Runcorn. He (Mr. Farrington) thought it was only fair to the Authority and himself that this assertion should not go uncontradicted. Far from that statement being correct, since 1880 there had been no less than 41 eases brought before the magistrates by the Authority for infringement of the Act, and 40 convictions bad been ob- tained. One case was withdrawn on payment of the Goats, which was tantamount to a conviction. He had issued a 'amnions against a boatowner to attend the next Daresbury Sessions, and this would retake a total of 42 cases since the passing of the Canal Boats Act. The gentleman might have meant that there was no inspector taking action with respect to the Education Act, but this was not within his province at all. He did not think anything had been done with respect to looking after the children in boats, but so far as the sanitary condition of the boats was concerned active measures had been taken; and be thought they would Oompare favourably with any other district in England. FRODSEAII MAIN Szwes —The minutes of the Frodsham Parochial Cemmittee, which were adopted, contained the following letter from Mr. J. Cunnah, secretary to the gas inspectors :—.‘ I are directed by the inspectors of the Frod- sham lighting district to inform you that they have had under consideration the application made by the Frodeham Parochial Committee to ventilate the main sewer by con- necting same with the gas pillars, but they do not pee their way to sanction the suggested arrangement, as the lanterns are taken off the pillars in the summer months, and a nuis- ance might arise therefrom."—Mr. Farrington was instructed to report to the next meeting what arrangement could be made for a ventilating shaft, and submit an estimate of the probable cost. This concluded the business.

I HUSBAND AIM WIFE. —By the ruling of one of the Judges of the Liverpool County Court (Mr. Thompson) a married woman's property rights are still very inferior to those of her husband. An unhappy couple who had sepa- rated had standing in their joint names an investment of .£l,OOO with the Mersey Dock Board. The wife took the bond away with her, and the husband sued her to recover possession of it. It does not appear in what way the pair acquired the money invested, but the Judge held that dur- ing their joint lives the husband was entitled to the custody of the bond and the coupons, but that he could only part with the coupons with the concurrence of hie wife. Nothing was said about the wife's means of possessing herself of her share of the proceeds of the coupons. THE SPLIT AMONGST THE TORIES.—The Daily News says :—The victory of Lord Randolph Churchill in the con- test at Sheffield, on Wednesday, is questioned by his op- ponents on the Conservative side. It is stated that though Lord Randolph secured an apparent majority of four ever Mr. Chaplin's nomination, this rests upon the assumption that the five members whose names appeard on both lists will vote for Lord Randolph in the forthcoming election as chairman of the council. It is claimed that the majority of these are Mr. Chaplin's friends, not Lorel Randolph's. Be- yond this Sir M. Hicks-Beach, whose name appeared in • neither list, is prepared to vote for the candidate favoured by the leaders of the patty. On Thursday the Central Con- servative Committee, of which Mr. Stanhope is chairman, resigned in a body. It is understood that this step was taken as a vsult of the meeting at Sheffield, which at letst , Jett doubtful the deposition of Lord Randolph Churchill ' from the chairmanship of the Council.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.

LONDON, TIICRSDAN. Affairs move so rapidly in these times that the tremonstra- , tion of Monday last has already become ancient history. But though it has passed away with the processionists, it has laft behind a memary and an effect which are likely rather to grow than to diminish. The procession itself was in point of numbers the most imposing ever seen in any ety. But more striking still was its orderly character and its unruffled good humour. Lord Salisbury, who probab!y sloes himself an injustice, affects not to understand the char- acter of an English crowd. Having first sneered at the working-man taking healthy exercise in the Perk, or harm- lessly peregrinating Pall Mall, he now finds in the very good humour of the procession an argument against the Woes:- nese of the popular feeling. I suppose he would have had , toem clench their teeth and shake their fists here, and there break a window. But Lord Salisbury is really too intelli- -.

e ordingly, though he had no official right to the place. roes was always made for him on the Front Opposition Bench whence ha used to rise and in that almost inaudible voice which deaf persons affect said a few words across the table. The minister rose and replied, the House generally gather- ing from his answer what the question was about, for Lord Ernest did not always place its terms on the paper. Lord Ernest never by any chance heard a word of the reply. But he was accustomed gravely to nod whilst the answer was being given, raise his hat in acknowledgement, when, the minister having resumed his seat, he felt sure the answer was complete, and then march off to his own teat on the back benches, a little scene at which the House was wont gently to laugh and genially to cheer. Then Lord Ernest Bruce went into the Lords; his grandson will in due time inherit the maiguisate, the present holder of the tCos being only two years younger than the dowager Menhioness.

Saturday is fixed for the marriage of a young lady whose face is familiar all over the world. Tbia is Miss Beatrix, eldest daughter of M. Da Manner. Readers of Punch, have, all unconsciously, watched her growth from the artless little girl wanting to know all kinds Lf things to the graceful maiden interested in balls and CI itiCali in the matter of partners. Most people in the literary and artistm world have been invited to assist at the ceremony, and St. George's, Hanover Square, will on Saturday enclose a remarkable congregation.

Talking about marriages an ingenious person has put forward the notion of what he calls a Marriage Benen't Association. The principle is very mach akin to that a the older established Burial Association. In both cases subscriptiena ars raid, and in both when the ceremony takeg place—whether it be burial or marriage—a sum of money is paid over Gu account of the suty=cription. This may be a . _
good thing, but it is painful to think of the girl, who in the first blush of hope (which I believe begins at the age of fourteen) commences to pay her subscription, and while
the long years roll on, no chance preeents itself to justify her clsiming, the premium. In Poch circumstances the
condition of the spinster would become increasingly desperate.

TRIP TO LLANDVD/40.—The united choirs of Trinity Church, Warrington' St. James's Church, Latchford, and Christ Church, Latchford, had an excursion on Monday to Llandudno, which proved on the whole a success, and WRS enjoyed by all. The party numbered about 300, and started from Bank Quay Station at 7-30 a.m. The weather was not of the most propitious character, rain falling for about an hour after the party arrived, but it eventually cleared off, aed the afternoon was very pleasant. The various places of interest were visited in turn, and the party started on the homeward journey at 8-10 p.m., arriving in Warrington about 11 o'clock. -

_ ORFORD SCHOOLS —On Sunday sermons were preached in the Orford Schoolroom, in aid of the Sunday and Day Schools. In the morning the Rev. E. J. Willcocks, M.A., preached from Jeremiah xvii., 7 and 8, "Blessed is the man that trusteth in the Lord, for he shall be as a tree planted by the waters, and that spreadeth her roots to the river."— In the evening the Rev. T. P. Williamson, vicar of Thelwall, preached from Psalms cxxvii. 4, prayer book version. The rev. gentleman urged the necessity of the culture of chil- dren physically, mentally, and spiritually, and strongly wrged the claims of the Orford Schools as worthy the sup- port of the inhabitants of that district. There was a large congregation on each occasion, and the collections realized about £l2. THR BIRTH AND Dna= RATE OF WARRINGTOX.—For week ending Saturday, July 19th, 1884. The mean temperature was 57 Fahrenheit, and therefore 149 degrees lower than preceding week. The maximum temperature 74 Fahrenheit, was recorded on the 131 inst., and the mi nimum temperature 40 Fahrenheit on the 19th inst. The rainfall measured •72 inches. The general direction of the wind was south-west. During the week, which was the 29th of the current year, 35 births and 18 deaths were reg ie• • ered The death rate from all causes was equal to 21-02 per 1,000, against 15 6 the average of the previous four weeke' and against 230 the corresponding week of last year. ' The deaths included 5 from measles, 1 ftom whooping cough, 1 from diarrhcet, 1 from phthisis, 1 from old age, 1 from prentatnre birth, 1 from kidney disease, and 1 from I train disease. One case of typhoid fever wss reported • under the requirements of the Act of Partistrent.—Jonst H. OORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.

DRUNKENNESS —John Alpin, an elderly man, was charged with having been drunk on the previous day, but on his pro- mising to leave the town he was discharged. SUSPICIOUS CHA.RACTERS.—Thomas Ogden a young man. and Anne Jones, an elderly woman, were brought before the Bench m suspicious characters.—lt appeared that on the previous day, which was "Fair day," the prisoners were noticed by In- specter Spinks and several constables to conduct themselves in a RUSDICiOUS manner amongst the crowd of people who had gathered in Buttermarkst and Sankey-streets. They were arrested, and on teeing separately charged gave somewhat con- tradictory accounts of themselves, both saying that they last Came from St. nelons. At first they denied any knowledge of each other, but it was a-certained that they had taken lodgings at a house as man and wife.—The Bench thought the police justified in arresting the prisoners on account of their suspicious condixt, but on promising to leave the town in " five minu:es" they were discharged. _ Tim Cum. Etta Ix THE MERSBY.—The cholera-infected members at the crew of the steamer St. Dunstan, now -lying in the Mersey, are going on well. A few of the men have been breualat ashore and placed in the hospital at Eromborough, which is completely isolated. The assistant medical officer of health considers the St. Dunstan now free from infection, and says there is no further cause for alarm. The ship, however, will be kept in quarantine for some time yet. SCHOOL BOARD MEETINU.

A monthly meeting of the Prescot School Board was held at the Clerk's office on Monday evening, when there were present Messrs W L Evans (chairman). C Spencelay, T P Hewlett, H Fogg, H Cross, (clerk), Cowherd (assistant clerk). Bayliss (inspector), and Miss McGregor (assistant mistress). MeosoMMee HOLIDAYS.—The midsummer holidays were fixed to commence for the following Friday. and were to ex- tend over a period of three weeks. It was also decided to present buns and oranges to each of the scholars and have a special distribution of prises at Christmas. ADVANCE OF SALARY. Mr James Ellison, assistant teacher of the boys school, applied for an advance of salary. —The Chairman explained that Mr Ellison had complained to him that £4O per annum was not sufficient, and he (the chairman) thought he was worthy of £5O per annum.—Mr Hewlett expressed the opinion that they °tight to keep salaries down at the present time. Mr Fogg ultimately moved, and Mr Hewlett seconded, that the salary of Mr Ellison be increased from £4O to £5O per annum and the motion was passed. THE ScaooL MASTERS.—The Chairman explained that they had at present two masters in the school, and he thought some definite position should be assumed for each. After some discussion Mr Hewlett proposed that Mr Grant's salary be £9O per annum, and that Mr Wilkinson's salary be £75 per annum, and that all monies received in grants from the Government over £lOO, should bst divided between them. —The motion was carried. RESIGNATION OF TICE HEAD haTRESS.— The Chairman read the resignation of Miss Duke, head mistress of the girls' school, which was accepted, and it was ordered that the clerk advertise for a successor.

ATTENDANCE AT SCHOOL.--The Clerk submitted the fol- lowing monthly return of attendances and fees :—Boys' school, No. on roll, 243, corresponding month last year, 230 ; attendances, 7,464, last year 7,532; attendances lost 2,013, last year 1,433; average 1913, last year 193 1 ; fees £lO 9e 2d, last year £ll Os lid. That was a large scheme for dealing with the sewerage of Wargrave and the township generally. The matter was being forced upon them, and arrangements were being made for the carrying off of the sewerage by proper drainage, and utilising it so that there would be no ill effects from it. The scheme was in course of preparation, and he hoped it would be carried out in the course of next year. He thought it would induce an i mproveinent in certain parts of the district, as more accommodation for workmen in the shape of houses was being delayed by their present bad sewerage system. More accommodation seemed to be very much needed; it was certainly for the workpeople at the Vulcan, arid he heard it was the same in other parts of the district. He hoped that would be remedied and that their sewerage would in future be properly dealt with. (Hear, hear.)—A. special meeting of the Commissioners to consider the suggested sewerage scheme was afterwards held in the Boardroom. There were present: Messrs Gooch (chairman), J W Emmett, Jas Fairclough, Thomas Stone, Thomas Hunt, James E Worsley (law clerk), and R Brierley (surveyor).—The Surveyor submitted amended plans with respect to the sewerage outtal I works near Red Bank; and it waa ultimately decided to adopt the plan. A motion was also passed that Mr Voiser, of Warrington, should act as valuer of the land required; and if Mr Legh's agent did not agree to that decision, that Mr Voiser should represent the Commissioners when the land was valued. VIADUCT WORKS ExCURSIONS.—The interest evoked by the annual excursions in connec:ion with the Viaduct Wag- gon Works and Institute at Earlestown, belonging to the London and North-Western Railway, was this year in no Sense below that of previous years. The selected destina- tions this year were London and Carnarvon, and the ex- ceedingly cheap rates at which passengers were conveyed to those places created great demand for the tickets. The return fares to the metropolis were 3s for one day. and 4, for three days; while the extension tickets (available for three days) for Carnarvon were issued at 2s each. A similar charge was made for the London tickets last year, and privilege was then abusei by a large number of persons, many of whom disposed of the tickets at a considerable pro- fit to themselves. As the excursions are arranged nominally for the benefit of the working-men employed by the railway company and their families, and it was definitely ascertained that other individuals obtained tickets to trade with them, the company this year imposed considerable restrictions capon the sale of the tickets. They were issued strictly to the workmen alone, and to members of the Institute, and it Is stated that the men were absolutely forbidden to let any Outside person have them. The passengers for London numbered about 1.200,and were conveyed in twe special trains which left Earlestown shortly after mid-night on Friday last. The arangements made for the safe and punctual despatch of the trippers were carried out by Mr. Young, the stationmaster and the officials under him, as efficiently as could have been expected. The special train to Carnarvon left Earleetown about six o'clock on the Saturday morning. and a large number of persons availed themselves of the op- portunity of visiting one of the principal places of interest in the principality of Wales. In every sense the excursions were a success, and so far as we have heard everyone thoroughly enjoyed the out.

THE EARLESTOWN CHURCH DISPUTE. THE PETITION TO REMOTE THE 'VICAR.

Ecclesiastical affairs in the parish of St. -John the Bap- tist, Earlestown, still remain in a very unsettled and un- satisfactory condition. On Sunday there was only a meagre attendance at each of the services, and at one of the services no person could be prevailed upon to go round with the offatory boxes, the result being no collection was made. At the forenoon service the Vicar baJ a new curate in attend- ance, but the importation was conspicuous by his absence in the evening. It has since been stated that he had left the parish en seeing the discreditable state to which church affairs bad been brought. The committee appointed at the public meeting of parishioners, held last week, to draw up a petition for presentation to the Bishop of the diocese, pray- ing for the removal of the vicar, have met with many promises of support. There can be no doubt the memorial will receive a large number of signatnres, but, naturally, con- siderable uncertainty prevails as to what effect it will have noon his lordship. The following is the wording of the peti- tion drawn up by the committee appointed for that purpose: "To the Right Reverend J. C. Rvle, D.D., Lord Bishop of Liverpool. The humble petition of the undersigned mem- bers of St. John ttte Baptist Church, Earlestown, showeth, That we desire to call the immediate attention of your lord- ship to the spiritual destitution of the above-named parish, which is undoubtedly the result of what is now known as the Earlestown Church scandal. Perhaps it is quite un- necessary to trouble your lordship with the pain- ful histoiy of the above, but we earnestly feel that being successful in erectitne a beautiful church and organ which has involved a large amount of time and money upon us, that your Lordship will be grieved to learn that our efforts have been met with such arbitrary treatment at the bands of our vicar (the Rev. T. R Matthews). We regret to say that he has driven our respected curate, wardens, and sidesmen, our organist and choir, and last, but not least, a splendid con- gregation numbering 500 from our church, and he has also been the means of our Sunday school being deserted by both teachers and scholars. Therefore it now seems impos- sible for any further good to come out of his mission in Earlestown, he being so bitterly opposed to the wishes of his parishioners. And if it lays in your Lordship's power to remove him by exchange of livings, we humbly pray that your Lordship will exercise that power at the earliest pos- sible date. Your petitioners will ever pray," dm. • The peti- tion can be signed by any parishioner; and all who desire to express their disapproval of the actions of the Vicar are requested to attach their names to it. It will be remembered that at the meeting of parishioners last week a hope was expressed that the large room of the Viaduct Institute could be secured in which to bold services for the " scattered flock" of St. John's, but this idea will now have to be abandoned. An application for the use of the room was duly made to the Committee of the Institute, who have since considered the matter. Ia their answer the committee stated that they could not see their way to let the room for services of a religious character.
NEWTON COMMISSIONERS. THE ANNUAL MEETING.

_ The annual general meeting of the Newton Improvement Commissioners and the ratepayers of the township was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday afternoon. The Commis- sioners present were Messrs. W. F. Gooch (chairman), J. W. Emmett, Thomas Stone, Thomas Hunt, James Fairclough, James E. Wursley (law clerk), and Richard Brierley (sur- veyor). The ratepayers were represented by Mr. Henry Houghton (assistant overseer), Mr. Sankey, and Mr. Rat- cliffe. _ _ .

THE ELECTION OF COMMISSIONERS —The Chairman, in commencing the business, said: I gave notice of the election of three Commissioners in place of Messrs. Thomas Stone, James Fairclough, and Thomas Hunt, all of whom were eligible for re-election. They have been the only gentlemen nominated, and consequently they have been re-elected as C >mmissionere for the miming year.—Mr. Thomas Stone returned thanks on behalf of himself and Mr. Hunt and Mr. Fairclough for the honour they had done to them in return- ing them unopposed as Commissioners for the ensuing year. He felt that the ratepayers had paid them a compliment, inasmuch as they had shown they had confidence in the way they had discharged their duties during their past term of office. He considered he was speaking on behalf or Mr. Fairclough and Mr. Hunt when he said that they had all acted conscientiously in doing what they considered best for the ratepayers of the district and their interests. (Hear, hear.) The expenditure was £5,225 10s 10d, leaving a balance of £389 0 101 d in hand. The gas works sinking fund account showed a balance of £379 lls 21 in the bands of Parr's Banking Company. The education account had the following balance in hand last year £32 4a. from the overseers of the township £110; total, £142 4s. The expenditure was £134 13s 4d, leaving a balance of £7 103 84. The accounts had been audited and found correct by Messrs. Richard Barton and Thos. Thomp- son, anditors.—The Chairman said he would be glad if someone would propose that the accounts be passed.—Mr Ratcliffe said that he saw that there had been some expen- diture in repairing the highways and roads in the townships. He saw in other districts that the county authorities con- tributed a portion of the expense, and he thought some steps should be taken by the Commissioners towards securing that for Newton. (Hear, hear.)—The Chairman : That matter has been before the court, and perhaps our Law Clerk will explain how the matter stands.—Mr Worsley said the Corn.; missioners had applied to the county authorities for one- half the cost of maintenance of the main roads in the town- ship, but the county authorities refused to pay it. Various deputations waited upon them without avail, until at last. acting under counsel's advice, the Commissioners instituted peoceedings in the Court of Queen's Bench .against the county authority to recover half the cost. The decision of be court was in favour of the Commissionera, who had recovered the expenses to which they were entitled. (Hear, hear.) But the county authority had since given notice of appeal against the de- eision.—The accounts were subsequently passed on the motion of Mr Ratcliffe seconded by Mr Sankey. Tar NEW CEMETERY : WRAT WILL THE RATE BB ? , —Mr Ratcliffe stated that they were now getting well on with the cemetery and he thought the ratepayers might be given some ROMS idea what the cost would be.—The Chair-

man: We have not the figures here at present. Mr Rat cliffs said he had heard a great deal of complaints from the ' property owners about the heavy rates put upon them. They would like to know what the cemetery rate would be. The present expensive form of street making was making things very heavy upon them, anl people would not go into the fields to build houses, but would rather erect them along the road aide. Roads were being made which would last nearly a thousand years.—The Chairman: That stands to the ad- vantage of the ratepayers in not having them to repair so often.—Mr Ratcliffe : Yes but it is to the disadvantage of the property owners.— The Chairman: As far as the pre- sent estimate goes it will be somewhere about 4d in the £. —Mr Brierley : It will depend very much upon what comes back again from the sale of graves. Some of the grave- yards in the district are not yet closed. APPOINTMENT OF Atturrons.—The Chairman remarked that it was the duty of that meeting to appoint auditors of the Board's acconnts for the ensuing year—On the motion of Mr. Sankey the retiring auditors, Messrs. Richard Barton and Thomas Thompson. were re-elected. VOTE OF TuarrEs.—Mr. Sankey moved, and Mr. Rd- cliffs seconded, a hearty vote of thanks to the Chairman, which was passed.—The Chairman, in responding, alluded to the new arrangements for the removal and disposal of the sewerage, and his remarks will be found reported elsewhere.

PRESSINTATION TO 4 FR-lE-24713L-Y-130C-IBTY MLNAGEII.-A pleasant gathering was held at the office of the local branch of the Liverpool Victoria Legal Friendly Society, 85, Cor- poration-street, on Saturday, when the collectors of the district presented to Mr John Garbutt, the district manager, a handsome centre seconds silver chronograph stop watch as a mark of respect in which he was held by those under hint. The watch bore a suitable inscription, and was handed to Mr Garbutt by Mr Thomas Bolton, of Prescot, on behalf of the collectors. Mr Garbutt acknowledged the gift, and ad- dresses were also given by Messrs Glover, Forter, and Burrows. Ca?roan or A FOWL-STEALISII.-At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday, William Hunter, a miner, was charged with stealing eight ducks and a hen, value 255, the property ef Ann Woodward.—About one o'clock on the morning of the previous day a soa of the prosecutrix (who lives at Island's-brow) was awoke by hearing a hen screech, and he thereupon got up and went to the ben cote. He found the door open and attempted to shut it, when the prisoner came out. A struggle took place, and the prisoner was ultimately secured. It was then ascertained that eight ducks and one hen had been killed by having their necks twisted.—The prisoner bad been previously convicted for felony, and he was now sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard I labour.

UNJUST WEIGHING MACHINES AT RAINFORD.—At the St. Helens Town Hall on Monday, James Middlehurst, landlord of the Junction Hotel, Rainford, was summlned for having an unjust weighing machine in Ws possession.— Superintendent Johnston stated that on the 17th instant he examined the defendant's machine and found that it was 141bs, against the seller_ when it was tested with a ton

weight. When he tested it at 15 cwt., however, it was I found to be correct. He could not account for the differ- I ence.—The defendant stated that when he tested the machine with small weights it was found correct, and there- fore relied on it being correct up to any weight —The Bench remarked that they thought there was a doubt whether they would be doing jestice in that case if they inflicted a fine, ' as it was evident that the defendant had been under the im- pression that the machine was correct. They would there- fore dismiss the case, but the machine should be made per- fectly right.--James Collier, of the Crank Hotel, was summoned for a similar offence.—Superintendent Johnston deposed that the machine was 161bs. wrong against seller at one ton, and was 4lbs. wrong at 16 cwt. The defendant was very obstinate when he went to examine the machine.— The Bench said they would dismiss that case on condition that the machine was at once made accurate; and the de- fendant promised to see that it was. DAMAGING LORD _DERBY'S TREES.—At the St. Helena Police Court on Monday, Lawrence Brannan and Francis Tansey, of Eccleston, were summoned for wilfully damaging a tree, the property of the Right Honourable the Earl of Derby. Neither of the defendants appeared.—Mr J 0 Swift said he appeared to prosecute the two defendants, both of whom resided at St. Helens, Tansey in Liverpool-street, and Brannan in Stanley-street. On the 30th ultimo, they broke a growing sycamore tree in the carriage drive of Lord Derby, on his estate at Rainford. The two defendants were seen in the drive near some sycamore trees. A girl named Eaves heard a noise as if one of the trees was being broken, and saw one of the defendants •, watching" while the other came from the direction of a tree which was afterwards found to have been broken. The defendants were afterwards followed by P. S. Smith, who was informed of the occur- rence, and on that officer getting up to them they each had a stick—cut from a sycamore tree—in their possession. A number of trees bad been planted for the purpose of forming an avenue, but during the last few years 60 or 70 trees had been broken, while during the last few days six bad been broken. It was most wanton damage and destruction that the young trees should be broken, simply to gratify an am- bition to possess a stick. He thought that looking at the circumstances of the case it was one calling for a substantial penalty. After evidence to the foregoing effect had been given, the Bench imposed a penalty of Sc and costs, and 25 6d damage on each defendant. CHURCH BAZAAR AT RAINFORD.-0/1 Thursday afternoon a bazaar was opened in the National Schools, Rainforcl, with the object of defraying the debt of £250 at present existing. upon the Rainford new church. There are three large stalls laden with useful, fancy, and ornamental articles, presided over by the following ladies :—Mrs Barnacle, Mrs Greener Mrs Dean, Mrs J Barton, Mrs J Whalley, Mrs R Birchall, Mrs James Birchall, Mrs J Fazakerley, Mrs B Smith, Miss Bradley, and Miss Webster. In addition there are refresh- ment and flower stalls. The bazaar is under distinguished patronage, the list including the Earl and Countess of Dprby and Sir Richard Cross. There is a good programme of addi- tional attractions, and hopes are entertained that the £250 will be raised and the parish church cleared of debt. Mr Clarke Aspinall, J.P., of Liverpool, in the absence of Mr G C Hale, Lord Derby's agent, performed the opening cere- mony, at which there were present the Rev Cam:it:art-, vicar of St Helens, the Hon Mrs Carr ; Rev J Btrnacle, vicar of Rainford ; Rev W W Bragg, curate Rev W Ber- ridge, Upholland ; Mr and Mrs H S Hall, Mr Joseph Robin- son, Mrs Richard Pilkington, &e.—Mr Aspinall, who was cordially received, said he thought the laity of both sexes and all ranks ought to make up their minds to be more real and more thorough in their practical work in connection with their religions professions. He I thought lair people—not intending unkindly—f re- quently expected too much from the clergy. The more the laity fairly did their work the better the ' clergy would be able to do theirs, for it was not the duty of the clergyman to do all the work connected with his church. The clergy had their responsibilities, and the 1 laity had theirs. It was impossible to have zeal and energy without sometimes overrunning what was called judicial discretion. He would rather have too much zeal than too little energy, for they would suffer less from the doings of an over-zealous person than from the inactivity of a whole tribe of jelly-fish people who had net energy enough to do either good or harm. (Laughter.)—A vets of thanks to Mr. Aspinall, moved by Mr. Joseph Robinson, having been carried, sales were proceeded with. LECTURE AT THE ST. HELENS ART EXHIBITION. On Tuesday evening a large number of ladies and gentlemen assembled in one of the rooms of the Imperial Buildings, Ormskirk-street, where the exhibition of pictures is at pre- sent being held, to hear an address, on "The origin, nature, and influence of the Fine Arts, by Mr. R. G. Kelly, of Bir- kenhead, painter of "The last man," one of the principal pictures of the exhibition. Dr. McNicoll presided, and in introducing the lecturer, he said in this age it did not belong to the people of St. Helens to devote themselves too much to the worship of the muses, the arts, or the graces, but to the God Mammon which was in their midst. He hoped ' that time would wean them from so close a devotion to that God, and that they might pay their respect and homage to the arts and sciences. It was very meritorious en the part of the members of the Exhibition Committee that they had instituted the exhibition, and they made another step in the right direction by bringing down a dis- tinguished artist to address them, one who had contributed to the exhibition, and one who was not only a painter, but ' a critic of paintings. (Applause.)—Mr. Kelly was warmly received. In a very comprehensive and instructive lecture he reviewed the subject chosen for his address. He remarked • thet it was one of general popularity, and its influence was felt so universally that he believed no apology was required , for its introduction. It dawned upon them from the earliest ages, and there were perhaps no people so rude but that they to some extent could acknowledge its influence. What they ' called the fine arts in effect seemed to be part of their nature • and they all sprung from the enjoyment of God's works. He spoke of the power of art in some cases as instilling men with bravery and filling others with virtue, and it created among all a love for the beautiful and filled them with flue sentiments. Before printing had made books cheap and education universal the artist was called upon to illustrate ; for the mass of the people the leading doctrines and inci- dents of the Bible. He controverted the idea which seemed • to:prevail among some people that the refinements of art I had a tendency to enervate a nation and in concluding said that the study of such subjects would enlarge their obser% vation, quicken their perception, exercise their judgment, , and be one great means of leading and enabling them to trace effect to cause, cause to effect, and all to God. (Applause.)—The proceedings concluded with hearty and deserving votes of thanks to the lecturer and chairman. On Friday, and succeeding nights, the curator will lecture on pictures in the exhibition, and give elocutionary enter- tainment; and on Saturday an excellent promenade concert will be given. The various schools will, in succession, have the privilege of visiting the pictures, and altogether, the venture promises to do much good in providing rational en- joyment for the people, and can safely be pronounced a suc- cess so far.

NOTES BY THE WAY. At St. Helens, on Saturday, the Victoria Rangers best the Albion Amateurs by 99 runs to 56. J. IJw.worth scoring 37 for the former, and H. Gerrard 26 for the latter.—The Fingerpost Amateurs defeated the Hardshaw Rangers as follow.; Amateurs. 66 (W. Gawty, 22 not out); hangers, 57 (T. Quinn, 22).—York-street Schools (2nd) and Garswood Park met at Denton's Green, the result of a good match being as follow.: York-street. 123 (P. Gee 36, A. Webster. not out, 80) ; Gars - wood, 167 (Masker 31, W. Woodward 30, J. Pilklegton 22). On Monday, In the match between If unpMire and Surrey at Southampton, the home team had lost seven wickets for 90 runs, as against 324, the result of the Surrey innings. On Tues- day Surrey made an easy victory with ten wickets to spare.— The game between the Philadephians and the Gentlemen of Sussex terminated at Brighton on Tuesday, the home team winning by ten wickets. Score :—Suasex, 302 and 46 for no wicket; Philadephians 181 and 164 —A great victory was ac- complished on Wednesday at Lords; : England over Aus- tralia, the home country winning with great ease by an innings and five runs. The success was gained by sterling cricket, and will do a great deal to reassure Englishmen of the supremacy of their country In the cricket field- Score :—Australians. 229 and 145; Engimd 379. On Saturday the match at the Trent Bridge Ground between Nottinghamshire and Yorkshire was brought to a conclusion Nottinghamshire' gaining a brilliant victory by seven wickets. Score: Yorkshire, 95 and 199; Nottinghamshire, 114 and 181. —Sussex met Kent at Tunbridge, and on the conclusion of the game the score stood, Sussex, 98 and 294; Kent, 116 and 163. —The match between Cheshire and M.C.O. and Ground was concluded at Stockport on Saturday, and resulted in a draw, but greatly in favour of Cheshire. At the else of the first day's contest Marylebone had got 185, to which Cheshire replied with 122 for six wickets. On Saturday Mr. Dennison, of Warrington, ran his score up to 58, being the last man out, when the total had reached 202 for the first innings. As time for drawing the stumps arrived Cheshire had 107 for four wickets, and the match was drawn, Cheshire wanting 48 runs to win and six wickets to fall. Warrington journeyed to Aigburth OR Saturday to meet the Liverpool team, whom they subjected to a defeat, securing an easy victory by 58 runs. Liverpool made a very poor beginning, the first live wickets going for 26 runs, but F. Williamson and A. J. Steel added 45 between them, and J. Homby rendered timely service with his 20, The Warrington team generally played a good all round game. and five of their men got into double figures, the In- nings closing for 161. Score: Warrington, 161; Liverpool, 103. At Brighton on Thursday. Sussex accomplished a remarkable batting performance against the Australians, running up a score of 387. Wyatt made 112 and Philips coming in towards the close of the innings put up 109, there being only nine wickets down for 387 runs. Philips is to be congratulated. The appreciation of the crowd took the shape of a subscription of 20 guineas.—At Aigburth the match between Liverpool and Free Foresters ended in a draw on Thursday, the scores being, Free Foresters 415, Liverpool 200 and 155.

SCHOOL ArrairniarcE ComurrrEs.—The monthly meet- ing of the St. Helens School Attendance Committee was held at the Town Hall on Wednesday Afternoon, when Councillor Wilcock presided. There was no business of im- portance before the committee, the School Inspectors' reports showing that the midsummer holidays had been during the past month. A MIDNIGHT ADVENTURE AT SUTTON.—Before Alderman Harrison at St. Helens Town Hall on ;Saturday, James Foster, a young man, was charged with assaulting Police- constables Brooks and Lowe,—P.C. Brooks stated that he was on duty in Sherdley Park about a quarter to two o'clock that morning when he saw three young men, of whom the prisoner Was one, coming up the path. He stopped them aud asked their names and business, but it was not until he threatened to lock them up that they gave him their right names. He let them go, and Foster picked up and threw two stones at him, one of which struck him on the hand and the other on the body. They then ran away.—Police-constable Lowe said he heard a constable's whistle, and was hurrying to the place from whence the sound proceeded when he met the three men running along Marshall's Cross-road. Foster threw a handful of dirt into his eyes which caused him to stop for about ten minutes. He then found that Foster had tumbled into a ditch. The other two men made off.—Prisoner was remanded until Monday, when he was fined 20s and casts for the assault on P.C. Brooks and 103 arid costs for assaulting P.C. Lowe. Greening (chairman), Appleton, Bonnell, Jolley, Blaekhurst, Brown, Derbyshire, Broadbent. Humphries, W. Houghton, Caldwell, Cooper, Forster, Greensll, Gibson, Swinton, Hunt, and J. C. Sutton (clerk).

div.head: TITHES.
div.p: TITHES.

The CLERK submitted an account amounting to £1 33 7d, being the charge for tithes on the land on which the Pad. gate Schools are erected.—Mr. BLACKIMRST asked if that was the tithe for the portion of land on which the schools stood or for the whole estate P—The CLERK said it would be the proportion of the tithe formerly paid by the tenant in respect of the land occupied by the schools.—Mr. BLACK- HURST : It seems to me a large sum for a small place like that.—Mr. Joriyy : What is the acreage P—The CLERK: Twelve acres.—Mr. GIBSON belieyed the tithes ran about 10s per Cheshire acre.—The Cwatimax thought the chair- man of the Schools Committee would make inquiry and fur- nish the information Mr. Blackburst wanted. He thought they ought to know.—Mr. BROWN moved that they do not nay the bill till they did know.—The CHAIRMAN said the bill was already passed.—The CLERK said they would be bound to pay it —lt was thus agreed that the Schools Com- mittee should inquire into the matter.

div.head: HOUSE COUMITTZE.
div.p: HOUSE COUMITTZE.

The minutes of the house Committee stated that Mr. Brown had been elected chairman in place of the late Major Cartwright.-0o the motion of Mr. Baows, seconded by Mr. APPLETON, the minutes were adopted.

SCHOOL COMMITTEE. A suggestion was made in the minutes of this committee that the Board should fill up the vacancy cause upon it by the death of Major Cartwright. It was recommended that the application of the Rev. Canon Dodd, Stretton, for the use of the band on Friday, the let August, be granted this year •, and also that the grant previously made and con- firmed by the Board be paid to the Rev. John Gardner, of Woolston Catholic Chapel, in consideration of the children of the schools attending there once a Sunday for divine worship.—Mr. DA,RBYSHIRE moved the confirmation of these minutes. The Rev. Mr. Gardner, he sad, was leaving, and he believed there was something over twelve months pay due to him. This he wished to be paid, and also if possible for the two or three month it hich had elapsed since the end of the twelve months. He (Mr. Derbyshire) thought this could not be done, but if it could Mr. Gardner ought to be paid up to ,1 the time he leaves. With regard to filling up the vacancy ' on the committee, he moved that Mr Gibson be appointed a member of the committee. Mr. Gibson, he said, lived at Thelwall, just over the river from the schools, and would make a very good member of the committee, and probably be very regular in his attendance. Mr. BROM/BERT seconded this proposal.—The CLERK mentioned that with regard to the payment of Mr. Gardner, they could only pay him from the Cate of the resolution of the Board.—The Citaintraw thought they might very safely leave that matter in the hands of the clerk. —The minutes of the cam- mittee were then confirmed, and the motion with respect to the appointment of Mr. Gibson as member of the committee pausal.

The CLERK reported, relative to the above cases, that he had, in accordance with the instruction of the Board, ap- peared befere the Newton magistrates, who were, as thee' always are, very courteous, and quite agreed with the viewE the put before them of the law in cOnnection with theta CASes. Mr. BuCkten, the clerk in attendance, called upon Min a fart days ago and syggested that it would be as well to issue fresh notices, and this he (Mr. Sutton) was willing to concur with on the understanding that the summonses should be re-issued witheut fees. He might say that in en- deavouring to enforce the law in the Board's behalf in that district he wished to move with moderation—(hear, hear) —and to do the duty in as fair and as moderate a spirit as possible. He bad said before the court that if anyone came forward and said that they would comply with the law, he would agree to the adjournment of the case for a month, and that if in that time the party had cereplied with the law they (the Board) would not apply even for costs. (Hear, hear.) The magistrates quite understood that. The Board, therefore, limited the cases to those who were deter- mined to resist the law. He might say that out of the 16 or 17 orders made it had only been necessary to summon six persons for non-compliance with the orders. The difficulty was that there were two or three people who had conscientious objections to vaccination, and these influenced other people who would otherwise readily com- ply with the law. (Hear, hear.) It was really necessary to bring those people who were the cause of this difficulty to the point of a penalty. He expressed satisfaction at the Petty Sessions with the fact that out of the whole of the Warrington Union Earlestown was the only district in which they experienced the least difficulty. Although there might be, in other parts of the Union, people who had doubts about vaccination, and some who even objected to it, they all complied with the law, and they had no difficulty except in this one district of Earlestown.—Mr. Aretxrcm said there was an Anti-Vaccination Society in Earlestown, and they influenced people who were not members of it. These anti-vaccinators objected on principle—at least they said it was principle—but he did not know whether it was or not. There was before the Board a bill from the county treasurer for the costa of summonses for vaccination pur- -1 poses in Earlestown, and all through it there was a great I vsriety in the charges. He saw that the lowest, for sum- mons and service, was 6s 6cl ; and the highest for summons, order, and service, was £1 Is 61. He could not see exactly where the difference in the charges lay, but what he wanted the Board to do WAR to ask for particulars in respect of these charges.—ln answer to a Guardian, Mr. Apprarrow said the 'total amount of the bill was £l2 Ms.—The CLERK said his attention had been before called to the difference in the ' charges, and he might take that opportunity of saying that in his jadgment the amount of fees charged was out of pro- portion to the quantity of work done. Of course, if the Clerk to the Justices was entitled to these Ifees, according to the scale in force, he could not see how they could avoid paying them. He noticed that Is ed was charged for summonses, and they had in that way pretty nearly £4 to pay for work that would only occupy a clerk in the office about two hours, and there was over 30s charged for serving summonses at 15 or 16 houses which Were in the immediate neighbourhood of each other. The variance there was in different counties and districts in fixing fees in magistrates' courts certainly seemed to be un- satisfactory. He noticed only last week in another county a person summoned under the Vaccination Acts asked for particulars of the fees which were given to him in court, and the fees for information, summonses, and copy was 2s ed. He had had occasion to write to one of the divisions of this county and the charges there were lees than here, but still if the scale of fees in force entitled them to demand these charges he did not know in what way to avoid payment. It seemed to him that the most reasonable course to take was that suggested by Mr Appleton—to ask the treasurer of the county or the clerk to the magistrates for the particulars of these fees. When they got these particu- lars he should be in a position to compare the charges with the scale of fees in force and see whether they were such charges as might be made.—Mr. Arregrow moved that the clerk be instructed to get a bill of particulars and investigate the matter.—Mr. CALDWELL seconded the proposal. He said they had heard a great deal about lawyers charges, and be had heard of a case the other day of a lawyer charg- ing £6O for very little work, and on the bill being taxed there was all but about £9 knocked off. (Laughter.)—Mr. DARBsswinz said he had been under the impression that they should have nothing to pay for these summonses. He thought that when a party committed a breach of the law and was summoned for it he had to pay the costs himself. —The CLERK mentioned that the solicitor referred to by Mr. Caldwell was a gentleman belonging to the midland coun- ties and not to this neighbourhood.—The Chairman : There is nothing of that sort here. (Laughter.)—The CLERK, con- tinuing, explained with regard to the remarks of Mr. Derby- shire that he had told the magistrates that in the case of those who complied with the orders he would not ask them to pay the costs. He had thought that would be the wisest course to take, as it would show that the Guardians wished to be as lenient as they could. (Hear, hear.)—Mr.Appleten's resolution was then passed. A letter wasTe-al;aVitlisli--thi7-1;;;Ii-rnight be allowed to play at the annual sports in connection with the Working- men's Club.—On the motion of Mr. BLecxamterr, seconded by Mr. CALDWELL, the request was granted. FILLING DP A VACANCY Mr. BLACRIIVRST moved that Mr. Broadbent be appointed a member of the Assessment Committee in place of the late Major Cartwright. Mr. Broadbent, he said, was a man of experience and a man of property, and he thought he would make a very good member of the Assessment Committee.— Mr. BONNELL seconded this proposal.—Mr. DARBYSHIRE, in supporting the proposal, said Mr. Broadbent was very well acquainted with the aristocratic property in the Union and the assessment of that property wanted increasing. (L;ugh- ' ter, and hear' bear.)—The proposal was also supported by Mr. Jolley, Mr. Caldwell, Mr. Appleton, and the chairman, and was carried unanimonsly.—Mr. BROADBENT, in acknow- ledging the kind manner in which he had been spoken of, said he hoped he would do his duty on the committee In an impartial manner. (Mr. Darbyshire : Hear, hear.)—This concluded the business of public interest.

Lord Shaftesbury on Wednesday presided at Willis's Rooms over a conference in connection with the Church of England Funeral and Mourning Reform Association' at which Mr. Beresford Hope, M.P., Mr. Seymour lladen, Mr. Samuel Morley, M.P., and Canon Erskine Clarke were amongst the speakers. The live shell which Lord Chas. Beresford unfortunately brought borne as a trophy from Alexandria has led to actions in four law courts. In the end the Assurance Corporation have had to pay to the Henry Small Arms Company the damages recovered from them by their workman who was drilling the shell when it exploded. • Tug Axcoais MURDER.—At Manchester Assizes, on Saturday, James Joseph Donnelly was indicted for the mur- der of his sister in Ancoats, on May 28th. The prisoner attacked his sister and mother with a razor, and inflicted , such terrible wounds upon the former that she died of her Injuries. The prisoner had been subject to epileptic fits since his youth, and the defence was that he committed the offence with which be was charged whilst suffering from a fit, and unanswerable for his acts. The jury found him guilty, but recommended him to mercy. Sentence of death was passed.

METHontsr FREE Citructi.—On Sunday evening the Rw. Robert Trotter preached a valedictoiy sermon in the above chapel, and brought his ministry at Frodsham, ex- tending over four years, to a close. THE Parma Cnuncli.—On Sunday morning and evening the Right Rev. Dr. Linton, Lord Bishop of Riverina (New South Wales), preached in the above church, on behalf of his diocese. Each of the services were attended by a large congregation, and the collections amounted to £2O is sd. THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTER.—A special meeting of the above committee was held at the Overseer's office, Frodsham' last week, when Mr. A Thomas, J.P.. presided. The Clerk read a letter from Mr. J. Cunnah. secretary to the Gas In- spectors, in which he stated as follows:—" I am directed by the Inspectors of the Frodsham Lighting District te inform you that they have had under consideration the application made by the Frodsham Parochial Committee to ventilate the main sewer by connecting same with the gas pillars, but they do not see their way to sanction the suggested arrange- ment, as the lanterns are taken off the pillars in the summer montbs, and a nuisance might then arise therefrom." The Inspector of Nuisances (Mr. Farrington) was instructed to report to the next meeting what arrangement could be made for a ventilating shaft, and an estimate of the pro- bable cost.

EDUCATION Dr ENGLAND.—The report Of the Committee of Council on Education, showing the result of the work of the past year of the Education Department, indicate that, out of a total estimated population of 26,921,703 in England and Wales, there were 4273,304 children on the school re- gisters, of whom 3,705,388 were present at the annual in- spection, being increases on the previous year of 83,692 and 162,646 respectively. The number of certificated teachers was increased from 35,444 in 1882 to 37,200 in 1883, the assistant teachers from 10,071 to 12,390, and the number of pupil teachers reduced from 28,285 to 26,428. A decrease in the number of half-time scholars on the registers from 177,126 to 164,410. The amount of the schoel income de- rived from the rates rose from £808,121 in 1882 to £840,947 in 1883; the amount derived from veluntary con- tribution fell from £724,846 to £719,089; and the amount of school pence increased from £1,585,928 to £1,659,743. The total cost of maintenance was £5,817,466, against £5,572,820 in 1882. On the subject of school attendance the Committee suggest that the number of school places Provided should be equal to one-sixth of the population, instead of one-fifth as at present. While they recognised the great improvement of recent years in the number and attendance of scholars, their efforts to secure still further progress must not be relaxed. There might be half a million of scholars more than at present on the registers of unaided and they iock with Confidence to this increase being off ected under tile new code. DIGGLE AND THE SHIP CANAL. AN AMUSING MEETING. One of the most amusing meetings ever held in Warring- ton took place at the Cu-operative Hall on Wednesday even- ing. Mr. W. Diggle, a gentleman who is well known in War- lento°, had announced by placard that he would deliver a !cloture on the Ship Camel and other subjects of interest to Warrinetonians, a charge of two pence being made for ad- mittance to defray expenses, the surplus, if any, to be given to the Infirm:ars. It was gmerelly anticipated thet the meeting would principally partake of the nature of "fun," and these anticipations were fulfilled beyond all expectation. At the time appointed for the meeting Co commence the hall Was filled aud the Chairman, Mr. Couocillor Dixon re- pared the audience for some hilarious enjoyment by asking them to allow the lecturer one hour in which to speak. another hour to be spent in discussion, promising thorn nom* genuine fun if they woald give Mr. niggle a fair hearing. The Chairman was about to call on Ms. Diggle to commence his lecture when Mr. Stirrup, who WAS seated in the hall, rose and remarked that he was as fond of a bit of fun as any of them present. If they wanted a bit of en- joyment, he said, they would give Mr. Digele fifteen minu- tes in which to speak and never say a word to interrupt him. He would be an enemy to the Ship Canal who die so inter- rupt, for if they gave Me. Diggle a quarter of an hour to himself they would have a good treat. (Laughter.)—Mr. Whitham : -Mr. Stirrup says a quarter of an hour and you say an hour P—Tin Chairman: Mr. Stirrup stipulates that no one is to speak for a quarter of an hour.—Mr. Stirrup: Give him a quarter of an hour, and I will promise you a treet —The Chairman: I am quite sure the meeting fully appreciates the presence of Mr. [Agate and I hope you will be kind enough to listen to him patiently and we shell no doubt be very mach benetitted.—Mr. Diggle, who was re- ceived with applause and laughter, said that he hoped that the audience would give him their attention, as the sub- ject was a difficult one, especially for a person who knew that all the parties before him were opposed is some measure to him. (Laughter.) He had appeared before them on the came queeticia before, but had never had an opportunity of being heard. He thought that they ebould always bear both sides of any question. (Laughter and disorder.)—The Chairman: I must ask you to be kind enough • to give him a hearing. Mr. Diggle proceeded that the question of the Manchester Ship Canal was occupying the attention of the country, and of this neighbourhood particularly, very seriously at present. He would give them reasoarewhy, in his opinion, the eleip canal would not affect the cotton trade as had been said would he the case, and when he had given those reasons they could draw their own conclutions He was not opposed to the ship canal if tie could think that it would be a benefit. The cotton trade was the staple trade of Lancashire and he would -iest go through it to show where it grew, how it came to Manchester, and how it went away front Manchester. Hay- inc enumerated verious countries whence cotton was expor- ted to the port of Liverpool, Mr. Diggle proceeded to re- mark that he had been in conversation with shipowaers and captains who were oompetent to form an opinion on tbe sub- :met. These men said that no shipowner would entrust his weasel in such a tortuoas caned He, Mr. Diggle, asked how that was? Well, there were fogs, there was frost. (A -.Mc.: There's rocks.) That was the most serious part of the business—(a voice: Give him a clap; laughter and die. order, during which Mr. Diggle refreshed himself with a glee, d water, remarking that he would rather have some- thins warmer and urging the meeting to keep quiet). These men said that no shipowner would let his vessel run the risks that they would have to do. They said, every man of them, that they would not undertake to navigate a vessel of theirs, would not run the risk of losing their reputations, under any such circumstances. These men—there were eight of them, and one had just come from the Suer —were competent to judge of the whole affair. (Cries of "Speak um, Diggle.) This was a most important piece of business. (Laughter and uproar.)—Mr. Stirrup: It is not fair, give the men a chance. He is quite wrong, lam opposed to him througheag, hat give him a hearing. I asked for a quitter of an hour and you did not give him a minute.—Mr Dig- gle: They said to me, where is your cargo l' (Renewed up- roar, daring which the speaker set down amidst applause 1 and ironical cheers.)—Mr. Stirrup thereepen rose to speak and was remarking that he had attended the great 1 demonstration at London when a Mr. Wilson rose and said that he bad not attended the meeting to hear that Mr. Stirrup had been to London. He had come to hear Mr. Rigel's. (Cries of" Sit down," "Shot up." and " Diggle.") lie should have his say and should appeal to the chairman for order. Mr. Stirrup had addressed them as Englishmen an he should address them as Englishmen Mr. Stirrup: We did not come to he you, we came to hear Diggle.—Mr. Wilson: I rise to protest against Mr. eVilliam Stirrup telling us that he went to London to see this great demonstration. I have not come here— ("Shut op ") to hear Mr. Stirrup give his description of the London demonstration. I have come here. (Derisive laughter, and a voice: " Write him down an ass.") I appeal to the chairman, I have come here to listen to Mr. Diggle--(rue Chairman (to the policemen aresent): Yon had better take this man out e--against the fartherance of the Ship Canal. Mr. Giggle kindly passed a chair down to him, upon which he carried it on to the platform, protesting that he would de- fend himself, the audience meanwhile indulging in up- , roirione laughter, and the Chairmen suggesting that Mr. Wilson would deliver a lecture the following night.—Mr. Wilson, who was almost inaudible, addressed the reporters, and said that the Chairman had brought an accusation against him.—The Chairman : They'll put you out if you tio aot go down.—Mr. Wilson was then induced te leave the platform.—Mr. Diggle : Well, now, gentlemen, we'll start at number one—(A voice : "1 diddle, diddle, diddle.") That man there should have brought his mother to look , after him. (Laughter.) Mr. Diggle proceeded to give his ' remarks upon the ship canal, but was constantly inter- rupted. Finally, he produced a packet of sweets, which he generously handed to the Chairman, which brought from the audience the cries of " Give us some humbugs." " Give him some toffee," "Two o' gin," ac. Mr. Wilson rose to 1 hand to the C utirman a note, upon which a facetious mem- ber of the audience asked the Chairman "to give that chap a big one." and Mr. Diggle accidentally upset his glass of water, a trilling circumstance which highly awned the meeting. At the request of the meeting Mr. Diggle again rose to confirm() his address, and used sound logic in the question" How can Igo on when you keep going on. I have only two minutes left now ?" (Voices : An exten- sion of time will he granted," and "Have another injutee.") Mr Diggle : PR just tell you a word or two—(Usse your ,totee)—Use my Dotes? 11l use my head, my notes are no good to this lot. He has been saying whatever he could, but there has been a dozen down there apd helf-amlemen up here interrupting him —Mr Wileon again rose, and requested that the note that ha had given to the chairmen should be read.—Mr Stirrup: Nothing surreptitious; let it be open and tnhinly, (Shouts of "Read that note," "Let ne have a song: and " I diddle, diddle, diddle.")—Mr Diggle : The Chairman wants you to go on and waste your time. I want to say a few words that are important to you. Fellow townsmen, I am aware—(" So we are ")—that the town is half way between Manchester and Liverpool, and might to be one of the moat populous in this country. (Laughter.)—(A Voice : You are trying to bribe him, Diggle by giving him sweets ) (Renewed laughter.)— Mr. Stirrup was abut to ask a queetien. when member of tht audience, who interrupted, was greeted with cries of " Bring him here," "He's a masher."—Mr Digele • Yes, but las a big baby.—Mr Stirrup asked Mr Diggle if he was not against the first plan that was proposed, becaese it did not take his coteages in ?—Mr Diggle I should have been very glad if it had taken my cetteaes.—Mr Wilson once more attempted to gain a bearing, and Mr Diggle proposed that he sheald "Shut up," which was duly seconded and carried, notwithstanding which Mr. Wilson persisted that he should have his say.—Mr. Diggle : Give me change for sixpence and I'll give him his twopence back.—The Chairman : You ought to give him fournence for this.--Mr. Wilson: The Chairman has made an assertion. I came here to listen to Mr. Diggle object to the Ship Canal. and to see whether he would promulgate any desirable scheme for the interests of Warrington. Mr. Stirrup tells you be went to London to see a procession, but I come not here to listen to Mr. Stirrup, but to Mr. Diggle. The Chairman made the assertion that I corns here to inter- rupt the meeting, but I say that it is a deliberate lie. What would you rather have next ? (Shouts of "Ship Canal," " Have it mixed," Waterworks," " Mixed beer," ha) Look at your papers in the morning and you'll see ynn are regular rough 'uns.—Mr. Diegle, having had another "go" at the Ship Canal, Mr. Stirrup rose to ask another queation—a legitimate one in plain Englieh. He i wisbel to off zr to Mr. Diggle two theories that there were at present, one was the infinite divisability of matter and the other the ultim Ate molecule. To which did he appertain. aughter.)—Mr. Diggle : That is a sert of jaw breaker. I'll do the hest I can, I'll answer it in this way. William, my friend, has been to London lately and has got so "high" , in his language I cannot make him out—After some time I had been spent in chaff and horseplay, Mr. Stirrup pro- posed that a vote of censure should be passed on the Lec- turer, which, was, however, negatived, and he was accorded three cheers —lu acknowledging the compliment, Mr. Diggle thanked the audience for their unruly conduct-- (laughter)—and the meeting terminated with three cheers for the chairman, who was designated as a "good sort," a parting wish being expressed that he would again provide so good a lecturer.—The proceedings then terminated.

div.head: WARRINGToN TOWN COUNCIL AND THE SHIP CANAL.
div.p: WARRINGToN TOWN COUNCIL AND THE SHIP CANAL.

On Wednesday evening a special meeting of the Warring. too Town Council was held in the Town Hill "in put.- LIIIIICO of the provisions of the Act of the 35th and 26ch Viet iria. cap. 91, igtduled 'An Act to authorise the applic dim of funds of municipal corporations and other govern- ing bodies in certain cases' for the purpose of considering, and, if thought desirable, of posing a resolution to contri- bute a sum equal to one penny in the pound on the rateable value of the borough towards promoting in Parliament • a 131 l to authorise the construction of a ship canal to Man- chester and for other purposes,' and to charge the earns noon the borough fund, borough rate, or other fund or rate, or ac- count of the said Council Apollo ible thereto." There were wesent at the Council meeting Aldermen Holmes,Chandler, Ktan, and Webster ; Councillors Broadbent, Brown, Bur- g.,3. Caldwell, Dixon, Mackie, Marsh, Milner. J. Pierpoint, W. Pisrpoint, Sutton, Wallineon, Whittle, and Tinsley ; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), and Churley (bo:ough treasurer). . _ . .
On the rootion of Alderman CHANDLEY, Secondod by. Ald..rmaa KEAN, Alderman Holmes was elected to the chair.

The TOWN CLERK said that as some doubts had been expressed on the question as to whether the Corporation had the power to vote a sum of money for the purpose men- ' tinned tie bad taken counsel's opinion, the opinion of Mr. I S. Wright, of the Temple, London, which was as follows: —" lam of ooinion that the Corporation have no power under the Borough Funds Act to contribute towards the ex- penses of promoting the Bal. The power given by that Act i 3 to pay for the promotion by the Corporation itself of Bills specifically relating to the borough, and not to contibute to th,a expenses of the promotion by other parties of a Bill only incidentally affecting the Corporation. It is, how- ever, open to the Council, if they think fit, to assent to the insertion in the Bill itself of a provision enabling them to subscribe after the passing of the Bill. Such resolution or provision, however, could not of course have any operation if the Bill is thrown out by the Commons committee, and there may 1)3 some difficulty on Standing Orders in getting such provision inserted in the Bill, but the passing of such a resolution might have some weight with the committee, especially if backed by a ratepayers' resolution. The rate- payers' resolution should not be under the Borough Funds Act, but should be passed at an ordinary public meeting." I Therefore, the Town Clerk continued, it seemed that the p-oposal if passel under the Borough Funds Act that night, according to Mr. H. S. Wright's opinion, would be of no value if passed. Mr. CALDWELL : Well, then, we can go home. (Laugh- ter.) Mr. BROADEENS thought that as they had been brought there that night they cauld hardly depart without making Some remarks. He had never considered that question at all as one ccnnected with being in favour or not being in favour of the Ship Canal. (Hear, hear.) The chairman (Alderman Holmes) himself although strongly in favour of the Ship Canal strongly disapproved of the course that was I recommended to the Council by the General Purposes Com- mittee. It now seemed to hint that whether they bad had that opinion from the Town Clerk or from counsel or not, already wiser counells had begun to prevail; and that al- though the Council, or the General Purposes Committee, which now consisted of the whole of the members of the Council, had been subject to a slight observation— Dr. Mama rose to a point of order. He thought it was exceedingly ungenerous to sky the least that they as a Town Council should discuss that question now that it was past their giving any positive assistance that day. (Hear, hear.) There was no doubt that what Mr. Broadbent and, those gentlemen who thought with him were saying would be duly reported, and it would( be very unkind and very un- generous to say the least that they should be considered as thus going in at the death and kicking—C" Oh, oh," and interruption ) Mr. BCRGEES rose to a point of order, upon which Dr. Mackie resumed his seat. Ti 4. CHAIRMAN said there was nothing before the meeting. Mr. Enos.nagisv said he would end with a resolution. He was going to say that they had been brought together at a meeting of the General Purposes Committee, and now they had been called together again. He thought it would have been very well if the opinion that they had jest had read to them bad been got earlier, so that they might have been saved that meeting. He concluded his remarks by moving that they adjourn. (Laughter.) Dr. MACKIE said he would second that proposal with great pleasure—under the eircurnstance—that they adjourn at once.
The CHAIIIIKAN: I think the meeting dissolves itseif as a matter of course. The meeting then terminated.
