div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY JULY 26. 1884
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY JULY 26. 1884

ACTION FOR LIBEL AGAINST A WARRINGTON NEWSPAPER CO. CLARKE V. MACKIE AND CO. This was an action for libel, the hearing of which was commenced on Tuesday afternoon, in the Niei Prius Court, at the Menctiester Assizes, before Mr. Justice Give and a special jury, and concluded on Wednesday afternoon. The plaintiff, Mr. George Clarke, a milk dealer, of Altrincham, claimed MO damages from the defendants, Meeers. Mackie and Co., of Warrington, proprietors of the Altrinehain and Boodon Gail-dime, for a libel whereby he alleged he nad been injured in his business. Mr. Ambrose, Q.O , and Mr. J. W. flemiltou were counsel for the plaintiff ; and Mr. Russell, Q.C., M.P.,. and Mr. Bradbury were for the defen- dants. Mr. Ambrose, in opening the case for the plaintiff, said that the libel in question was published in the defendants' newspaper on April 12th of the present year. At that time , typhoid fever had broken out in the district of Altrincham. An article heeded "A Horrid file " appeared in the Altyincharn and Bowdon Guardian on the data named, in which it Was imputed that the outbreak of fever was due to milk supplied to the residents by the plaintiff, and that the milk had become contammated with the germs of the disease in consequence of the unclean conduct of a milk boy who was in the service of the plaintiff, and who was suffer- lug from diarrhoea, having subsequently become an in- patient at the :ucal hospital, where it was found that he had typhoid fever. The Article professed to be based on a repeat of Dr. Fox, medical utficer of health for the Altrincham Rural Sanitary Authority, but was an entire misreading of that report. Toe learned counsel suggested that the article ' WAS inserted in the newspaper in order to create a sensation and to increase the circutation_of the defendant? newspaper, i but it had nearly ruined the plaintiff, who estimated his loss I at £4 per weee- Toe plaintiff was then called, and give evidence as to the falling off in his business consequent upon the publication of the article complained of. He WAS cross-examined at considerable length as to ttie dates on vvhicb his customers discontinued taking his milk, and also as to the time when Spillsbury, the youth who took out the milk, and whose 4 .in- duct formed the subject of the libel, first exhibited signe of illness.—George Spalsbury, 19 years of age, said that he I had been in the employ of the plaintiff for the last six I months, and WAS in the habit of carrying out the milk. He I WAS taken ill on the 10th of March, and suffered from head- ache, but was then able to work. He did not suffer from diarrhoea.. Did not know he was suffering from fever until he WAS in the hospital. He denied having been guilty of the conduct imputed to him. Cross-examined : Did not feel out of sorts on the 3rd Mime, but on the 10th. WAS not suffering from looseness at the bowels. Was not aware that when he was ill at home Dr. Gotland called and asked his mother if he were not suffering from diarrhce I, and did not tell Dr. Golland at the hospital that he had been compelled to leave the cart two or three times.—Eliz a Clarke, wife of the plaintiff, said that she superintended the sending out of the milk, aud bad never seen anything wrong with the milk or the carts either when they had gone out or returned.— Joseph Hill, of Altrincham, said that he was a customer of the plaintiff's. He read the article in the Altriachanb and Bowdon Guardian entitled "A Horrid Tale," and had then reduced his supply from the Plaintiff. By Mr. Ambrose : There had been a great deal of talk about typhoid fever in , the district. He had heard the plaintiffs milk mentioned in connection with it. The stories of the milk having to do with the communication of typhoid did not improve his taste for milk.—Henry H. Belshaw, of Albert-road, Sale, soil that after leadiog the article in the defendants' paper he ceased to be a customer of the plaintiff. Mr. Ambrose said that he had several other witnesses whom he could call, but who would only give evidence to the same effect as that given by Mr. Balehaw. Mr. Russell ceetended that no case had been made out, and a lengthy legal argument ensued, alter which hie Lord- ship overruled the contention, and the case was proceeded i with.

Mr. Russell, addressing the jury, said that he would endeavour to place the matter before them in such a way that they would be able to follow him. Let him stati the position of the parties. The defendant's position was that of the editor and manager of the paper in question, which, he believed, belonged to a limited company, in which the defendant was one of the most considerable proprietors. His learned friend had described Dr. Mackie in away be thought that gentleman would be st.rprised to hear—as a sensational editor of a kind of society paper, who Was looking out for sensational ptragrapbs with which to delight the readers of the Altrinchara and Bowdon Guardian. He was not much acquainted with that very respectable and, he believed, ancient publication, but from the slight acquaintance that he bad he should be inclined to describe it, as no doubt an exceedingly wieful but very uninteresting publication, con- taining a great deal of, he doubted not for its readers, most useful and valuable information, but upon the dullest sub- jects to the general reader. (L 'tighter.) The last thing that it could be accused of WAS that it was a sensational paper. Having referred to the outbreak of fever, he described the efforts of the medical gentlemen of the district to trace its source. Those gentlemen came to the conclusion that the contagion was spread by milk, and from circum- stances that came to their knowledge inspected the premises of a farmer named Taylor, from whom Clarke had his milk. It was then found that the persons who had taken the I disease were getting their milk front Clarke, and were upon one round only, the one in which the services of the bay Spillsbury were brought into requisition. It Was also ascer- tained that the boy Spillsbury was at the hospital suffering from the fever, and the idea WAS that his hands were polluted and the contagion carried to the milk. The learned conneel then reviewed the acions of the medical men, to show hew they had arrived at their opinions. Dr. Fox, be said, as a matter of duty in the in- terests of the people wrote his report for tee Altrincharn Rural Sanitary Authority, who, seeing the importance of the metter, passed a resolution exonerating Taylor's farm from any suspicion' anti ordering that a copy of the resolu- tion be sent to each of the Cheshife papers and that copies be printed for circulation. Dr. Fox forwarded hie report to the defendants' paper, with the request that it should he published. Accordingly the detendents puhliehad it, and there WAS not a shadow or shade of suspicion for saying that Dr. Meckie had the slightest particle of ill-feeling towards I ear, Clarke, or the slightest desire to procure a sensational I story for the purposes of his paper. Ile had not a reporter , waiting at the Board-room to pick -up what he could, and did not move in the in Atter until he received a aelsort from Dr: Fox and a request for its publication. He (Mr. Russell) admitted that the defendant bad unquestionably misread the report of the medical officer and put a construction upon it that it was not meant to hear. On a date subsequent to that upon which the alleged libel appeared it was stated in the defen- dants' piper that the plaintiff was himself in no way to blame ter what might have been done by the boy Spillsbury, and that he could not have known of it. The article was based upon the report of the medical officer, and it was pub- lished in the interests of the public, lie then called wit- nesses for the defence. Alexander Mackie was first called. He said that be had been editor of the defendants' paper since its publication 21 or 22 years ago. He received a letter accompanied with a report, from Dr. Fox, and when he got the letter he con- sidered that the outbreak ketie a matter of great public inter- est. He knew nothing personally about the plaintiff. The Paper was pre-eminently an agricultural and commercial one, and not political, and he was following up his usual course in giving what information he could in reference to agricul- Carat 'fluters. He had no other feeling. He had known Dr. Fox by report but not personally: he was well known as a gentleman whom they had communications from before— Was he in your opinion a high authority on this matter? I think a very high authority.—Who is Dr. Fox? He is the medical authority for the Altriocham Union Rural Sani- tary Authoritv.—Mr. Ambrose 7 Are you a medical man? No, L.L.D.—What University ? In America, I received it chiefly for inventions and literary work.—ln what Univer- aity? Grenfield in Tennessee, twelve ye trs ago.—How much did it cost you? Nothing whatever. (Laughter.) He had received and read the resolution. The communi- cation from Dr. Fox WAS received shortly before the time for going to press, and as it was from Dr. Fox he took it as I gospel and handed it over to the manager to be at once prin- ted.—Do you not think that what was authorised WAS the Publication of the resolution alone? Ido not. The reso- lution would have the effect of re-instating Mr. Taylor's milk in the estimation of the public.—You published Dr. Fox's report in addition to the resolution? Yes. And in addition to the article complained of you published the re- port of Dr. Fox in a separate column? I think it was printed the one immediately after the other. You had a leader headed 4°A Horrid Tale !" I bad —ls that the alleged libel ? Yes.— Yon began: "A. tale which will turn the atom,chs of our Altrincham readers comes to us from," and so on. You have got it in three places in the piper? I think not.—Elis Lordship: The advertisement is not a report.—Mr Amlsrose : You have get the subject then. You thought this matter of very great importance? I did.—You say " A tale that will turn the stomachs of our Altrincham readers comes to us from the highest official source ICI the Rural Sanitary Au- thority. . . In plain English, milk pails have been used I for the filthiest purposes by a boy affected with diarrhoea, whose occupation it Was to take milk to his MOOD era." Do you mean by that that the boy had used the milk-pails sea commode. Do you mean to convey that by this passage? I cannot answer that yes or no.—l must ask for yes or no, and you can give your explanation afterwards. It is the usual course, and Ido not know that von are different to anyone else.—l understood from Dr Fox's report that the pails had been used.—Understanding that did you mean to convey by this statement In your paper, to the readers of your paper, that milk-pails had been used by the boy as a commode? C did.—And when Dm Ciolland and Mules in a letter on the 10th of April wrote to your paper repudiating that such inference was to be proved from Dr Fox's report, you still adhered to the aceueation ? I did, for I had a letter in the meantime from Dr Fox, confirming the opinion, as I thought, the interpretaticn which I had put upon it. I believe since then he has repudiated ' that and asserted that I took too strong a view lof his words.—Nothwithstanding that Dr. Mules and Dr. Crollaod wrote calling your attention that it Was not war- ranted by the report von still to tintained that it was a proper statement of Dr. Fox's report? Yee.—ln further cross- examination, witness said Dr. Fox did not say in plain English that the pails had been so used, else his report would not have required re-translation. He reminded thr learned counsel that he bad only had the manuscript les°, than an hour in his possession' owing to the exigencies of printing, and, probably, if he hid had time to read it more he should not have put the same strong construction on it.— Farther cross-examined, witness said that he bad received a
number of letters on the subject. and had only inserted thoes of medical men, whom be allowed to disease the matter in

his columns.—Mr. Russell: Are you still of opinion that ex- creta had got into the cams? Certainly.—ls it a fact that from the first article that appeared on the 12th April up to the 3rd March the whole of your editorial cointnesta did not occupy a quart.- rof a plumn ? Yes.—And is it a fact that . .
----- you published letters relieving Clarke fromt all pereonal blame? It is.

The,Judge said that at present he WAS of opinion that there I was no lawful occasion for the article, and the otily question I was whether those portions of it in which special damage was alleged were true or not. He thought the resolution passed by the Altrincham Local Board, requesting that pro- minence might be given to their advertisements—which was a very proper one--did not authorise the publication of the report, and ke very much doubted whether the request to publish it justified the publication. . _

Dr Fox, Dr Arthur Rsnsome, and Dr Mules, medical officer of health for Bowdon Local Board District, gave evidence that according to their opinion the outbreak of typhoid fever was attributable to the milk supplied by the plaintiff. Dr Fox stated that the Board were anxious that the report should be published —Dr Golland and Dr Blesse also gave evidence in support of that given by the other medical gentlemen.
Mr. Ambrose, in Answer to the Judge. submitted that the case was not one in which he was bound to prove special damage..

The Judge said that according to a reported case the allegation was not an attack upon a man's character or his conduct, but it was solely an allegation disparaging his goods. Mr. Ambrose : This is an attack upon the way in which a man carries on his business. The Judge : No, it is an attack upon the goods which he sells.

Mr. Ambrose: It could not happen if he carried on his business properly. The Judge: I do not see how he is to be responsible for what a boy does when be is not there.—Continning, his Lerdship said it was perfectly clear, so far as the report went, that there was no allegation that the plaintiff's milk cans were not kept clean. That part of the libel did not ap- pear to be true, and with regard to that of course the ques- tion would be whether that was a case for special damage. If it was a case for special damage, the plaintiff would be entitled to a verdict. In any way it seemed to him that it only came to a disparagement of the man's goods, and not to an attack upon his character. Mr. Ambrose submitted that he was entitled to claim 'vindictive damages, because there was clear evidence of I malice. The Judge slid if that were so he should leave the ewe- ' lion to the jury. Mr. Russell, in an address to the jury, remarked that his I learned friend had certainly been rather offensive to Dr. Mackie, asking him about his degree, where he got it, and what he had paid for it, but those were questions that had nothing to do with the case. He then reviewed the evidence at length. Mr. Ambrose said that if they wanted any proof of how people felt the smallest imputation upon anything that af- fected them in their profession or trade, he did not think that they could have better proof than the way in which Dr. Mackie kieked at his (the learned counsel's) presumption, when he ventured to put to him a question with reference to by what title he held the degree of doctor. lie was very sorry if his had put a (lineation that he should not have done, if it was so very delicete a question that Dr. Mackie did not like to answer it. One wondered if he were ashamed of that degree and title, but one would think that if so he would not have it on all occasions paraded and that it would not have been paraded on that occasion. He thought that it WAS a proper question to ask in a case of that kind, to ascer- tain the exact position of the defendant. He was very sorry if he had put anything to Dr. Mackie that had hurt his feelings. They saw how touchy people were as regarded aavthing that affected their position. He followed hi pro- fession as editor of the paper and was indignant for it to he known that he was not L L.D. of any of the English or recognised universities. He (the learned counsel) wished that yr. Mackie had had the Same regard for the feelings of others, especially before he sat down to write the article which formed the subject of the present action. Counsel then criticised very severely the actions of the various medical gentlemen concerned in the case, speaking at con- siderable length. The Judge summed up the case, and observed that it was of a peculiar character. It was an action for damages for I disparaging the goods which the plaintiff sold. There were two grounds upon which the defendant sought to defend himself. It was admitted that he published the statement in , question, and that the statement disparaged the goods in which the plaintiff dealt, and the grounds of defence were, I first, that the statement was published with lawful cause, and, secondly, that it was true. The question as to whether the statement was published with lawful cause was one of law for him (the Judge), and whether he was right or not in regard to thee might be a matter to be questioned here- after; but he held that it WAS net a lawful occasion, that it Iwas not an occasion in which either the duty or the interest I of the defendant juetitied, or required, or excused the publi- cation of the document, and consequently that was a ground of defence which could not be set up in that Court. The other ground of defence WAS one of fact, and wan therefore I entirely for the jury. It.was whether or not the s: atemeat wee true. If toey found that it was a true statement, then their verdict should be for the defendant, and the plaintiff would not have a came if the statement were partially true, should that part welch Was true have caused the damage. He thought the jury would be of opinion that if Dr. Mackie said no more than Dr. Fox said in his repert, the result would have been 1 the same; people would have nothing to do with a man who sold polluted milk, no matter. how that pollution was oc- casioned. If the jury, on the medical evidence, came to I the conclusion that Dr. Fox in his report gave the real I cause of the outbreak, then they would be entitled to find a verdict for the defendant. If, as had been alleged, the jury came to the conclusion that the defendant had published the article with the intention of injuring the plaintiff in his businese, they would t.e entitled to give him damages be- yond the actual damages he had sustained; and further, if they thougnt the defendant had published the statement with perfect recklessness as to whether it injured the plain- tiff or not, but with the desire of increasing the circulation of his (the defendant's) paper, they would be equally en- titled to give the plaintiff damages over and above the actual danmees proved. If, on the other hand, they he. , lieved the defendant published the article because he honestly believed it to be a matter of public interest, with no desire to injure the plaintiff, and with no personal feel- , ine against him, then they might very fairly nay that it was not a cage in which he should ho puniebed after he had made good the dun tem which the plaintiff lied sustained. After a brief conenrratien, the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff;, damages, £5O.

formation of the House of Lords itself. I only hope, that should Mr. Gladstone re-introduce the measure during an autumn session that the Lords will again reject it. Should they accept it, I cannot imagine a more ridiculous position for a body of men to be placed in. Their impotence will be so manifest, that, should the people forbear forcing the reform upon them, it mast surely come from within their own .body.

We have long ceased to disregard any vetoing power the Queen may be supposed to posers,. Her Majesty bee seen well to move with the spirit of the age. ThiS has been a possibility to her as an individual If it is not possible to the House of Lords, the people must know the reason why. I might take up your space by recounting the various reasene given by the Lords for rejecting this impertant measure, but not one of them would be the true one. The fact, and it was well known by Mr. Gladstone that had he made it his first important measure, coupling it or otherwise with Redistribution, its fate would have been the same, and the work of a Liberal parliament thrown away. It must not for a morcent be thought that the Radical opposition to the existence of a House of Lords is mere sentiment. Iheir opposition is based upon something more tangible, and were I asked to point to something where in a condensed form face could be gleaned and reasons given I should point to the Financial Reform Almanack. The rejection of the Reform Bill is a small matter, merely the proverbial feather. The people must be given to understand that, in the words of John Bright, "the Public Service is neither more nor less than a gigantic system of out-door relief for the aristocracy of Great Britain." And whether the Liberal party choose or not to make use of the services of such men as Lord Granville or Lord Dalhousie, it will never for a moment put a stop to the deep and anxious feeling enter- tained by the people that the Lords think sornerhing like a fulfilling the pr pheliee When all the hest (finagles gm, the hs,st offices.

The British aristocracy may he compared to the centipede, each scion can put its foot down in a dozen places at once, and what shall we say of the moral character of a few of these legislators by Divine right ? True, the Duke of Marb botough is trying honestly to make his living as a cab pro- prietor, but what of his little peccidilnem that might bring misery into other homes? Then there is Lord St. Leonardo and the servant girl. The police reports tell us the magis- trates in such a case wink at a lord's gross misconduct. A list might be given, not at all a short one, of noble lords, who born in the purple and clairoing the right to make laws for "Church" and State, are leading lives the immorality of which calls for the immediate attention of the Salvation Army.

As showing the degraded state of pauperisation the lords have reached, we have 261 dukes, marquises, an earls, who have relatives ve the number of 4,536 who are employed by the nation, and the offices they hold number 9,228, their salaries received since 1850 reach the paltry sum of £66,241,242. One nobleman (?) has kindly palmed on the nation seven sons, one grandson, two nephews, and one niece. Very few heads of families amongst the working- classes have such opportunities as these for disposing of their families In studying our Parliamentary systetn the mind becomes completely mystified. There seems so much room for reform, and the possibility of doing this so easy, that the wonder if,' why have we allowed it to go the length it has in abuse? The electorate has in so many instances chosen memkers of the aristocracy to represent them, that in looking over the naraes of morn- hers one is astonished at the stupendous amount of influence possessed by the noble pauper classes. It is only by a diligent searching and analysis that he true i position of affairs is revealed to us. The House of Commons I numbers amongst its members 270 gentlemen who are directly connected with the Upper House, either by birth or marriage. While thi!r state of things exists, it matters not, Liberal or Tory in power will think little of the work- ing classes. It is a sorrowful sight to see at times how anxious we are to gat a noble lord to speak lat our meetings, or to take the chair at great popular gatherings. We little think of it being so much dust thrown into our eyes, a sop deftly placed before us intended to keep "the great unwashed" in order. But the present action of the House of Lords demands that the people at once organise ler such an agita- tion as we have not seen since the repeal of the Corn Laws. The I'eers must be told— That there's on earth a yet atuuster thing, Veiled though it be, thin Lords and King. July 14, 1994. CLIFFORD DM.

div.p: XetterO to the editor.
SUNDAY CLOSING.

Sir,—" Cipt tin Cattle," evidently fully conscious of the excessive weakness of his cise, attempt.s ia his last very " gin and wate-y" effusion to blind ! your readers as to the real question at issue Iby resorting to "chaff and banter," and that of a very poor quality. Ile also gives expression to ideas and statements, some of which althou,,h• nut accurate ere cer- ; !Anil" unique. For instance it is. to say the least of it, I "original ' to refer to " Merchants, manufacturers, and shopkeepers" as "the folks who help to embitter life," and on the other hand to describe the publicans as "benefactors of their race." In the some way the" Captain" (who surely ' must have been "spirituous'', " inspired when he penned his last epistle) defends Sunday " boozing " because it leads to Monday " playing." Well, sir, seeing that "there's nowt as queer as folk," one must not be surprised in these days of " monstrosities " to find odd cases of individuals whose in- tellecrs have received such a " twist " some time or other that they can defend or bolster up any cause however rotten I may be. Again, the " Captain " tells us that we must not imagine " that Letotelism will do away with misery ; it will only aggravate, it." What a terribly deluded lot of beings we "abstainers " must be. Our lives must be a gigantic sham, and the pleasure that we sup- pose we feel in the cosiness and cleanliness of our homes, and in the happiness of our families, is, according to "Captain Cattle," a farce, and only a thin gauzs like covering, which is too flimsy and transparent to prevent the keen penetration of my opponent from witnessing the horrible misery underlying it all. One thing, however, is quite certain, and that is. tbat if our life on this little planet called Earth is a miserable one, we "enjoy " it for a longer period than do either the " modera- tors " or the "topers." But. Mr. Editor, joking apart (for, after all, this is far too serious a 'natter to be settled in a humourous vein), we have two men before our, borough at the present time, each of whom aspires on behalf of the constituency to represent our views in the National Parlia- ment. What I want to know is this—will William Crostield or Gilbert Greene!l he the better man to vote for on the temperance question ? Let the local temperance society ask Sir Gilbert straight out whether er not he will sappoit such a measure as! have indicated, and if lie refuses to do so let them use every righteous means of inducing all religious and social reformers, whether Liberal or lory, to do all they can to secure his defeat at the next General Yours, SOCIAL REFORMER.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS.
div.p: THE HOUSE OF LORDS.

Sir,—What most Radicals desired has come to pass. The House of Lards, a body of men responsible to no constitu- ency, has dared to thwart the wishes of a majority of the people's representatives. No Radical CAR well be sorry at this. That a majority of the Bishops should have deter- mined to vote with the Government only proves their keen- ness of vision. Conn.cted with the people as they are through tbe rectors, -vicars, curates, &c, they know well that the people are fast making up their Minds to sweep away a chamber whogle members claim their seats by right of mere accident of birth. It will go- bard with the Bishops when the reckoning day comes if they are not able to point to one good action, to one vote given through sympathy for the people's cause. That the people of England should have been content to allow an hereditary chamber to exist so long speaks well for their moderation. It will be seen that I do not press for the entire and complete a olition of the second chamber, but if this chamber insists upon its rights to rej.et a measure having for its object the reforin of the House of lommons. then I say decidully the people must at once ace o it that 205 arrogant lords skall no longer block the way. the action taken by the Lords has made this possible. We nust at enc-i commence an agitation, not only for the lass- oing of the R..iforin Bill, but for the most complete trans-

div.head: BUILDING SOCIETIES.
div.p: BUILDING SOCIETIES.

Sir,—A letter entitled " Idil iding Societies," and signed 'A Paying Member," appeared in last week's issue of your contemporary, the St. _Helens Newspaper, which letter, as von will see from the enclosed cutting, contained sortie attacks, studiously formal, upon come of the officers of a local building society, whose annual meeting was very fully reported in your columns on July sth, from which the St. Helens Newspaper evidently took a briefer account the fol- lowing week. I addressed a letter last Thursday to the editor of the St Helens Newspaper in reply, from which he extracted two or three sentences, and placed at the end of "A Paying Member's" letter in his Saturday's issue. As he has not published my letter in his subsequent issue of Tries- day last, will yon kindly accord to me the courtesy of in- serting in your columns a copy thereof enclosed, which °courtesy is denied to ins, for reasons of his own, by the editor of your contemporary, and oblige, yours faithfully, JNO. FRED. BOOTH. 35, Church-street, St. Helens, July 23rd, 1884. LCOPY To the Editor of The St. Helens Newspaper. Sir,—a. cOmmunication, purporting to be written by "A Paving Member" of one of our local Building Societies, which appears in your issue of Tuesday last, seems to !lie to call for some reply, to which I trust you will give equal prominence. lam sorry that ' A Paying Member," who says he was present at the annual meeting of the society, which took place a fortnight ago, should have had his feeling of sick- ness prolwnged over such a period of time, as to permit of three separate reports of the proceedings being published in the local papera before he could eject his bilious attack upon some of the officers of the society It is a pity for his own sake, becodiss if he had only mustered tap a little courage when at the meeting and asked his questions and made hie °barges when the chairman asked if anyone bad anything to say pertaining to the business of the society, the" kind of sickening feeling" which came over him might have been allayed at once by a little wholesome information ; he might have been spared the pains of stomach or of mind he has en- dured since the meetinu, and he would at any rate have been saved, what was to him no doubt the painful necessity of asking his ques!ions and making his charges and ipsinua- tions through the medium of a newspaper, and under the nm de plume loak of "A Paying Member." Perhaps, after all, his moral nature is so constituted as to make him think the latter mode of proceeding the more manly and courageous of the two. If "A Paving Member " really thought at the meeting that the management of tbe society in question ought to be ehanged,why opened he not his mouth,and endeavour to pre- vent the unanimous re-election of the old officers. The chairman himself referred to the fact of his re-election year after year by the shareholders, as a proof of the conalence they had in him, and asked "ft the management has not been satisfactory, why should we have been re-elected ?" •"ri,en, air, what was his nephew, Mr. Booth, doing? He is the land surveyor to the society, and he should have known all about it."

I have field the appointment of land surveyor to tbe society for about two year., during which time I have not surveyed a scptere yard of land, nor valtied any property for a mortgage to the society, nor received a farthing in virtue of such race, which though merely a nominal one. had to be tilled up according to the rules of the society. The bulk of the properties in the society's posiession were first dealt with 10 or 12 years ago, long before I became oven a member of the society.
The respected name of Mr. Lacey is silo dragged into this personal attack, but a;I "A Payinc Member" can say about him is that there is a street at Widnes called Lacey- street.

Then "A Paying Member" "thought that when they were reducirr the secretary's salary they should at the same time have 'docked' the other salaries until at all events there lea fair dividend for members." As there are no other salaries paid iu connection with this society beyond that of the secretary, it is difficult to see how they could very well be " dockeq," but it is not very difficult to see that "A Paying Member" is guilty of making either ignorant or malicious imputations.

Sir, there is an element of suspicion about the whole of "A RiVirlZ Meinher's " communication, which cannot but lead one to doubt the bona Ales of the writer. It bears the impress of a familiar band, which is not unaccustomed to the anonymous mode of personal attack and insinuation adopted on tne present occasion. The singling out of one or two officers of the society for attack, and the general ignorance of the history and working of the society displayed, are evidences which would lead one to surmise that the anonymous writer of the letter is not en- titled to call himself "A Paying Member." If mach MU- mite he correct, then tbe only term morally applicable to the writer would be a word of two syllables that is not con- sidered a parliamentary expression. On the other hand, if the letter be a bona-fide production of " A Paying Member "of the society in question, he con- demie himself, on the hie of his own letter, as a coward. Which ever cap fits, or" clears his conscience," he is wel- come to it.—Yours, dec., _

JOHN FRED. BOOTH. St. Helene, July 17th, 1884. [lt in contrary to our rule to insert letters referring to com• municationn which have appeared in another journal, but as Mr. Booth has been dented access to the columns of oHr cmitemporary, we make an eXCeptionin this caeF;,-- ED. EX.]

Tha‘VARRINGTON WATERWORKS COMPANY AND Tian CANAL.—We understand that the directors of this com- pany have btren enabled to withdraw their petition against the Manchever Ship Canal Bill, having obtained clauses from the promoters giving the fullest possible protection to the rights and interests of the company. Several members of the Board, with Mr E J Nicholson (the Law Clerk) have been in London busily engaged in the settlement of this matter, with remits which are entirely satisfactory. There are to be two capacious subways under the canal in the neighbourhood of Stockton Heath, through which all the mains of the company on that side will be carried, and which are to be constructed etf such dimensions as will pro- vide, not only for the present, but for all possible future requirements ; also various other provisions for the company's benefit, which have been specially granted to them. The petition was withdrawn on Tuesday, and ao undertaking given by the promoters of. the Canal Bill for the insertion of the elausea in the Bill.

CONSECRATION OF THIS BISHOP OF RIPON.—At West- minster Abbey, on Friday forenoon, the consecration took place of the Rev. R W. Boyd Carpenter, Bishop elect ot Ripon, the ceremony being performed by the Archbiehop of York, assisted by the Bishops of London, Rochester, DW- I:ism, Litchfield, Liverpool, and Newcastle. THE CLAIMANT.—SeveraI friends visited the Tichborne Claimant in Portsea Couvict Prison, on Friday, and found him in good health and spirits. He will be released on the 24th October next from Pentonville Prison. whither be will be removed a week previously. The Central News is in- formed that "it is intended to take some very serious proceedings against some distinguished persons on his release." COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—Twn chartarmasters, named John Hyde and Thomas Parks, sustained shocking injuries on Friday at Smith-lane Col iery, Lower Gomel, Edgley, by an explosion of gas. The two men descended the pit for the pureose of preparing the working for their men to resume work, and were indiecreet enough to tree naked candles in- stead of safety lamps. An explosion of gas and cartridges followed, and both men were frightfully burnt. Hyde is in a precarious slate. SUICIDE IN PRISON.—A. remarkable case of suicide in ' gaol was discovered in Newcastle-on-Tyne on Friday morn- ing. The Deputy-Governer of Her Majesty's Prison on making his usual survey found a prisouer named John Thompson, 41 years of age, dead and suspended from a ven- tilator by a rope which he had formed by tying together about twenty-seven inch lengths of °Awn rope. The de- ceased was underaoing eighteen months' imprisonment with hard labeur for two serioes assaults upon girls. THE WESLEYAN COEFERENCE.—The Wesleyan Confer- ence met on Friday morning in Burslem at the usual time, the Rev. Dr. Oreaves in the chair. Thirty-three ministers became supernumeraries owing to failure in health or ad- vanced age, amongst them the Reve. Edward Lightwood, George Curnock, and Samuel Walker. Six supernumeraries return to tall work. The list of candidates for ordination and preachers on trial were carefully gone through. Several notices of motion were given of no public Interest. CONFERENCE OF CONSERYATITE EDITORS.—A. conference of Editors connected with Conservative newspapers was held at the Carlton Club on Friday afternoon. The meeting was called for two o'clock. A Large number of journalists- attended to meet Lord Salisbury and Sir Stafford Northcote. The Central News says about no Conservative journalists were present, representing chiefly the provincial press.—Sir Stafford Northcote, in opening the proceedings, remarked that. considering the intimate relations that should exist between the leaders of the Conservative party and the news- papers devoted to the same interests, there certainly did pre- vail a coneiderable amount of apathy: Ira his opinion there ought to be more frequent and closer communication between the proviocial Conservative press and the Conser- vative leaders and associations, both local and general, for the purpose of supplying truthful information with regard to party matters and the various political questions coming before the country.—ln response to an invitation, a number of editors spoke Of the great difficulties under which Conservative journalists laboured in obtaining reliable information on party matters, especially in the Parliamentary lobbies. All the speakers em- phatically repudiated any idea of requiring pecuniary subsi- dies. Lord Carnarvon, whe spoke after the general discussion, said be cordially agreed with the preposition that the editors were fully entitled to any information they could be fairly and rightly given. The Marquis of Salisbury, who was very warmly received, said the question was how was the infor- mation to be imparted, and to whom. For his own part he had given the matter much attention, but had often felt that to give information to one and to forget or ignore another newspaper er jourualist was practically to create an unde- sirable monopoly. Means should certainly be taken to give them information without prejudicing or impairing that in- dependence which was the most precious privilege of the Conservative Press. The editors and many of the Conser- vative leaders were to dine together in the evening at the Criterion.

THE PRE3WENTIAL ELECTION, PITTSTIORG, FIZIOAr.—The National Prohibition Parts' Ilan nominated Mr. William Dani&, of Maryland, for the Vice-Presidency of the United States. EARTHQUAKE AT MASOWAH. SOUAKIM, Fitil)kY II Nx.—Farther particulars regarding the earttiquake at Massawah state that nearly all the houses in that town have b,eu destroyed or damaged by the shock. All the ships in the harbour were seen to rock violently. The inhabitants were greatly alarmed and flied toward& the inte- rior.

- - - - - ---- A Cabinet Council, which met at two o'clock yesterday, did not separate until four o'clock. Mr. L. M. Wynne, of Netherworton House, near Banbury, will be the Conservative candidate for Banbury. At a meeting of Liberals of East Devon, yesterday, it was decided to contest both seats at the next election. Five thousand colliers in the Rhondda Valley, under Mr. D Daviea, M.P., have received two and a half per cent. advance.
When the stamps were drawn at Brighton yesterday the Australians bad made in first innings 223 runs for the loss of 6 wickets.
At the annual meeting of the City Liberal Club, London, yesterday, a vote of confidence in the Government was unanimously passed.
In the (4ueen's Hench Division, on Friday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, the case of Weldon v. Senaple was continued. Dr. Ruddiforth was re-called and further ex- amined.

A Lloyd's telegram from Portland, Dorset, on Friday morning, says the steamer Navarino, of Glasgow, arrived there on Thursday night, on fire. Assistance was rendered by ELMS. Minotaur and the fire was subdued. At a large meeting of miners held at Hednesford, near Rageley, it was resolved not to resume work until the em- ployers had conceded the men's demands. 31ARSHILLES, FRIDAY, 9 5 A. M.-- -;;;;;317. deaths from cholera were registered here last night. TOULON, FRIDA.Y —ThOre were 15 deaths here from chob.ra last night, five of which occurred in the Ben Recon- tre Hospital, three in the town, and seven in the suburbs. It 13 feared that the present stormy weather will Cause a re- crudescence of the epidemic. More than 000 persons have left Toulon during the last two days for Ariege and able departments in the Pyrenees

LISION, FRIDAY. —intelligence received from Huelva re- ports that in consequence of the arrival off the port of a steamer. having some cases of cholera on board, a number of the inhabitants of Huelva, se:zed with panic, left, the town, and crussed the frontier into Portugal. They bad arrived at Castro Marim.

WRECK OF A SPANISH STEAMER. MADRID, FRID AFTHRNOON.—AD English schooner has picked up anothur ho it containing 15 survivors of the craw and passengers of the wrecked Cuban mail steamer Gijon and has landed them at Mums.

LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS The House met e 4-0. BILLS ADVANCED.—On the motion 0 Earl BEAUCHAMP, the Contagions Diseases (Animals) Act, MS, Districts Bill was read a second time.--The Naval Discipline Act Amend- ment Bill was read a third time.

THE CONFERENCE —Earl GRANTILLE, replying to E Delawarr' said the Conference on Egyptian affAirs would meet on Monday, when some decision might be come to enabling the Government to make an early statement on the subject to both Houses of Parliament. •g. The House then adjourned.mows so) HOUSE OF COMMONS r csnwi AG) The House met at four o'clock.

. . Quxstrotes.—Sir W. Hancorirr, teplying to IMr. T. Egerton, said with regard to the complaint furnished him of the inconvenience suffered by members coming to the House last Monday, he did not think the blame attached to the police.—Lord HARTINGTON, replying to Lord Cecil, said he had consulted the Chancellor of the Exchequer, and it had been decided, unless some unfmeen necessity should arise which would cause large expenditure, not to present a supplementary estimate in rela- tion to the defence,. of Egypt.—Mr. GrAnsToNE intimated the Medical Acts Amendment Bill would be withdrawn.— Mr. PARNELL asked whether the Government would at the autumn session reintroduce the Poor Law Guardians (Ire- land) Bill, which the Lords rejected on Thursday night?— Mr. GLADSTONE said the limited time of the autumn session would not admit of tbat being done. THE Tax on CARRIAGES.—On the motion to go into Committee of Supply. Lord ALGERNON PancY moved that in the opinion of the Howse the taxes on carriages were ex- ceptional in their charader, injurious to trade, and should , therefore be abolished. He did not see why gentlemen's ' yachts should be free from a tax which was imposed on a country doctor's carriage.—Mr. COWEN seconded the resolu- tion, and said the present tax was a direct injury to trade.— The Crrexcatton of the EXCHEQUER could not accept the resolution, because if passed it would give the carriage tax priority for repeal over other taxes, such for instance as the tobacco duties, revision of death duties, bouee tax, the duties on tea, coffee, and dried fruit, railway duties, rnarine Mem, since, and a number of others.—After further discussion, the resolution was rejected be 33 to 38. BIISCELLANEOUS.—Mr. MACFARLANE said as the attention of the Government was now fully directed to the move- ments of Russia in Central Asia he should not proceed with his motion.--Mr. Ssum, called attention to the last elec- tion of Guardians for Newry Union and Local Board neg- lecting to bold inquiry into charges made against the re- turning officer.—Mr. TREVELLAN did not think the papers submitted made out a case against the returning officer, but he world urge the Local Board to re-consider the decision they arrived at regarding the inquiry.—Mr. SEXTON Celled attention to the delay in trying the Tubbercurry prisoners.— The SOLICITOR-GENERAL for IRELAND regretted that the men were not tried at the last Sligo Assizes: He promised a speedy trial in .Dublin.
Service Estimates, votes for reformatory and industrial schools, and Broadmoor Criminal Lunatic Asylum were agreed to.

The house in question had been visited the previous night by Inspector Church and a constaWee who found there four women and three SoLtiers. The house was only adapted for two persons.—lreepector Norman : was there last Thai-shy, and found a number of known characters, and We caused it to he visited.—Mr. Hunt : have heard of girls of Viand 17 staying at the house of the elder prisoner; Winifred Galway, a girl abouc 16, was there when Inspector Norman went.— rho defen tants were or- dered to find securities of £lO each for their good behaviour for six moathe, and to ewer into their own recognisances of , £2O, or go to etisoli for two months. Tn MAYM/ AsD MAYORESS AT THE LORD MAYOR'S• RECBErION.—On IVednesdey evening, in accordance with annual custom, the Lord Mayor of London and the Lady Mayoress gave it hell at he Mansion House to meet the ! mayors and prnvosts nt the United Kingdom, among those present beim.: the Mayor and Mayoress of WarrinZton (Alderman and Mrs. Harrison). The State apartments of the Lord Mayor's official residence were very tastefully decorated with dowers and ferns, and brilliantly illuminated. The guests, numbering over 1,000, were received in the saloon en their arrival by the Lord Mayor, who wore his State robes, and the Lady Mayoress, attended by the Sword and Mace hearers and the City Marshal, and accompanied by the Sheriffs and Under-Shsriffs of London and Middlesex. There were present in all 120 ineyore of the English cities and towns, 'one Irish mayor (Mr. Smlth wick, M.P., Meyor of Kilkenny), and twelve Septch p:ovosts. with their wives. The aldermen and mainbere of the Court of Common Cons- Cil were invited to meet them. Maser of the town clerks were also proseat. Dancing to the music of the Hon. Artillery tompany's band was commeeced ahoist ten o'clock, and con- tinued till a late hoer. supper was served in the old ba'l rooms, and dancing ;afterwards was kept up till an early hour in the morning.

CADISHEAD, SERMONS.—Two excellent discourses were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel on behalf of the organ fund, on Sun- day, by the Rev. J. Stevison, of Manchester. The congre- gations were geed, with a full chapel in the morning. There were special anthems sung by the choir on the occasion, under the leadership of the schoolmaster, Mr. Gatenby. The collections were about the average. PATRICROFT.—The foundation stones of a new Wesleyan Chapel in Patricroft were laid on Saturday. There was a large attendance, and great interest was manifested in the proceedings. Toe stones were laid by four ladies placing on each stone a purse of gold. The president of the Wes- leyan Conference, the Rev. T. M'Cullagh, gave a masterly exposition of Methodist doctrine and polity. The collections amounted to more than £3OO.
